e: BOOK VI. The religion of the Mexicans, that is, their gods, temples, priests, sacrifices, and oblations; their fasts and their austerities; their chronology, their calendar, and their festivals; their rites at the birth of their children, at marriages, and at funerals. eligion, politics, and economy are the three things which R          chiefly form the character of a nation, and without knowing them one cannot have a complete idea of the genius, the inclinations, and the enlightenment of any people. Now the religion of the Mexicans, of which we must speak in this book, was a mass of errors and of superstitious and cruel rites. Such weaknesses of the human spirit are inseparable from every religion that has its origin in the caprice or the fear of men, as has been made only too plain even in the most cultivated nations of antiquity. If one wishes to make the comparison, as we do elsewhere, between the religion of the Mexicans and that of the Greeks and Romans, we shall find the latter more superstitious and more ridiculous, and the former more inhuman. Those celebrated nations of ancient Europe multiplied their gods excessively because of the mean conception they had of their power; they confined their dominion within narrow limits, defamed them with the most atrocious crimes, and befouled their worship with the most execrable obscenities, which the Doctors of Christianity justly cast in their teeth. The Mexicans held their gods to be less imperfect, and in their worship, superstitious as it was, no action contrary to decency took place. Teotl, a word far more like the Theos of the Greeks in meaning than in pronunciation; but they used certain epithets highly expressive of the greatness and the power which they conceived in him. They called him Ipalnemoani, that is, He by whom we live, and Tloque Nahuaque, He who has all in himself. But the knowledge and the worship of this supreme being were obscured among them by the crowd of gods which their superstition invented. They believed that there was an evil spirit, the enemy of mankind, to whom they gave the name of Tlacatecolotl (Rational Owl), and they said that he often let himself be seen by men in order to harm them or to frighten them. Concerning the human soul, the barbarous Otomis believed, from what is reported, that it came to an end together with the body; but the Mexicans and all the other civilized nations of Anahuac held it to be immortal. Yet they did not consider the privilege of immortality so proper to the rational soul as not to grant it also to the souls of brutes. (*) They distinguished three places for souls separated from their bodies. They believed that the souls of soldiers who died in war or as prisoners in the hands of their enemies, and those of women who died in childbirth, went to the house of the Sun, whom they imagined to be the Lord of glory, and there led a life of surpassing delight: that every day at the rising of the Sun they celebrated his birth and accompanied him with hymns, dances, and the music of instruments as far as the zenith: that there the souls of the women came out to meet them, and with the same rejoicing conducted him down to his setting. [p. 5] (several unbelievers of our century foolishly go on imagining), those nations could not have invented a dogma more suited to encourage Bk. VI. their soldiers than one that assured them so weighty a reward after death. They added, furthermore, that after four years of that glorious life those spirits passed on to animate clouds and birds of lovely plumage and sweet song, remaining always free to rise again into heaven and to come down to earth to sing and to suck the flowers. The Tlaxcalans believed that all the souls of the nobles, after death, animated beautiful and melodious birds and noble quadrupeds, and those of the commoners, weasels, beetles, and other vile animals. Whence it is seen that the preposterous system of the Pythagorean transmigration, which has taken such deep root and spread so widely in the countries of the Levant, found its partisans in those of the West as well. (a) The souls of those who died drowned, or struck by lightning, or of dropsy, tumors, sores, or any other such infirmity, like the souls of children, at least of those who were sacrificed to Tlaloc, god of water, went, as the Mexicans said, to a cool and pleasant place called Tlalocan, where that god dwelt and where every sort of delicate food and of pleasure abounded. In the enclosure of the great temple of Mexico there was a place where they believed that on a certain day of the year all the children sacrificed to Tlaloc were present, invisible. The Mixtecs were persuaded that a great cavern, which lay in a very high mountain of their province, was the gate of Paradise; and therefore all the lords and nobles had themselves buried near that cavern, in order to be nearer to that place of delights. And yet it was seriously promoted not long ago by a Frenchman in a book printed in Paris under this extravagant title, L'an deux mille quatre cent quarante. To such excesses does freedom of thinking in matters of religion lead. [p. 6] which was, from what they said, a very dark place, where there Bk. VI. reigneda god called Mictlantecuhtli (Lord of hell) and a goddess named Mictlancihuatl. They believed, as it seems to me, that hell was situated in the center of the earth; (b) but they were not persuaded that the souls suffered there any other pain than that which the darkness of the dwelling may perhaps have caused them. The Mexicans had, like all the other civilized nations, a distinct notion, though one altered with fables, of the creation of the world, of the universal Flood, of the confusion of tongues, and of the dispersion of peoples, and all these events they had represented in their paintings. (c) They said that when men were drowned by the Flood, there were saved, in a little boat, only a man named Coxcox (to whom others give the name of Teocipactli) and a woman called Xochiquetzal, who, having landed on the earth near a mountain called by them Colhuacan, had many children; but all were born dumb, until a dove from the top of a tree imparted languages to them, but so different that no one was understood by another. The Tlaxcalans fancied that the men who escaped from the Flood were transformed into monkeys, but that little by little they recovered speech and reason. (*) Among the particular gods worshiped by the Mexicans, who were many, though not so many as those of the Romans, thirteen were the principal and greatest, in whose honor they consecrated that number, as we shall see. This was the greatest god who was worshiped in § 2. The gods of provithose countries, after the invisible God, or Supreme Being, of whom dence and of heaven. we have spoken. His name means shining mirror, from the one that his idol had. He was the god of Providence, the soul of the world, the Creator of heaven and earth, and the Lord of all things. They always represented him as young, to signify that he never grew old, nor weakened with the years. It was believed that he rewarded the just with many blessings and punished the vicious with sicknesses and other evils. At the corners of the streets there were stone seats, where this god might rest whenever he wished, and no one was permitted to sit on them. Some said that he had descended from heaven by a rope made of spiderwebs, and had persecuted and driven out of that country Quetzalcoatl, high priest of Tula, who afterward was himself consecrated a god. His principal idol was made of teotetl (divine stone), which is a black and shining stone like black marble, and it was dressed in festive attire. It had gold earrings, and from the lower lip there hung a little crystal tube, inside which there was a little green or blue feather, which at first sight seemed a gem. His hair was bound with a little gold cord, from the end of which hung an ear of the same metal, with certain vapors of smoke painted on it, which, according to their interpretation, represented the prayers of the afflicted. The whole chest was covered with solid gold. On both arms he had gold bracelets, in the navel an emerald, and in the left hand a gold fan edged with most beautiful feathers and so well burnished that it looked like a mirror, in which they meant to signify that he saw everything that happened in the world. At other times, to signify his justice, they represented him seated on a stool surrounded by a red cloth, on which were figured some skulls and bones of the dead, in his left hand a shield,

(*) The latter was a goddess and the former a god, whom they imagined to dwell in heaven in a glorious city abounding in pleasures, and from there to watch over the world and to give mortals their inclinations, Ometecuhtli to men, and Omecihuatl to women. They related that this goddess, having borne many children in heaven, gave birth at one delivery to a flint knife; whereupon the children, in disdain, threw it down to the earth, and in falling there were born from it sixteen hundred heroes, who, aware of their noble origin, and seeing themselves without servants, since all men had perished in a great calamity (d), agreed to send an embassy to their Mother, begging her to grant them leave to create men who might serve them. The Mother replied that if they had thoughts more noble and more elevated they would make themselves worthy to live with her eternally in heaven; but since the dwelling on earth pleased them, they should go to Mictlantecuhtli, god of hell, and ask him for some bone of men already dead, from which, sprinkling it with their own blood, they would have a man and a woman, who would then multiply; but they should guard well against Mictlantecuhtli, since, once he had given the bone, he might immediately repent. In accordance with this instruction of the Mother, Xolotl, one of the heroes, went to hell; and having obtained what he sought, he at once set off running toward the surface of the earth; whereupon Mictlantecuhtli, in disdain, ran after him; but, being unable to overtake him, returned to hell. Xolotl, in his headlong flight, stumbled, and as he fell the bone broke into unequal pieces. e: Apotheosis of the deified by those nations. They said also that, once the human race Sun and of the Moon. had been restored and had multiplied, each of the aforesaid heroes, or demigods, had among men his servants and partisans, and that, there being no longer a Sun, since the one that had been there had come to an end, the heroes assembled at Teotihuacan around a great fire, and told the men that the first of them who should cast himself into the fire would have the glory of becoming the Sun. A man bolder than the others, named Nanahuatzin, at once hurled himself in, and descended to hell. Meanwhile, as all remained in expectation of the outcome, the heroes made a wager with the quails, the locusts, and other animals on the place in the sky from which the new Sun was to be born, and since it was not guessed by those animals, they were at once sacrificed. At last the Sun was born in that quarter which from then on was called the East; [p. 10] but scarcely had it risen above the horizon when it stopped; which Bk. VI. the heroes perceiving, they sent word to it to continue its course. The Sun replied that it would not do so before seeing all of them dead. This reply caused the heroes no less indignation than fear; whereupon one of them, called Citli, taking a bow and three arrows, shot one at it; but the Sun, bending aside, avoided the blow. He hurled the other two, but could never strike it. The Sun then, in disdain, turned the last arrow against Citli, and drove it into his forehead, of which wound he died afterward. The others, dismayed at their brother's misfortune, and finding themselves unable to prevail against the Sun, resolved to die at the hands of Xolotl, who, after opening the breast of all his brothers, killed himself also. The heroes before dying left their garments to their servants, and even after the conquest by the Spaniards certain old mantles of the Indians were found preserved with singular veneration, because they believed them to have been received as an inheritance from those ancient heroes. The men remained melancholy at the loss of their lords; but Tezcatlipoca ordered one of them to go to the house of the Sun, and from there to bring music to celebrate his festivals, and told him that for such a journey, which was to be made by sea, a bridge of whales and turtles would be made for him, and that he should go continually intoning a song which he gave him. The Mexicans said that this was the origin of music and of the dances with which they celebrated the festivals of their gods; that from the sacrifice which the heroes made of the quails arose that which they themselves made every day of these birds to the Sun, and from what Xolotl did with his brothers, the barbarous sacrifices of human victims, which afterward became so common in that land. Similar to this fable was that which they related of the origin of the Moon, namely, that Tecuciztecatl, another of those men who gathered at Teotihuacan, imitating the example of Nanahuatzin, cast himself also into the fire; but the flame having by then slackened, he did not become so luminous, and was transformed into the Moon.

He was among the Mexicans, § 4. The god of the air. and all the other nations of Anahuac, the god of the air. They said that he had been high priest of Tula, white, tall, and corpulent, with a broad forehead, large eyes, long black hair, and a thick beard; that out of love of decency he always wore a long robe; that he was so rich that he had palaces of silver and of gems; that he was very industrious, and had been the inventor of the arts of casting metals and of cutting gems; that he was most wise and most prudent, as he made known in the laws he left to men, and above all that he was a man of austere and exemplary life; that whenever he wished to publish some law in the kingdom, he had a crier go up on the mount Tzatzitepec (hill of cries), near the city of Tula, and his voice could be heard as far as three hundred miles; that in his time maize grew so large that a single ear was a load suited to the strength of one man; that the gourds were as long as a human body; that there was no need to dye cotton, since it grew naturally of every color; and in the same fashion was the greatness and the abundance of all other fruits and seeds; that there was then an incredible multitude of most beautiful and melodious birds; that all his subjects were rich; and, to put many words into one, the Mexicans imagined the pontificate of Quetzalcoatl to have been as happy as the Greeks imagined the reign of Saturn, to whom he was also similar in the misfortune of exile; for while he was in such prosperity, Tezcatlipoca, wishing, I do not know for what reason, to drive him out of that country, appeared to him in the form of an old man, told him that it was the will of the gods that he betake himself to the kingdom of Tlapallan, and at the same time offered him a drink, which Quetzalcoatl took willingly, in the hope of acquiring by it the immortality to which he aspired; but scarcely had he taken it when he felt himself moved

e: B2 [p. 12] by such a desire to go to Tlapallan that he set out on the road at once, Bk. VI. accompanied by many of his subjects, who all along the way went making festival for him with music. They said that near the city of Cuauhtitlan he pelted a tree with stones, which all remained fixed in its trunk, and that near Tlalnepantla he stamped his hand on a stone, which the Mexicans showed to the Spaniards after the conquest. When he had arrived at Cholula, the citizens detained him there, and charged him with the government. Besides the decency of his life and the sweetness of his manners, what contributed to the esteem in which the Cholulans held him was the aversion he showed to every sort of cruelty, so much so that he could not bear to hear war spoken of. To him, according to what the Cholulans said, they were indebted for the art of casting metals, in which they afterward excelled, for the laws by which from then on they governed themselves, for the rites and ceremonies of their religion, and also, as some affirmed, for the ordering of the times and their calendar. After having been twenty years in Cholula, he resolved to continue his journey to the imaginary kingdom of Tlapallan, taking with him four noble and virtuous youths. In the maritime province of Coatzacoalco he dismissed them, and sent word through them to the Cholulans that they might be assured that after some time he would return to console and to govern them. The Cholulans placed the reins of government in the hands of these youths, out of regard for their beloved Quetzalcoatl, of whom some said that he disappeared, others that he died on that same coast. However that may have been, Quetzalcoatl was consecrated a god by the Toltecs of Cholollan, and made the principal tutelary god of their city, where in his honor they built in the center of it a high mount, and on it a sanctuary, and another mount, with its temple, was afterward built for him at Tula. From Cholula his cult spread throughout all that country, where he was venerated as god of the air. He had temples in Mexico and elsewhere, and several nations, even enemies of the Cholulans, had in the city of Cholula itself temples and priests dedicated to his worship, and from all countries [p. 13] went to that city to make their devotions, and to fulfill their vows. The Cholulans preserved with the greatest veneration certain little Bk. VI. green stones, well carved, which they said had been possessed by him. The Yucatecans boasted that their lords were descended from Quetzalcoatl. Barren women commended themselves to him in order to become fruitful. The festivals they held for him were great and very famous, especially in Cholula in the Teoxihuitl, or divine year, which were preceded by a rigorous fast of eighty days and by frightful austerities carried out by the priests consecrated to his worship. They said that Quetzalcoatl swept the road for the god of water; because in those countries the wind ordinarily precedes the rain. Dr. Sigüenza believed that the Quetzalcoatl deified by those nations was none other than the Apostle St. Thomas, who announced the Gospel to them. He promoted such an opinion with exquisite erudition in a work (e) which, like several others of great merit written by him, had the misfortune of being lost through the negligence of his heirs. In this work he made a comparison of the names of Didymos and of Quetzalcoatl, (f) of their dress, their doctrine, and their predictions, and examined the places through which they went, the traces which they left, and the portents which their disciples published. Since we have not seen the aforesaid manuscripts, we abstain from censuring such an opinion, to which, in spite of the respect which we bear to the sublime talent and the great learning of the author, we cannot in any way assent. Several writers of Mexico have persuaded themselves that some centuries before the arrival of the Spaniards the Gospel had already been preached (e) Of this work of Sigüenza, Vetancurt makes mention in his Teatro mexicano, and Dr. Eguiara in the Biblioteca mexicana.

e: (f) Vetancurt, where he makes the comparison of the names of Didymos and of Quetzalcoatl, says that this name is composed of Coatl, twin, and Quetzalli, gem, and that it signifies Precious Twin. But Torquemada, who knew Mexican perfectly, and had from the ancients the interpretation of those names, says that Quetzalcoatl means Feathered Serpent. In fact, Coatl properly signifies Serpent, and Quetzalli Green Feather, and only by metaphor are such names given to the twin and to the gem. [p. 14] preached in America. The reasons which those authors had are severBk. VI. al: crosses found at different times and in different places (g), which appear to have been made before the arrival of the Spaniards; the fast of forty days observed by many peoples of the New World, (h) the tradition which existed of the future arrival of foreign and bearded people, (i) and the human footprints impressed in several stones, which are thought to be those of the Apostle St. Thomas. (j) I have never been able to persuade myself of such an opinion; but to examine such monuments requires another work, quite different from this. Tlaloc, otherwise Tlalocatecuhtli (Lord of paradise), was the god of water. Of those of Yucatán Father Diego López de Cogolludo, a Franciscan, makes mention in bk. 2, ch. 12 of his History. Of that of the Mixteca Father Burgoa, a Dominican, in his Chronicle, and the Chevalier Boturini in his work. Of that of Querétaro a Franciscan religious of the College of Propaganda of that city wrote; and of that of Tepic the learned Jesuit Segismundo Taraval, whose manuscripts were preserved in the College of the Jesuits of Guadalajara. That of Tianquiztepec was discovered by the Chevalier Boturini, and he makes mention of it in his work. The crosses of Yucatán were adored by the Yucatecans because of the instruction, as they affirmed, of their great prophet Chilam-Cambal, who warned them that when certain bearded men should come ashore in that land from the east, and should see them adoring that sign, they should embrace their doctrine. Of all these monuments we shall speak in the Ecclesiastical History of Mexico, if God deigns to favor our designs. (h) The fast of forty days proves nothing, since those nations likewise observed fasts of three, of four, of five, of twenty, of eighty, of a hundred and sixty days, and even of four years, as we shall see later, and that of forty days was certainly not the most common. (i) In Book V we have set forth our opinion on the omens of the arrival of the Spaniards. If the prophecies of Chilam-Cambal were genuine, he could, without being a Christian, have been enlightened by God to foretell Christianity, just as Balaam was likewise enlightened to announce the birth of our divine Redeemer. There lived, they said, in Coatepec, a place near the ancient city of Tula, a woman most devoted to the worship of the gods, called Coatlicue, Mother of the Centzonhuitznahuac. One day, on which, as usual, she was occupied in sweeping the temple, she saw descend through the air a ball formed of various feathers; she took it, and kept it in her bosom, intending to use the feathers afterward for the adornment of the altar; but when she looked for it after she had finished sweeping, she could not find it, at which she was exceedingly astonished, and much more when she felt herself, from that moment, pregnant. The pregnancy grew until it was recognized by her children, who, although they suspected nothing of the Mother's virtue, yet fearing the dishonor which the birth would bring upon them, determined to prevent it by parricide. Their resolution was not so secret that the Mother did not become aware of it, being extremely afflicted at having to die at the hands of her own children; but suddenly she heard a voice issuing from her womb, which said to her, Do not be afraid, my Mother; for I shall save you, for your highest honor and my own glory. e: Boturini, as one who was not very conversant with the Mexican language, derives this name from Huitziton, leader of the Mexicans on their migration, and affirms that this same leader was none other than that god; but besides that such an etymology is too forced, that alleged identity was wholly unheard of among the Mexicans, who, when they began their migration led by Huitziton, were already adoring, from time immemorial, that god of war. The Spaniards, not knowing how to pronounce the name of Huitzilopochtli, called him Huichilobos. [p. 19] guilty, and he fell upon the others with such fury that, in spite of their Bk. VI. efforts, their arms, and their entreaties, all were killed, and their houses sacked, and the spoils of these he presented to his Mother. Such an event put men into such consternation that from then on they called him Tetzahuitl, terror, and Tetzauhteotl, terrible god. This god, having become the tutelary god of the Mexicans, was he, according to what they said, who led them for so many years on their migration, and established them on the site where afterward the great city of Mexico was founded. Here they raised to him that superb temple, which was so celebrated even by the Spaniards themselves, in which every year they held for him three very solemn festivals, in the fifth, ninth, and fifteenth months, besides those which they held for him every four years, every thirteen years, and at the beginning of each of their centuries. His statue was gigantic, and represented a man seated on a blue stool, from whose four corners four great serpents were seen to issue. His forehead was blue; but the whole face was covered with a mask of gold, and another like it covered the nape of his neck. On his head he had a fine plume formed in the manner of a bird's beak, on his neck a necklace composed of ten figures of human hearts, in his right hand a serpentine and blue staff, and in his left a shield, on which there were five balls of feathers arranged in the form of a cross; and from the upper part of the shield there rose a little banner of gold with four arrows, which the Mexicans said had been sent to them from heaven to perform those glorious actions which we have seen in their history. He had his body encircled by a great serpent of gold, and adorned with several figurines of animals made of gold and of gems. Each of these ornaments and insignia had its particular significance. Whenever they deliberated on making war, they implored his protection with prayers and sacrifices. Among their gods he was the one to whom the greatest number of human victims was sacrificed. Painalton (swift, or hasty), god of war and vicar of Huitzilopochtli. Just as they invoked this god in the wars which they undertook after serious deliberation, so they invoked Painalton in sudden emergencies, such as an unexpected attack by enemies. This they did by having the priests run through all the wards of the city with the image of this god, which was venerated together with those of the other gods of war, calling upon him with cries, and offering him sacrifices of quails and other animals. All the men of war were then obliged to run to arms for the defense. § 7. Mixcoatl, goddess of hunting, and the principal deity of the Otomis, who, because they lived in the mountains, were for the most part hunters. The Matlatzincas also honored her with particular worship. In Mexico she had two temples, and in one of them, called Teotlalpan, they held for her in the fourteenth month a great festival with many sacrifices of wild animals. Opochtli, god of fishing. They believed him the inventor of nets and of the other instruments for fishing; whence he was especially venerated by fishermen, as their patron. In Cuitlahuac, a city situated on a small island of the lake of Chalco, Amimitl, god of fishing, was much revered, who in all likelihood was not distinct from Opochtli, except in name. Huixtocihuatl, goddess of salt, and celebrated among the Mexicans for the salt works which they had not far from the capital. They held a festival for her in the seventh month. They honored her annually with sacrifices of human victims, and with particular hymns which they composed to praise her. Tezcatzoncatl, god of wine, and called also by other names for the effects caused by wine. (**) He had a temple in Mexico, where there were four hundred priests consecrated to his worship, and where every year in the thirteenth month they held a festival for him and the other gods his companions. Ixtlilton (he who has the black face) seems to have been also a god of medicine; because to his temple they brought sick children, that he might heal them. Their parents brought them, and made them dance before the idol (if they were in a condition to do so), suggested to them the prayers with which they were to ask for health, and then made them drink a water which was blessed by the priests consecrated to this god. Coatlicue, or Coatlantona, was the goddess of flowers. She had a temple in Mexico called Yopico, where the Xochimanqui, that is, the makers of nosegays of flowers, held a festival for her in the third month, which fell precisely in the season of spring. Among other things they presented to her nosegays of flowers charmingly interwoven. We do not know whether Coatlicue was the same as the one whom some imagined to be the Mother of Huitzilopochtli. Tlazolteotl was the god whom the Mexicans invoked to obtain pardon for their misdeeds, and to avoid the infamy which these might bring upon the guilty. The principal devotees of this wicked deity were lascivious men, who sought his protection with sacrifices and oblations. (l) Xipe (**) They also gave the god of wine the names of Tequechmecaniani, Strangler, and of Teatlahuiani, Drowner. (l) The Chevalier Boturini affirms that Tlazolteotl was the shameless and plebeian Venus, and Macuilxochiquetzalli the Pronuba Venus; but it is certain that the Mexicans never attributed to their gods those shameful excesses with which the Greeks and Romans defamed their Venus.

VI. smiths, (m) who was held in great veneration among the Mexicans; for they were persuaded that all those who neglected this worship would be punished with several infirmities, and particularly with the itch, with abscesses, and with grave ailments of the eyes and of the head. They were especially notable, however, for the cruelty of the sacrifices which they made to him at the festival they were accustomed to celebrate in the second month. Nappatecuhtli (four times lord) was the god of the makers of mats. They said that he was very kindly and ready to pardon the injuries done to him, and very generous toward all. He had two temples in Mexico, where they held a festival for him in the thirteenth month. Omacatl was the god of rejoicing. Whenever the Mexican lords gave some great banquet, or had some public rejoicing, they carried the image of this god from the temple and set it in the place of the festival, believing that they would expose themselves to some misfortune if they failed in this. Tonantzin (Our Mother) was, as we believe, the same goddess Centeotl of whom we have already spoken. She had a temple on a mountain three miles distant from Mexico toward the north, and the peoples came there in crowds to venerate her, with an astonishing number of sacrifices. Today at the foot of the same mountain there is the most famous sanctuary of the whole New World, dedicated to the true God, to which people flock from the most distant countries to venerate the most celebrated and truly miraculous image of the most holy Madonna of Guadalupe, that place of abomination being transformed into a place of propitiation, and the Lord abundantly pouring out his graces on behalf of those peoples in the place bathed with so much blood of their ancestors. II, where we set forth the tragic death of the Princess of Colhuacan. This goddess had a temple in Mexico, where in the eleventh month they held a most solemn festival for her. The Tlaxcalans paid her particular worship, and the midwives venerated her as their protectress. Almost all the Spanish writers confuse Teteoinan with Tonantzin; but they were without doubt different. Ilamatecuhtli, for whom the Mexicans held a festival on the third day of the seventeenth month, seems to have been a goddess of old age. Her name signifies nothing other than Old Lady. Tepitoton (little ones) was the name which the Mexicans gave to their Penates, or household gods, and to the idols which represented them. Of these little idols the kings and the lords were required to have six in their houses, the nobles four, and the commoners two. In the public streets they were to be seen everywhere. Besides these gods, who were the most notable, and others whom we pass over so as not to weary the readers further, they had two hundred and sixty, to whom as many days were consecrated. These gods communicated their names to such days, and they are the ones that are read in the first thirteen months of the Calendar. The very gods of the Mexicans were for the most part those of the other nations of Anahuac; they varied only in greater or lesser celebrity, in some rites, and sometimes in names. The god most celebrated in Mexico was Huitzilopochtli, in Cholula and in Huexotzinco Quetzalcoatl, among the Totonacs Centeotl, and among the Otomis Mixcoatl. The Tlaxcalans, though eternal rivals of the Mexicans, worshiped the same deities also; indeed their favorite god was the very Huitzilopochtli of the Mexicans, but under the name of Camaxtle. The Texcocans, as confederates, friends, and neighbors of the Mexicans, conformed in almost everything with them. The ordinary material the gods. of which they were made was clay, and several kinds of stones and woods; but they also made them of gold and other metals, and some of gems. On a high mountain of Achiauhtla in the Mixteca, Benito Fernández, a celebrated Dominican missionary, found a little idol called by the Mixtecs the heart of the People. This was a most precious emerald four fingers long and two wide, on which was carved the figure of a little bird, and around it that of a little serpent. The Spaniards who saw it offered fifteen hundred sequins for it; but the zealous missionary, before all the people, and with great ceremony, reduced it to powder. The most extraordinary idol of the Mexicans was that of Huitzilopochtli, which they made of several kinds of seeds kneaded with human blood, of which we shall speak later. The idols were for the most part ugly and horrible by reason of the extravagant parts of which they were composed, to represent the attributes and functions of their gods.

e: They acknowledged the alleged divinity of such gods with prayers, with genuflections and prostrations, with vows, with fasts and other austerities, with sacrifices and oblations, and with several rites, partly common to other nations and partly peculiar to their religion. They commonly made their prayers on their knees, and with their faces turned toward the east, and for this reason they built their sanctuaries for the most part with the door to the west. They made vows both for themselves and for their children, and that of consecrating them to the service of their gods in some temple or monastery was frequent. Those who stumbled or slipped on some journey and were in peril made a vow to visit the temple of the god Omacatl, and to offer him incense and paper. They often made use of the name of God to confirm the truth. The formula of their oaths was this: Cuix amo nechitta in Toteotzin? Perhaps our God does not see me? [p. 25] me? And naming the principal god, or some other to whom they bore Bk. VI. particular devotion, they kissed the hand after touching the ground with it. Such an oath carried great weight in trials for clearing oneself of any crime of which they were accused; because they were persuaded that there was no man so rash as to dare to abuse the name of God with the evident peril of being most severely punished by heaven. The mythology of the Mexicans did not lack metamorphoses, or § 9. transformations. Among others they related that a man named Their transformations. Yappan, having undertaken to do penance on a mountain, was tempted by a woman and fell into adultery; for which he was immediately beheaded by Yaotl, to whom the gods had given the commission of watching over his conduct, and by the same gods he was transformed into a black scorpion. Not content with such a punishment, Yaotl carried it out also on Tlahuitzin, the wife of Yappan, who was likewise transformed into a blond scorpion, and Yaotl himself, for having exceeded the limits of his commission, was changed into a locust. They said that the shame of that crime was the reason why scorpions shun the light and hide under stones. The Mexicans and the other peoples of Anahuac had, like all the § 10. The great temple of civilized nations of the world, temples, or places set apart for the ex‐ Mexico. ercise of religion, where the people assembled to render worship to their gods, and to implore their protection. They called the temple Teocalli, that is, House of God, and Teopan, place of God, which names, after they embraced Christianity, they gave with greater propriety to the temples erected in honor of the true God. The city and the kingdom of Mexico began with the building of the sanctuary of Huitzilopochtli, or Mexitli, from whom the city took its name. This edifice was then a poor hut. Itzcoatl, the first conquering king of that nation, enlarged it after the capture of Azcapotzalco. Moctezuma I, his successor, built a new temple, in which there was some magnificence. e: and [p. 26] Bk. VI. and dedicated that vast temple, which was designed by his predecessor Tizoc. This was that temple which the Spaniards so much celebrated after having ruined it. We could wish that their exactness in the measurements which they have left us had been as great as was their zeal in destroying that proud monument of superstition; but so great is the variety with which they wrote that, after having labored to combine their descriptions, I have not been able to satisfy myself about the measurements, nor should I ever have been able to form an idea of the architecture of this temple, had it not been for the image which the Anonymous Conqueror sets before our eyes, the copy of which we give here, although in the measurements we conform more to his account than to the image. We shall say, then, what we have found true by the prolix comparison of the descriptions of four eyewitnesses, leaving aside that of which we are in doubt on account of the confused account of the authors (n). This (n) The four eyewitnesses whose descriptions we have combined are the Conqueror Cortés, Bernal Díaz, the Anonymous Conqueror, and Sahagún. The first three stayed several months in the palace of King Axayacatl near that temple, and saw it every day. Sahagún, although he did not see it entire, still saw some part of it, and was able to recognize the site which it occupied. Gómara, although he did not see the temple, nor ever stayed in Mexico, had his information about it from the Conquerors who saw it. Acosta, whose description Herrera and Solís copied, instead of describing the great temple describes another, quite different. This author, although otherwise worthy of trust, did not stay in Mexico until sixty years after the conquest, when nothing remained of the temple. In a Dutch edition of Solís an unfaithful image of the great temple was published, which was later published by the authors of the General History of Voyages, and is found again in the edition of the letters of the Conqueror Cortés made in Mexico in 1770; but, that the carelessness of those who made this edition may be seen, let a comparison be made of that image with Cortés's account. He says in his first letter (though hyperbolically) that the great temple of Mexico was higher than the tower of the Cathedral Church of Seville, and the aforesaid image scarcely shows seven or eight perches, or toises, of height. Cortés affirms that five hundred Mexican nobles fortified themselves in the upper court of the temple, and in the space which that image represents there could not be more than sixty or eighty men. Finally (omitting many other contradictions) Cortés says that that temple consisted of three or four bodies, and every body had, as he speaks, its corridors, or terraces, and in the image the whole is represented as a single body without such corridors.

e: This great temple occupied the center of the city, and comprised, to‐ Bk. VI. gether with the other temples and buildings attached to it, the whole site of the great cathedral church, part of the main plaza, and part also of the streets and the buildings around it. The wall which enclosed that place in a square was so large that within its enclosure, according to the Conqueror Cortés, a town of five hundred households could have stood. (o) This wall, built of stone and lime, was quite thick, eight feet high, crowned with battlements made in the shape of snail shells, and adorned with several stone figures made in the form of serpents: whence they gave it the name of Coatepantli, or wall of serpents. It had four gates at the four cardinal points. The east gate faced a wide street which led to the lake of Texcoco; the other three faced the three principal streets of the city, the widest and the straightest, which were continuous with those built on the lake, leading to Iztapalapa, to Tacuba, and to Tepeyacac. Above the four gates there were as many armories, most abundantly supplied with every sort of offensive and defensive arms, where in case of need the troops went to arm themselves. The floor, or court, which lay within the enclosure of the wall, was curiously paved with stones so smooth and polished that the horses of the Spaniards could not move upon them without slipping and falling. In the middle of the court there rose a vast oblong edifice (p), entirely solid, covered D2                         with (o) The Anonymous Conqueror says that what was within the enclosure of the wall looked like a city. Gómara affirms that the wall was a very great crossbow shot long on each side. Torquemada, having said the same as Gómara in bk. 8, ch. 11, afterward in ch. 19 affirms that the circuit of the wall was more than three thousand paces: which is evidently false. Dr. Hernández, in his lengthy description of that temple, which is preserved in manuscript in the library of the Escorial, and which Father Nieremberg used in his Natural History, gives each side of the wall two hundred Toledan braccia, which make about eighty-six perches.

e: (p) Sahagún makes the temple perfectly square; but the Anonymous Conqueror, both in his description and in the figure he left us, represents it as oblong, such as those of Teotihuacan are, which served as the model for all the others. [p. 28] with square and equal slabs, and composed of five stages, nearly equal Bk. VI. in height but unequal in length and breadth, since the higher ones were narrower. The first stage, or the base of the edifice, was more than fifty perches long from east to west, and about forty-three wide from north to south. (q) The second stage was about one perch shorter and narrower on every side than the first; the third had as much less than the second, and the others in the same proportion; so that above each stage there remained a space or level, along which three or even four men abreast could walk around the next stage. The stairs, which were on the south side, were of large, well-worked stones and consisted of one hundred and fourteen steps, each a foot high. Nor was it a single continuous stair, as the authors of the General History of Voyages and the publishers of the Letters of Cortés in Mexico represent it; but it was divided into as many stairs as there were stages of the edifice, in the manner seen in our figure; so that, the first stair having been climbed, one could not ascend the second without making a circuit on the first level around the second stage; nor, the second stair having been climbed, could one arrive at the third without likewise going around on the second level, and so on with the others. This can be better understood by looking at the figure which we present, which is made after that of the Anonymous Conqueror, (r) though corrected as to the measurements from the description of the same author and of other historians. On the fifth and last stage there was a level, or small oblong plaza (which we shall call the upper court), which had (q) Sahagún gives the first stage 360 Toledan feet on each side; but this is the measure of its length. Gómara gives it fifty brazas; but this is the measure of the breadth. 360 Toledan feet make 308 Parisian feet, or a little more than 50 perches. Fifty brazas, or estados, make 257 Parisian feet, or nearly 42 perches. e: Kircher’s work entitled Oedipus Aegyptiacus. [p. 29] had forty-three perches (s) in length and thirty-four in breadth, and Bk. VI. was as well paved as the floor, or lower court. At the eastern end of that level two towers rose to a height of fifty-six feet, a little more than nine perches. Each was divided into three stories, of which the lowest was of stone and lime, and the other two of well-worked and painted wood. The lowest story, or base, was properly the sanctuary, where on a stone altar five feet high the titular idols were placed. One of these two sanctuaries was consecrated to Huitzilopochtli and to the other two gods of war, and the other to Tezcatlipoca. The other stories were intended for keeping certain things belonging to the worship of the idols, and the ashes of some kings or lords who out of particular devotion had so provided. Both sanctuaries had their door to the west, and both towers ended in a very beautiful dome of wood; but there is no author who sets forth the interior arrangement and the ornamentation of the sanctuaries, nor even the thickness of the towers; wherefore the one that we represent in our figure is not even certain, but was put in only by conjecture. This, too, we can affirm without danger of error: that the height of the edifice, without the towers, was not less than nineteen perches, and with the towers exceeded twenty-eight. From that height one saw the lake, the cities around it, and a great part of the valley, and it was, according to what eyewitnesses affirm, the most beautiful view in the world. In the upper court was the altar of the ordinary sacrifices, and in the lower court that of the gladiatorial sacrifices. e: (s) Sahagún, whose measures Torquemada adopted, gives the upper court no more than seventy Toledan feet square, which make ten perches; but it was not possible that in so narrow a space five hundred Mexican nobles could have taken their stand to fight against the Spaniards, as Cortés affirms, and much less if we believe Bernal Díaz, who says that the Mexicans fortified in that temple were four thousand, besides other companies that were up there when those nobles climbed up. [p. 30] night there was a perpetual fire, which they kept up and preserved Bk. VI. with the greatest care, because they feared that if it should ever go out they would have to suffer the most terrible punishments of heaven. In the other temples and religious buildings included within the enclosure of the aforesaid wall there were up to six hundred braziers of the same size and shape, and at night, when they were all lit, they formed a delightful spectacle. § 11.    In the space between the wall and the great temple, besides a plaza Buildings annexed to for the religious dances, there were more than forty smaller temples the great temple. consecrated to other gods, several colleges of priests, some seminaries of youths and boys of both sexes, and many other buildings scattered around the whole circumference, of which, for their singularity, it will be necessary to give some account. Among these temples the most considerable were those of Tezcatlipoca, of Tlaloc, and of Quetzalcoatl. All of them, though different in size, were alike in form, and all had their façade turned toward the great temple, whereas the other temples outside that enclosure were built with the façade toward the west. Only the temple of Quetzalcoatl differed in form from the others; for whereas they were quadrangular, that one was round. The door of this sanctuary was the mouth of an enormous stone serpent armed with teeth. Several Spaniards who out of curiosity entered this diabolical temple afterward declared the horror which they felt at the entrance. Among the other temples there was one called Ilhuicatitlan, dedicated to the planet Venus, where there was a great column, and on it painted or carved the image of that star: before which, at the time of its appearance, they sacrificed prisoners to it. The colleges of priests and the seminaries contained within the enclosure of the aforesaid temples were several: in particular we know of five colleges, or monasteries, of priests, and of three seminaries of youths; but there were certainly more, since the number of persons consecrated to the worship of the gods found there was excessive, as we shall shortly say.

e: Among the notable buildings included within that enclosure, be‐ Bk. VI. sides the four armories over the four gates, there was another near the temple: Tezcacalli (house of mirrors), so called because its walls inside were covered with mirrors. There was another small temple called Teccizcalli, entirely adorned with shells, and it had an attached house where at certain times the king of Mexico retired to make his prayers and his fasts. Besides this there was a house of retreat for the high priest, called Poyauhtlan, and others also for private persons. They also had a good hospice for lodging the distinguished strangers who out of devotion went to visit the temple, or out of curiosity to see the grandeurs of the court. There were several ponds in which the priests bathed, and fountains whose water they drank. In the pond called Tezcapan many bathed on account of a particular vow made to the gods. Among the fountains there was one which they called Toxpalatl, whose water was esteemed holy; they drank it only at the most solemn festivals, and outside of them no one was permitted to take it. (t) There were places for raising birds that were sacrificed, and gardens where flowers and fragrant herbs were cultivated for the adornment of the altars, and also a little wood in which mountains, crags, and rocks were artificially represented, and from there they went out to the general hunt, of which we shall speak elsewhere. They had rooms intended for guarding the idols, the ornaments, and all the property of the temples, among which were three halls so large that the Spaniards were amazed when they saw them. But the buildings most notable for their singularity were: a great prison, in the manner of a cage, where they kept the idols of the conquered nations as if imprisoned; and others in which they preserved the skulls of the sacrificed, some of these being mere heaps of bones, where they stood piled up, and in

[p. 32] in the others there were skulls set in the walls, forming by their Bk. VI. arrangement and symmetry several figures not so much curious as horrible to behold, or else strung in good order on poles. The largest of these buildings, called Hueitzompan, though it was not within the enclosure of the wall, was nevertheless not far from it, facing the main gate. This was a vast oblong mound of earth, made in the shape of a half pyramid. At the lowest part it was a hundred and fifty-four feet long. One ascended by a stair of thirty steps to the level above, where there were erected seventy or more very tall beams, pierced from top to bottom and scarcely four feet apart from one another. From the holes of one beam to those of the next, rods were passed across, and on each of them a certain number of skulls were strung through the temples. On the steps of the stair, too, there was a skull between one stone and the next. Moreover, on one side and the other of the same edifice there were two towers made, as far as could be seen, only of skulls and lime. Where some skull happened through excessive age to break, the priests put in another, a fresh one taken from the heaps of bones, so that neither the number nor the symmetry should ever fail. The skulls of the common victims were kept stripped of their skin; but those of the lords and of famous captains they tried to preserve with their skin, beard, and hair: which made those trophies of their barbarous superstition still more frightful. So many were the skulls preserved in this and in other similar buildings that, some of the Spanish conquerors having taken the trouble to count those which were on the steps of the aforesaid edifice and on the rows of the beams, they found a hundred and thirty-six thousand. (u) Whoever may want a more detailed account of the buildings that were within the enclosure of the wall of the great temple may read the account of Sahagún in Torquemada (u) Andrés de Tapia, one of Cortés’s captains and one of those who counted the skulls, related it to the historian Gómara, as the latter bears witness in ch. 82 of his History of Mexico.

The Anonymous Conqueror counted, as he affirms, 190 towers among those of the temples and those of the palaces. Bernal Díaz says that they exceeded a hundred; but it is to be believed that these two authors counted only those most notable for their height. Some later authors wrote that those towers were as many as the days of the year. [p. 34] there is a devout sanctuary of the Mother of the true God; but on acBk. We are wholly ignorant of its measurements; but its circumference at the lower part is not less than half a mile. (x) One climbs to the summit by a road made in a spiral line around the pyramid, and I climbed it on horseback in 1744. This is that famous mountain which the Chevalier Boturini believed to have been built by the Toltecs to take refuge in, in case another flood, like that of Noah, should come upon them, and about which so many fables were spread. There still survive the famous buildings of Teotihuacan, three miles to the north of that place, and more than twenty from Mexico toward the northeast. These vast buildings, which served as the model for the temples of that country, were two temples consecrated, one to the Sun and the other to the Moon, represented in two idols of enormous size made of stone and covered with gold. That of the Sun had a great cavity in the breast, and in it the image of that planet in the finest gold. The Conquerors profited by the metal, the idols were broken to pieces by order of the first bishop of Mexico, and the fragments lasted in that place until the end of the last century, and perhaps are still there. The base, or lower stage, of the temple of the Sun is a hundred and twenty-eight perches long and eighty-six wide, and the height of the whole edifice corresponds to its bulk. VI. as those of the great temple of Mexico; but at present they are not to be seen, because they are partly in ruins and covered everywhere by a great quantity of earth. Around the same buildings many little mounds are seen, which, as is believed, were so many small temples consecrated to other planets and stars, and because all that site was full of religious structures of this kind it received from the ancients the name of Teotihuacan. The number of temples that there were in the whole Mexican empire was very great. Torquemada persuaded himself that there were more than forty thousand; but I believe that they exceeded that number by far, if one wishes to count even the small ones; for there was no inhabited place without a temple, nor any place of some size that did not have many. The structure of the large temples was for the most part like that of the great temple of Mexico; but there were also many of quite different architecture. Some consisted of a single pyramidal stage and one stair, others of one stage and several stairs, as is seen in the following figure, which is a copy of another published by Diego Valadés in his Rhetorica Christiana. [p. 36] large. Each temple had its own possessions and lands, and also its own Bk. VI. farmers to work them. From these was drawn everything needed for the maintenance of the priests, as well as the firewood, which in no‐ § 13. table quantity was consumed in the temples. The priests who were Revenues of the temples. stewards of the temples often betook themselves to the aforesaid possessions; and those who served on them thought themselves fortunate to contribute by their labor to the worship of the gods and to the support of their ministers. In the kingdom of Acolhuacan those twenty-nine cities which provided what was necessary for the royal palace were also obliged to provide for the temples. It is to be believed that that tract of country which bore the name of Teotlalpan (Land of the Gods) was so called because the possessions of the temples were there. To this were added the countless oblations which the devout made every day spontaneously, of every sort of provisions, and the first fruits which they offered in thanksgiving for timely rain and for the other benefits of heaven. Near the temples were the granaries, where they kept the grain and all the provisions belonging to the support of the priests, and what remained over each year was distributed to the poor, for whom there were hospitals in the large places. The multitude of the priests corresponded to that of the gods and § 14. of the temples of the Mexicans, and the veneration which they paid Number and differ‐ to their ministers was in no way inferior to the superstitious worship ent ranks of the priests. of their deities. The prodigious number of priests that there were in the Mexican empire may be conjectured from that which there was within the enclosure of the great temple of Mexico, which amounted, according to what several ancient historians affirm, to five thousand. Nor should this occasion wonder; for the priests consecrated in that place to the service of the god Tezcatzoncatl were four hundred.

e: Every temple had a good number of priests: wherefore I should not consider rash one who dared to affirm that the number of priests of the whole Mexican empire was not less than a million. Contributing greatly to the multiplication of such ministers was the supreme respect which they paid to the priesthood [p. 37] and the esteem in which they held the employment of serving at the worship of the gods. The lords vied with one another in consecrating Bk. VI. their sons for some time to the service of the sanctuaries. The lower nobility employed their sons in the outer tasks, that is, in carrying wood, in stirring up and keeping up the fire of the braziers, and in other similar ones, both groups persuading themselves that they could not aspire to a greater honor than that of serving the worship of their gods. There were several orders and ranks among the priests. The supreme heads of all were the two high priests, to whom they gave the names of Teoteuctli (divine lord) and of Hueiteopixqui (great priest). This eminent dignity was not conferred except on persons of great distinction, both for their birth and for their probity and for their knowledge of the ceremonies of their religion. The high priests were the oracles whom the kings consulted in the gravest affairs of state, and without their opinion no war was undertaken. These were the ones who anointed the kings after their election, and who opened the breast and tore out the heart of the human victims at the most solemn sacrifices. The high priest in the kingdom of Acolhuacan was always, according to what some historians say, the second-born son of the king. The one of the Totonacs was anointed with elastic resin mixed with the blood of infants, and this they called divine anointing. (z) Several authors affirm the same of the one at Mexico. From what we have said it can be understood that the high priests of Mexico were heads of religion only with regard to the Mexican nation, not to the other conquered nations; for these, even after having been subjected to the crown of Mexico, kept their own priesthood independent. The insignia of the high priests of Mexico was a tuft, or tassel, of cotton hanging from the breast, and on the principal festivals they put on gorgeous garments, in which were figured the emblems of that god whose festival they were celebrating. The high priest of the Mixtecs on solemn festivals dressed in a tunic, in which were represented the principal events of their mythology, over it a white rochet, and over all a large cope; on his head he wore a plume of green feathers curiously woven, with some little figures of their gods; from his shoulders hung a cotton tassel, and another from his arm. After this supreme priestly dignity, the most considerable was that of the Mexicoteohuatzin, which was conferred by the high priests. His office was to watch over the observance of the rites and ceremonies and over the conduct of the priests who had charge of the seminaries, and to punish delinquent ministers. To fulfill all the obligations of so ample an office, he had two vicars, the Huitznahuateohuatzin and the Tepanteohuatzin. The latter was the superior general of the seminaries. The principal insignia of the Mexicoteohuatzin was a little bag of copal, which he always carried with him. The Tlatquimilolteuctli was the steward of the sanctuaries; the Ometochtli, the chief composer of the hymns that were sung at the festivals; the Epcoacuiltzin (*), the master of ceremonies; the Tlapixcatzin, the choirmaster, who not only ordered the music but supervised the singing and corrected the singers. Others were immediate superiors of the colleges of priests consecrated to various gods, whose names we omit, in order not to give the readers further trouble. VI. guardian or minister of God. In each ward of the capital (and the same is to be believed of the other large cities) there was a preeminent priest, who was like the parish priest of that district, to whom it belonged to order the functions and acts of religion of that ward. All these parish priests were subject to the Mexicoteohuatzin. Among the priests were apportioned all the ministries of their reli‐ § 15. gion. Some were sacrificers, and others diviners; these composers of The offices, the dress, and the life of hymns, and those singers. Of the singers, some sang at certain hours the priests. of the day, and others at certain hours of the night. Some had charge of the cleanliness of the temple, others of the adornment of the altars. To the priests belonged the instruction of youth, the ordering of the calendar and of the festivals, and the mythological paintings. Four times a day they incensed the idols, that is, at daybreak, at noon, at sunset, and at midnight. This last incensing was done by the priest whose turn it was, and the most distinguished ministers of the temple took part in it. To the Sun they made nine incensings every day, four at different hours of the day and five at those of the night. For the incensings they used for the most part copal or some other aromatic resin; but at certain festivals they made use of Chapopotli, or Jewish bitumen. The censers were ordinarily of clay; but there were also some of gold. Every day the priests (at least some of them) dyed the whole body with ink made from the soot of Ocotl, which is a species of very aromatic pine, and over this ink they painted themselves with ocher or with cinnabar, and every evening they bathed in the ponds that were within the enclosure of the temple. e: [p. 40] dressed all in black, like the common priests of the other nations of Bk. VI. the empire. They never cut their hair; so that many of them wore it so long that it reached to their legs. They wore it braided with thick cords of cotton and smeared with ink, forming of it a heavy mass no less inconvenient to carry than loathsome and horrible to behold. Besides the ordinary anointing with ink, they used another, extraordinary and more abominable, every time they went to make sacrifices on the summits of the mountains or in the dark caverns of the earth. They took a good quantity of poisonous insects, such as scorpions, spiders, and worms, and also small serpents, burned them in some brazier of the temple, and pounded the ashes in a mortar together with the soot of Ocotl, with tobacco, with the herb Ololiuhqui, and with some living insects. They presented this diabolical compound in small vessels to their gods, and then anointed the whole body with it. Thus anointed, they advanced intrepidly into any danger whatever, persuading themselves that neither the wild beasts of the woods nor the most noxious insects of the earth could do them any harm. They called it Teopatli, that is, divine medicine, and they esteemed it efficacious against several infirmities; and therefore they often brought the sick and children to the priests, to have them anointed with it. The boys who were brought up in the seminaries had the task of gathering such little animals; so that, accustomed from that age to such a trade, they lost all horror of it, making themselves familiar with such beasts. Nor did the priests make use of this ointment alone against illnesses, but they also employed superstitious and ridiculous blowings, and a certain water which they blessed in their fashion, especially the priests of the god Ixtlilton, which they made the sick drink. The priests practiced themselves in many fasts and austerities; they never got drunk; indeed, they rarely drank wine. The priests of

e: Tezcatzoncatl every day, after the end of the singing with which they celebrated their god, put on the ground [p. 41] a bundle of three hundred and three reeds, according to the number Bk. VI. of the singers, among which only one was pierced; each took his own at random, and he who drew the pierced reed was the only one who might taste the wine. During the whole time that they were employed in the service of the temple, they refrained from touching any woman other than their own wives; indeed they affected such composure and modesty that whenever they chanced upon some woman they fixed their eyes on the ground so as not to look at her. Any excess of incontinence on the part of the priests was rigorously punished. The priest who in Tehuacán was convicted of having violated chastity was handed over by the priests to the people, and by night they beat him to death with clubs. In Ichcatlan the high priest was obliged to remain always within the temple and to abstain from all dealings with any woman whatever; and if through his misfortune he failed in any of these obligations, he was mercilessly torn to pieces, and his bloody limbs were presented as an example to his successor. Those who through their sloth did not rise for the nocturnal ministries of the temple had boiling water poured over their heads, or else had their lips and ears pierced, and if they did not amend this or any other fault, they were plunged into the lake and dismissed from the temple at the festival which they held for the god of water in the sixth month. The priests lived for the most part in community under certain superiors, who watched over their conduct. Among the Mexicans the priesthood was not by its nature perpet‐ § 16.

e: The priestesses. ual. There were indeed some who consecrated themselves for their whole life to the ministry of the altars; but others only for some time, either in fulfillment of some vow of their fathers or out of particular devotion. Nor was the priesthood attached to the male sex, since there were women dedicated to the immediate service of the temples. They incensed the idols, tended the sacred fire, swept the court, prepared the oblation of food which was made daily, and presented it with their own hands to the idols; but they were wholly excluded from the ministry of sacrificing and from the preeminent [p. 42] dignities of the priesthood. Among these priestesses some were from Bk. VI. their most tender age consecrated by their parents to the service of the temple; others, again, by a particular vow which they made on occasion of some illness, or to obtain from the gods a good marriage or the prosperity of their families, served in that ministry a year or two.

e: The consecration of the former was done in this manner. As soon as the girl was born, her parents offered her to some god and informed the parish priest of that ward, and he the Tepanteohuatzin, who was, as we have already said, the superior general of the seminaries. After two months they carried her to the temple, and put into her little hands a small pomegranate and a little clay censer with a little copal, to signify her destination. Every month the visit to the temple and the oblation were repeated, together with that of some pieces of tree bark for the sacred fire. When the girl reached the age of five, her parents delivered her to the Tepanteohuatzin, and he placed her in some seminary of girls, where they were instructed in religion, in good morals, and in the occupations proper to their sex. Those, however, who entered to serve for some personal vow had their hair cut off before anything else. Both kinds lived in great modesty, silence, and retirement under their superiors, never communicating with men. Some rose about two hours before midnight, others at midnight, and others at daybreak, to stir up and keep alive the fire and to incense the idols; and although in this ministry they worked together with the priests, there was nevertheless some separation between them, the men forming one wing and the women another, these and those in sight of their superiors, so that no disorder might occur. Every morning they prepared the oblations of food to be presented to the idols, and swept the lower court of the temple, and the time which remained to them after these and other religious occupations they spent in spinning and in weaving fine cloths for the garments of the idols and for the adornment of the sanctuaries. About nothing was there such zeal as about the continence of these virgins. Any [p. 43] crime in this matter was unpardonable; if it remained entirely secret, the young offender sought to appease the wrath of the gods by fasts Bk. VI. and austerities, since she feared that in punishment of her fault her flesh would rot. When the virgin consecrated from her infancy to the worship of the gods reached seventeen or eighteen years, an age at which they were for the most part married, her parents sought a husband for her, and having found one they presented to the Tepanteohuatzin, on small round dishes curiously varnished, a certain number of quails, and a certain quantity of copal, flowers, and foods, with a well-composed speech in which they thanked him for the care and diligence employed in the education of their daughter and asked his permission to settle her in marriage. The Tepanteohuatzin granted it with another speech, exhorting the young woman to perseverance in virtue and to the fulfillment of the obligations of marriage. Among the different orders or congregations that there were, both § 17. Different orders of of men and of women consecrated to the worship of certain particu‐ religious. lar gods, that of Quetzalcoatl is worthy of mention. In the colleges or monasteries of both sexes dedicated to this imaginary god a singularly rigid and austere life was led. The dress of the inmates was quite modest; they bathed every day at midnight, and kept vigil until two hours before day, singing hymns to their god and exercising themselves in various austerities. They had liberty to go to the mountains at any hour of the day or night to shed their blood: which was granted them on account of the reputation of virtue in which they were held by all. The superiors of the monasteries took the same name of Quetzalcoatl, and had such authority that they visited no one, except the king when it was needed. These religious were consecrated to their order from infancy. The parents of the child invited the superior to a dinner, and he sent one of his subordinates. The latter carried the child to him, who, taking him in his arms, offered him with a prayer to Quetzalcoatl, and put around his neck a necklace, which he was to wear until the age of seven years. When F2 [p. 44] the child reached two years of age, the superior made a small incision Bk. VI. in his breast, which, like the necklace, was a token of his consecration. As soon as the boy was seven years old, he entered the monastery, after having listened to a long speech from his parents, in which they reminded him of the vow made by them to Quetzalcoatl, and exhorted him to the fulfillment of the same vow, to good morals, to submission to his prelate, and to praying to the gods for his parents and for the whole nation. This order was called Tlamacazcajotl, and the religious Tlamacazque. Another order was consecrated to Tezcatlipoca, which they called Telpochtiliztli, that is, the youth, since it was composed of young men and boys. They were likewise consecrated from infancy, almost with the same ceremonies as those of Quetzalcoatl; but they did not live in community, each living in his own house. They had in each ward of the city a superior who governed them, and a house where at sunset they gathered to dance and to sing the praises of their god. Both sexes took part in this dance; but without the slightest disorder, on account of the vigilance of the superiors and the severity with which offenders were punished. Among the Totonacs there was a kind of monks dedicated to their goddess Centeotl. They lived in great seclusion and austerity, and their life, superstition and vanity aside, was truly irreproachable. Into this monastery none entered but men of more than sixty years, who were widowers, removed from all intercourse with women, and of good life. There was a fixed number, and when one came to die they substituted another. These monks were held in such great esteem that they were consulted not only by common persons, but even by the highest nobility and by the high priest. They listened to the consultations sitting on their heels, with their eyes fixed on the ground, and their replies were received, like oracles, even by the Mexican kings themselves. They busied themselves in making historical paintings, which they delivered to the high priest, that he might communicate them to the people.

But the most considerable function of the priesthood, and the principal act of the religion of the Mexicans, were the sacrifices, which they Bk. VI. made now to obtain some grace from heaven, now to thank it for benefits received. This is a subject which we should very willingly § 18. omit, if the laws of History permitted it, in order to spare the readers Common    sacrifice of human victims. the displeasure which the description of so much abomination and cruelty will cause them; since although there has hardly been any nation in the world that has not used the same sacrifices, one will hardly find any that carried them to such an excess as we shall see in the Mexicans. We do not know what the sacrifices of the ancient Toltecs were. The Chichimecs remained a long time without using them, having at first neither idols, nor temples, nor priests, nor offering to their gods the Sun and the Moon anything other than herbs, flowers, fruits, and copal. The inhumanity of sacrificing human victims did not enter the minds of those nations until the Mexicans by their example removed from the minds of those people the first ideas impressed by nature. What they spread abroad about the origin of such barbarous sacrifices has already been set forth by us elsewhere; as also what is found in their histories concerning the first sacrifice of the four Xochimilca prisoners made by them when they were in Colhuacan. It is to be believed that in that time, when the Mexicans were isolated on the lake, and especially when they were under the dominion of the Tepanecs, the sacrifice of human victims must have been very rare, since they neither had prisoners nor could acquire slaves to sacrifice. But after they extended their dominions and multiplied their victories, sacrifices were frequent, and at certain festivals the victims were many. The sacrifices varied in number, place, and manner according to the circumstances of the festivals. For the most part the victims died with the breast opened; but others were drowned in the lake, others died of hunger shut up in the caverns of the mountains, and others finally in the gladiatorial sacrifice. The most common place was the temple, in whose upper court

VI. temple of Mexico was a green stone (presumably jasper), convex on top, about three feet high, equally wide, and more than five feet long. The ordinary ministers of the sacrifice were six priests, of whom the principal was the Topiltzin, whose dignity was preeminent and hereditary; but in each sacrifice he took the name of that god to whom it was made. For this function he put on a red garment, similar in form to the scapular, or pazienza, of our religious, and bordered with cotton tassels; on his head he wore a crown of green and yellow feathers, in his ears gold earrings and green gems (perhaps emeralds), and in his lower lip a pendant of turquoise gem. The other five ministers were dressed in white garments of the same form, but embroidered with black, and wore their hair tied up, their heads bound with strips of leather, their foreheads armed with little disks of paper painted in various colors, and the whole body dyed black. The pitiless ministers carried the victim, quite naked, to the upper court of the temple, and after pointing out to the bystanders the idol to whom the sacrifice was made, that all might adore it, stretched the victim out upon the altar destined for such a function: four priests held the feet and arms, and another held the head fast with an instrument of wood made in the manner of a coiled serpent, which he put on the neck; and because the altar was convex, as we have said above, the victim remained arched, with the breast and belly raised, and prevented from any movement. The inhuman Topiltzin then approached, and with a sharp knife of flint very swiftly opened the breast and tore out the heart, which, still palpitating, he offered to the Sun, and then threw at the feet of the idol; thereupon, taking it up again, he offered it to the same idol, and then burned it, keeping the ashes with veneration. If the idol was gigantic and hollow, they were accustomed to introduce the heart of the victim into its mouth with a golden ladle. The Zapotecs sacrificed men to the gods, women to the goddesses, and children to I know not what little deities. This was the most ordinary manner of sacrificing, with some circumstances of greater cruelty, as we shall see below; but they had other kinds of sacrifices, though rare. At the festival of Teteoinan the woman who represented this goddess was beheaded on the shoulders of another woman. At the festival of the arrival of the gods the victims were put to death in the fire. At one of the festivals which they made to Tlaloc they sacrificed to him two children, one of each sex, drowning them in a certain place in the lake. At another festival of the same god they bought three little boys of six or seven years, and, shutting them up with abominable inhumanity in a cave, left them to die of hunger and of horror. But the most celebrated sacrifice among the Mexicans was that § 19. which the Spaniards called, not without reason, the Gladiatorial. An officer or soldier of the Mexicans, furnished with better arms, went up to fight with him. Everyone can consider the efforts of that unfortunate man to escape death, and of the Mexican not to lose his reputation before the great crowd that gathered to such a spectacle. If the prisoner was vanquished, a priest called Chalchiuhtepehua came at once, and, dead or still alive, carried him to the other altar of the common sacrifices, and there opened his breast and tore out his heart, and the victor was applauded by the multitude and rewarded by the king with a certain military insignia.
