e: Concerning the number of victims that were sacrificed annually we can affirm nothing, since the opinions of the historians are too vari‐ Bk. VI. ous. (C) The number of twenty thousand, which is what is believed to come nearest the truth, if it comprises all the men sacrificed in the § 20. Number of sacrifices Mexican empire, does not seem to me excessive; but if it is restricted, uncertain. as some authors claim, to children alone, or to those sacrificed only on the mountain of Tepeyacac or in the capital, it seems to me altogether improbable. It is certain that there was no fixed number of sacrifices, but one always proportioned to the number of prisoners that were taken in war, to the needs of the state, and to the quality of the festivals, as was seen in the Dedication of the great temple of Mexico, in which the cruelty of the Mexicans passed beyond the bounds of probability. But it cannot be doubted that they were always many; for the conquests of the Mexicans were most rapid, and in their frequent wars they did not try so much to kill the enemy as to take them prisoner for the sacrifices. If to these victims are added the slaves who were bought for the same end, and several criminals who were condemned to expiate their crimes in sacrifice, we shall find a number much greater than that which Monsignor Las Casas claimed, too intent on clearing the Americans of all the excesses of which the (C) Bishop Zumárraga, the first bishop of Mexico, in a letter of his of June 12, 1531, written to the General Chapter of his Order assembled at Toulouse, says that in that capital alone 20,000 human victims were sacrificed annually. Some cited by Gómara affirmed that the number of those sacrificed reached 50,000. Acosta wrote that there was a day on which five thousand were sacrificed in various places of the Mexican empire, and some day on which twenty thousand were sacrificed. Others believed that on the mountain of Tepeyacac alone twenty thousand were sacrificed to the goddess Tonantzin. Torquemada, citing, though unfaithfully, the letter of Bishop Zumárraga, says that twenty thousand children were sacrificed annually. On the contrary, Monsignor Las Casas, in his refutation of the bloody book of Dr. Sepúlveda, restricts these sacrifices to so small a number that he scarcely leaves one to believe that there were ten, or at most a hundred. The Mexicans were accustomed, at their festivals, to dress the victim in the same garb and the same insignia as the god to whom he was to be sacrificed, and thus dressed he went about the whole city asking alms for the temple, accompanied by a guard of soldiers so that he should not escape. If by chance he fled, the corporal of the guard was put in his place as a penalty for his negligence. They were also accustomed to feed the victims well and to fatten them, just as we fatten several kinds of animals. The religion of the Mexicans was not confined to sacrifices of this kind: they made them also of various species of animals. They sacrificed quail and sparrow hawks to Huitzilopochtli, and hares, rabbits, deer, and coyotes to Mixcoatl. To the Sun they offered quail daily. Every day, when the Sun was about to rise, several priests stood in the upper court of the temple, with their faces turned to the east and each with a quail in his hand, and at the rising of that planet they saluted it with music, and cutting off the heads of the quails, offered them to it. This sacrifice was followed by the censing, accompanied by a great din of musical instruments. They also offered to their gods, in acknowledgment of their dominion, various species of plants, flowers, gems, resins, and other insensible things. To Tlaloc and Coatlicue they offered the first fruits of flowers, and to Centeotl those of maize. The oblations of bread, of various pastes, and of cooked food which they made to their gods were so abundant that they sufficed to satisfy all the ministers of the temple. The priests in the temple, the fathers of families in their houses, and the judges in their tribunals used to burn incense toward the four cardinal winds every time they had to pronounce sentence on any grave case, whether civil or criminal. But the censing among the Mexicans and the other nations of Anahuac was not only a religious act toward their deities, but also a merely civil homage toward the lords and the ambassadors. The cruelty and the superstition of the Mexicans were imitated by all the nations conquered by them or neighboring on their empire, with no other difference than that among these nations the number of such abominable sacrifices was smaller, and that certain particular circumstances attended them. The Tlaxcalans, at one of their festivals, fastened a prisoner to a high cross and shot him with arrows, and at another festival beat to death with clubs another prisoner bound to a low cross. Equally famous were the inhuman and frightful sacrifices which § 21. the people of Cuauhtitlan celebrated every four years to the god of Inhuman sacrifices at Cuauhtitlan. fire. One day before the festival they planted six very tall trees in the lower court of the temple, sacrificed two female slaves, and then flayed them and took the bones out of their thighs. The next day two distinguished priests dressed themselves in the blood-stained skins, and taking those bones in their hands, began to descend the steps of the temple at a solemn pace, but together with frightful howls. The people, crowded at the foot of the temple, said in a loud voice: Behold, our gods are now coming. As soon as they reached the lower court, they began, to the sound of musical instruments, a dance which lasted almost the whole day. Meanwhile the people went on sacrificing so great a number of quail that at times they reached eight thousand. Since these men were so pitiless toward others, it is no wonder that they were inhuman even toward themselves. The Mexicans, accustomed to the bloody sacrifices of their prisoners, became equally § 22. lavish of their own blood, not judging the great quantity which their Austerities and fasts of the Mexicans. victims shed to be enough to slake the diabolical thirst of their gods. The austerities which they practiced, whether in penance for their offenses or in preparation for their festivals, cannot be read of without a shudder. They maltreated their flesh as if it were insensible, and poured out their blood with as much prodigality as if it were a superfluous fluid of the body. The shedding of blood was frequent, and daily, among certain priests, and to these they gave the name Tlamacazqui. They pricked themselves with the very sharp thorns of the maguei, and pierced various parts of the body, especially the ears, the lips, the tongue, and the flesh of the legs and arms. Through the holes which they made with these thorns they put little pieces of cane, at first slender, and as their penance advanced ever thicker. The blood that came out they gathered carefully in branches of the plant Acxojatl. The number of canes to be used each time was for the most part fixed; after they had served once, they were kept as a testimony of their penance. Besides these and other austerities, of which we shall make mention below, vigils and fasts were very frequent among the Mexicans. There was hardly a festival for which they did not prepare with fasts of more or fewer days, according to what their Ritual prescribed. Their fast, so far as we can deduce from their history, consisted in abstaining from meat and from wine, and in eating only once a day: which some did at midday, others afterward, and many remained without taking anything until evening. They generally accompanied the fast with vigil and with the shedding of blood, and during that time access to any woman, even to their own wives, was not permitted them. Among the fasts there were some general ones, which the whole people was bound to observe, such as that of five days which preceded the festival of Mixcoatl, in which even the children were included, that of four days before the festival of Tezcatlipoca, and, as we suspect, that also which was made to the Sun. (F) For this fast the king withdrew to a certain place in the temple, where he kept vigil and shed blood according to the custom of his nation. Other fasts bound only certain individuals, such as that which the owners of the victims kept on the day before their sacrifice. e: (F) The fast which was made to the Sun was called Netonatiuhzahualo, or Netonatiuhzahualiztli. Dr. Hernández says that it was made every two hundred or three hundred days. We suspect that it fell on the day I Olin, which came around every two hundred and sixty days. [p. 54] with many rooms, where they withdrew to perform such a penance. Bk. VI. At one of the festivals all those who held any public office, after serving through the day in their office, went in the evening to that retreat for the same purpose. In the third month the Tlamacazqui, or penitents, kept vigil every night, and in the fourth month they were accompanied in the vigil by the nobility. In the Mixteca, where there were many monasteries, before the firstborn sons of the lords were put in possession of their states, they were subjected for an entire year to a rigorous penance. They conducted the firstborn with a great retinue to a monastery, where, stripping him of his garments, they clothed him in rags smeared with olli, that is, elastic resin, rubbed his face, belly, and back with certain stinking herbs, and handed him a lancet of itztli, that he might draw blood. They constrained him there to a rigid abstinence, subjected him to the hardest labors, and punished him severely for any fault whatsoever. When the year was completed he was led back to his house with great pomp and with music, after four maidens had washed and cleansed him with scented waters. In the principal temple of Tehuacán there lived four priests famous for their austere life. Their dress was that of poor people: their dinner was reduced to a loaf of maize of about two ounces and a vessel of atolli, that is, gruel of the same grain. Every night two of them kept vigil, employing all that time in singing hymns to their gods, in offering them incense, which they did four times in the course of the night, and in sprinkling their own blood on the braziers of the temple. The fast was continuous throughout the four years that they remained in that life, except on the day of festival which came every month, on which they might eat as much as they wished; but for every festival they prepared themselves with the usual austerities, piercing their ears with maguei thorns and passing through the holes as many as sixty pieces of cane of different thicknesses in the manner already described.

e: After four years four other priests took their places to lead such a life; and if before reaching that term any of them died, another was sub‐ Bk. VI. stituted, so that the number should never fall short. So great was the fame of these priests that they were venerated even by the kings of Mexico themselves; but woe to him who, to his misfortune, violated continence; for if after a diligent inquiry the crime was found to be true, he was put to death by clubbing, his corpse burned, and the ashes scattered to the wind. There was seen at times, on the occasion of some public calamity, an extraordinary fast made by the high priests of the Mexicans. To carry it out the high priest withdrew to a wood, where he had a hut made, covered with ever-green boughs, since where the first ones began to dry up, other new ones were put in their place. Shut up in this hut, deprived of all communication with men, and without any other food than raw maize and water, he spent nine or ten months, and sometimes a year, in continual prayer and frequent shedding of blood. This fast was not obligatory, nor did all the high priests make it; nor did he who undertook it make it more than once in his whole life; and to tell the truth, it is not likely that he would be left with strength to repeat it, in case he survived so rigorous and long an abstinence. § 23. Also very famous in that country was the fast of the Tlaxcalans in Celebrated penance the divine year, in which they held a most solemn festival to their god of the Tlaxcalans. Camaxtle. e: [p. 56] were usually more than two hundred, on the very high mount Bk. VI. Matlalcueye, on whose summit there was a sanctuary dedicated to the goddess of water. The Achcauhtli went up to the summit to make his oblation of gems, of precious feathers, and of copal, and the others remained halfway up the ascent, praying their goddess to give them strength and courage for the penance. They then came down from the mountain, and had knives of itztli made for themselves, and a great quantity of little rods of different thicknesses. The workmen who made these instruments had to fast five days before making them, and if any knife or little rod broke, it was reckoned a bad sign, and was attributed to the fast having been broken by some artisan. Then began that of the Tlamacazqui, which lasted no less than a hundred and sixty days. On the first day they made a hole in the tongue, to introduce the little rods, and although the pain they felt was great, and the blood they shed still greater, they forced themselves to intone hymns to their god, repeating this cruel operation every twenty days. When the first eighty days of the priests’ fast had passed, the general fast of the people began and continued for as long again, from which not even the foremost leaders of the republic were exempt. No one was permitted during all that time to bathe, or to eat chili pepper, with which they were wont to season almost all their food. To such excesses of cruelty were those nations carried by their fanaticism. § 24. e: much as the account of the festivals which they held for their gods, and of the rites which they observed in them; but before entering upon this subject, it is necessary to give an account of the division they made of time, and of the method they had in counting the days, the months, the years, and the centuries. What we are about to say on such a subject has been investigated at great length and verified by men well informed, and worthy in every respect of the greatest credence, who applied themselves with the utmost zeal to this study, [p. 57] examined the ancient paintings with diligence; and they informed Bk. VI. themselves from the best-instructed Mexicans and Acolhuas. We profess ourselves particularly indebted for these lights to the apostolic religious Motolinía and Sahagún (from whose writings Torquemada took whatever good there is in him), and to the most learned Mexican Don Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora, whose opinions we have found true through the examination which we have made of several Mexican paintings in which the months, the years, and the centuries are clearly represented by their own figures. The Mexicans, the Acolhuas, and all the other nations of Anahuac distinguished four different ages, with as many Suns. The first, Atonatiuh, that is, Sun, or age, of water, began with the creation of the world, and continued until the time when, together with the first Sun, nearly all men perished in a general inundation. The second, Tlaltonatiuh, age of earth, from the general inundation to the ruin of the giants and the great earthquakes, with which the second Sun likewise ended. The third, Ehecatonatiuh, age of air, from the destruction of the giants to the great whirlwinds, by which all men perished together with the third Sun. The fourth, Tletonatiuh, age of fire, from the last restoration of the human race, as we have said in the Mythology, until the fourth sun and the earth shall be destroyed by fire. This age they believed would end at the close of some one of their centuries, and this seems to have been the cause of the noisy festivals which they held to the god of fire at the beginning of every century, as in thanksgiving for having restrained his voracity and postponed the end of the world.

e: Concerning the reckoning of the century, of the years, and of the months, the Mexicans and the other civilized nations kept to the same method as the ancient Toltecs. Their century consisted of fifty-two years, divided into four periods of thirteen years each, and of two centuries was composed an age, called by them Huehuetiliztli, that is, old age, of a hundred and four [p. 58] years. (G) To the end of the century they gave the name Toxiuhmolpia, Bk. VI. which means Binding of our years, because in it the two centuries were joined to form an age. The years had four names, which were Tochtli, Rabbit, Acatl, Cane, Tecpatl, Flint, and Calli, House, and with these, with different numbers, the century was composed. The first year of the century was I Rabbit, the second II Cane, the third III Flint, the fourth IV House, the fifth V Rabbit, and so on to the thirteenth year, which was XIII Rabbit, with which the first period ended. They began the second with I Cane, and continued with II Flint, III House, IV Rabbit, until completing it with XIII Cane. Likewise the third period began with I Flint, and ended in XIII Flint, and the fourth began with I House, and ended together with the century in XIII House: so that, there being four names and thirteen numbers, there was no year that could be confused with any other. (H) This can be more easily understood from the table of the century which we shall give below. The Mexican year consisted, like ours, of three hundred sixty-five days; for although it was composed of eighteen months, each of twenty days, which make only three hundred sixty, they added also after the last month five days, called by them Nemontemi, that is, useless; because in them they did nothing but visit one another. The year I Rabbit, the first of their century, began on February (G) Some authors give to the age, or old age, the name of century, and that of half century to the century; but this matters little, provided that the method of counting the years and the division of time are not altered in substance. (H) The Chevalier Boturini asserts, against the common opinion of the authors, that not all the centuries began with I Rabbit, but sometimes with it, sometimes with I Cane, or I Flint, or I House. He is mistaken here too; for both from the older authors who were better informed and from the paintings which I myself have examined it is established for us that the Mexican century always began with I Rabbit. That author says moreover that in four centuries the same name or character with the same number was never repeated; but how is it possible that it should not be repeated in the course of 208 years, when the characters are no more than four, nor the numbers more than thirteen, as he himself confesses?

But when the century was ended, the year began again on February 26, as we shall say below. The names which they gave to their months were taken both from the operations and from the festivals which they carried on in them, and from the accidents of the season in which they fell. The cause of such a variety was without doubt the same diversity that results from our leap years, of which those authors perhaps did not take notice. The editors of the edition of Cortés’s Letters made in Mexico in 1770 put as the first month that of Atemoztli, which in our table is the sixteenth. But Motolinía, whose authority is of greater weight, puts, as we do, the Atlacahualco first, and with him agree Torquemada, Vetancurt, and Martín de León, Dominican. In order not to weary readers, we pass over the weighty reasons which we have for believing this opinion true.

Although the signs, or characters, signified by these names were distributed in the aforesaid order for the twenty days, nevertheless in counting them no regard was had to the division of the months, nor to that of the years, but to certain periods of thirteen days (like those of thirteen years in the century), which ran on without interruption even after the month, or the year, was ended. The first day of the century was I Cipactli, the second II Ehecatl, or wind, the third III Calli, or house, and so on to the thirteenth, which was XIII Acatl, or cane. The 14th day began another period, counting I Ocelotl (tiger), II Quauhtli (eagle), etc., until the month was completed with VII Xochitl (flower), and in the second month they continued counting VIII Cipactli, IX Ehecatl, etc. Twenty of these periods made in thirteen months a cycle of 260 days, and in all this time the same sign or character was not repeated with the same number, as can be seen in the Calendar which we shall give below. On the first day of the fourteenth month another cycle began, with the same order of characters and the same number of periods as the first. If the year did not have, beyond the eighteen months, the five days Nemontemi, or if in these days the periods were not continued, the first day of the second (L) Cozcaquauhtli is the name of a bird described by us in the first book. Xochitl; but since the period of thirteen days was continued, as in fact it was continued through the Nemontemi days, the signs or characters accordingly changed place, and the sign Miquiztli, which in all the months of the first year occupied the sixth place, occupies the first in the second year, and on the contrary the sign Cipactli, which in the first year had occupied the first place, has the sixteenth in the second year. To know what the sign of the first day of any year whatever must be, there is this general rule. Every year Tochtli begins with Cipactli, every year Acatl with Miquiztli, every year Tecpatl with Ozomatli, and every year Calli with Cozcaquauhtli, always giving to the sign of the day the same number as that of the year: so that just as the year I Tochtli has for its first day I Cipactli, so II Acatl has II Miquiztli, III Tecpatl has III Ozomatli, IV Calli has IV Cozcaquauhtli, etc. (M) From what we have said, the particular esteem is evident in which the number thirteen was held among the Mexicans. Of thirteen years were the four periods of which the century was composed; of thirteen months was their cycle of 260 days, and of thirteen days the periods of which we have made mention. The reason for such an esteem was, according to Dr. Sigüenza, that this was the number of their greater gods. The number four seems to have been somewhat less prized by them. Just as they counted in their century four periods of thirteen years, so they counted thirteen periods of four years, and at the end of each of these periods they held extraordinary festivals. We have already mentioned elsewhere both the fast of four months and the Nappapohuallatolli, or general audience, to be held every four months. (M) The Chevalier Boturini says that the year of the Rabbit always began on the day of the Rabbit, the year of the Cane on the day of the Cane, etc., and never on the days indicated by us; but we must place greater faith in Sigüenza, who was much better instructed than Boturini in Mexican antiquities. The system of this Chevalier is fantastic, and full of contradictions.

As for the civil government, they divided the month into four peri‐ Bk. VI. ods of five days, and on a fixed day of each period the fair, or great market, was held; but because in political matters too they were governed by principles of religion, this fair was held in the capital on the days of the Rabbit, of the Cane, of the Flint, and of the House, which were their favorite signs. The Mexican year consisted of 73 periods of thirteen days, and the century of 73 periods of thirteen months, or cycles of 260 days. It cannot be doubted that the Mexican, or Toltec, system concern‐ § 26. e: Mexican antiquities, is that, knowing the excess of a few hours of the solar year over the civil, they made use of intercalary days to equalize them; but with this difference with respect to the method established by Julius Caesar in the Roman calendar, that they did not insert one day every four years, but thirteen days (using for this too the number thirteen) every fifty-two years: which for regulating time amounts to the same. At the close of the century they broke, as we shall say elsewhere, all their crockery, fearing that with it the fourth age, the Sun, and the whole world would also come to an end, and on the last night they performed the famous ceremony of the new fire. Once by means of the new fire they had made themselves secure, as they believed, of a new century granted them by the gods, they employed the thirteen following days in providing themselves with new crockery, in making new garments, in repairing the temples and the houses, and in making all the preparations for the great festivals of the new century. These thirteen days were the intercalary days, marked in their paintings with blue dots: they did not count them in the century already completed, nor in the following one, nor did they continue in them the periods of days, which proceeded [p. 63] always numbering from the first to the last day of the century. When the intercalary days had passed, they began the new century with the Bk. VI. year I Tochtli and with the day I Cipactli, on the 26th of our February, as at the beginning of the preceding century. I would not dare to publish such anecdotes had I not assured myself by the most weighty testimony of Dr. Sigüenza, who, besides his great erudition, his critical sense, and his truthfulness, was the man who employed the greatest diligence to clarify these points, now consulting the best-instructed Mexicans and Texcocans, now studying their histories and paintings. The Chevalier Boturini affirms that more than a hundred years before the common era of Christianity the Toltecs corrected their calendar, adding, as we do, one day every four years, and that this was in use for some centuries, until the Mexicans established the method already indicated: that the cause of the new method was the coincidence on one day of two festivals, the one movable, of Tezcatlipoca, and the other fixed, of Huitzilopochtli, and that the Colhuas celebrated the latter and omitted the former: whereupon Tezcatlipoca, angered, predicted that in time the monarchy of Colhuacan would come to an end, the worship of the ancient gods would cease, and the Colhuas would be left subject to the worship of a single deity never seen or understood, and to the dominion of certain strangers who would come from distant countries: that the kings of Mexico, aware of this prediction, ordained that whenever two festivals fell on the same day, the principal festival should be celebrated on that day and the other on the day after, and that the day usually added every four years should then be omitted, and that afterward, when the century was completed, the thirteen omitted days should be added. But I do not wish to trust this account. Two things will indeed seem strange in the system of the Mexicans: the one, that they did not regulate their months by the course of the Moon; the other, that no particular character is to be found which distinguished one century from another. Divination.  of the  years, served the Mexicans for their superstitious prognostications, predicting either the good or the evil fortune of children from the sign under which they were born, and the happiness or misfortune of marriages, of wars, and of every other thing from the day on which they were undertaken or carried out; and for this reason they considered not only the proper character of every day and of every year, but also the dominant one in every period of days or of years; since the first sign or character of any period was dominant throughout it. Of the merchants we know that when they wished to undertake any journey, they took care to begin it on some day of the period in which the sign Coatl (serpent) was dominant, and thereby promised themselves good fortune in their trade. Those who were born under the sign Quauhtli (eagle) were believed destined to be scoffers and sharp-tongued, if male; if female, talkative and shameless. The concurrence of the year and of the day of the Rabbit was esteemed the most fortunate. § 28. In Tlaxcala there were dances both of the nobles and of the commoners, all clothed in animal skins and adorned with gold and silver. In the third month, which began on April 7, the second festival of Tlaloc was celebrated with the sacrifice of some children. The skins of the victims sacrificed to Xipe in the preceding month were carried in procession to a temple called Yopico, which was within the enclosure of the great temple, and deposited in a cave that was there. In this same month the Xochimanqui, that is, those who dealt in flowers, celebrated the festival of their goddess Coatlicue, and presented to her little bunches of flowers curiously arranged. Before this oblation was made, no one was permitted to smell those flowers. Every night of this month the ministers of the temples kept watch, and for this reason made great fires; whence the month had the name Tozoztontli, or little vigil. The fourth month was called Hueitozoztli, or great vigil; because in it not only the priests kept watch, as in the preceding one, but also the nobility and the commoners. Ten days before, a priest was dressed in the same garb, and adorned with the same insignia as that god, and went out of the temple with a little bunch of flowers in his hand and a little clay flute, which gave out a sound far too shrill. Turning his face first toward the east, and then toward the other three cardinal winds, he blew the flute loudly, and then, taking up a little dust from the ground with one finger, carried it to his mouth and swallowed it. On hearing the sound of the flute all knelt down. The criminals, thrown into extraordinary terror and consternation, begged that god with tears to grant them forgiveness of their faults, and not to permit them to be discovered to men. The men of war asked him for courage and strength against the enemies of the nation, great victories, and abundance of prisoners for the sacrifices; and all the rest of the people, performing that same ceremony of taking and eating the dust, implored with bitter weeping the clemency of the gods. The sound of the flute was repeated in the same manner on all those days preceding the festival. One day before, the lords brought a new garment to the idol, which the priests put on it at once, and they kept the old one like a relic in some chest of the temple, adorned the idol with particular insignia of gold, and with beautiful [p. 69] feathers, and raised the curtain which always covered the door of the Sanctuary, so that that image of their god might be seen and adored Bk. VI. by all who stood around. When the day of the festival had come, the people gathered in the lower court of the temple. Some priests, painted black and dressed in the same garment as the idol, carried it down on a litter, which the young men and the virgins of the temple girded with thick ropes composed of many strings of toasted maize, and they put one of these strings on the idol’s neck, and a garland on its head. This rope, a symbol of the dryness which they sought to avoid, was called Toxcatl, which name was given also to the month on account of such a ceremony. All the young men and the virgins of the temple, as well as the grandees of the court, wore similar strings on their necks and in their hands. Then a procession was formed through the lower court of the temple, where flowers and fragrant herbs were strewn: two priests incensed the idol, which others carried on their shoulders. Meanwhile the people stayed on their knees, striking their backs with thick, knotted cords. When the procession was over, and the discipline with it, they carried the idol back to its altar, and made it copious oblations of gold, gems, flowers, feathers, animals, and foods, which the virgins prepared, and other women, who by a particular vow went that day to serve at the temple. These foods were carried in procession by the same virgins, led by a distinguished priest dressed in a strange garment, and then the young men carried them to the dwellings of the priests, for whom they were destined. The sacrifice of the victim representing the god Tezcatlipoca was then performed. This was a young man, the most handsome and best formed of all the prisoners. They chose him a year in advance, and throughout this time he went dressed in the garb of that idol: he walked freely about the city, but always escorted by a good guard, and was adored by all as the living image of that supreme deity. e: [p. 70] him all the pleasures of life. On the day of the festival they conducted Bk. VI. him with a great retinue to the temple of Tezcatlipoca; but before arriving, they dismissed his wives. He accompanied the idol in the procession, and when the hour of the sacrifice came, they stretched him on the altar; and the high priest with great reverence opened his breast and tore out his heart. His body was not, like those of the other victims, thrown down the steps, but was carried in the arms of the priests, and beheaded at the foot of the temple: his head was strung on the Tzompantli, where were the skulls of the victims sacrificed to Tezcatlipoca, and his legs and arms, cooked and seasoned, were served at the tables of the lords. After the sacrifice there was a great dance of the young collegians and of the nobles, who took part in the festival. At sunset the virgins of the temple made a new oblation of bread kneaded with honey. This bread, together with I know not what other things, was set before the altar of Tezcatlipoca, and was destined as the prize of the young men who, in the race they ran up the steps of the temple, remained victors; who were also rewarded with a garment, and celebrated no less by the priests than by the people looking on. The festival was brought to an end by dismissing from the seminaries the young men and the virgins who were by now of an age suited to marriage. The young men who remained mocked them with satirical and burlesque sayings, and threw at them knots of rushes and other plants, reproaching them for abandoning the service of the gods for the pleasures of marriage: which was permitted them by the priests, as an outlet for youth. In the same fifth month the first festival of Huitzilopochtli was § 32. Great festival of celebrated. The priests made a great statue of this god, of the stature Huitzilopochtli. of an ordinary man. They made its flesh of the dough of the Tzohualli, a certain edible seed, and its bones of the wood Mizquitl, or acacia; they clothed it in cloths of cotton and of maguei, and a mantle of feathers: they set on its head a little parasol of paper adorned with beautiful feathers, and above it a small bloodstained knife of flint, [p. 71] on its breast a gold plate, and on its garment were seen several figures Bk. VI. representing the bones of the dead, and the image of a man torn to pieces: by which they intended to signify either the power of this god in battles, or the terrible vengeance which, according to their mythology, he took on those who conspired against the honor and the life of his mother. They placed this statue on a litter built upon four wooden serpents, which four principal officers of the Mexican army carried from the place where the statue was made as far as the altar where it was set up. Several young men, forming a circle, and joining together by means of certain arrows which they held in their hands, some by the shaft and others by the point, carried before the litter a piece of paper more than fifteen perches long, on which were probably painted the glorious deeds of that wicked deity, which they went along singing to the sound of musical instruments. When the day of the festival had come, a great sacrifice of quails was made in the morning, whose heads were torn off and which they then threw at the foot of the altar. The first to make such a sacrifice was the king, then the priests, and finally the people. Of so great a multitude of quails a part was seasoned for the tables of the king and of the priests, and the rest was kept for another time. All those who attended the festival carried clay censers, and a certain quantity of bitumen of Judea, to burn and with it to incense their god, and all the coals that were used there were then put into a great brazier called by them Tlexictli. On account of such a ceremony they called this festival the incensing of Huitzilopochtli. The dance of the virgins and of the priests followed immediately. The virgins wore their faces painted, their arms adorned with red feathers, on their heads garlands made of strings of toasted maize, and in their hands certain split canes with little flags of cotton or of paper. The priests wore their faces painted black, their foreheads armed with little paper disks, and their lips smeared with honey: they covered their private parts

The musical instruments, which in other dances occupied the center, were in this one kept outside and hidden, in such a way that, while the sound was heard, the musicians were not seen. A year in advance there was chosen, together with the victim of Tezcatlipoca, the prisoner who was to be sacrificed to Huitzilopochtli, to whom they gave the name of Ixteocale, which means wise lord of heaven. Both went about together throughout the year; but with this difference, that they adored the victim of Tezcatlipoca, not that of Huitzilopochtli. When the day of the festival came, they dressed the prisoner in a curious garment of painted paper, and put on his head a miter made of eagle feathers with a plume at the top. On his back he carried a small net, and over it a little bag, and in this attire he mingled in the dance of the courtiers.

e: The most singular thing about this prisoner was that, although he was to die that day, the hour of the sacrifice was nevertheless in his own power. Whenever he pleased, he presented himself to the priests, in whose arms, not on the altar, the sacrificer broke open his breast and tore out his heart. When the sacrifice was ended, the priests began a great dance, which lasted all the rest of the day with some intervals, which they made in order to repeat the incensing. In this same festival the priests made a slight cut in the chest and belly of all the children of both sexes born within the preceding year. This was the sign, or mark, by which the Mexican nation recognized itself as specially consecrated to the worship of their [p. 73] tutelary god; and this is also the reason why several authors came to Bk. VI. believe the rite of circumcision established among the Mexicans. (P) But perhaps the Yucatecans and the Totonacs practiced it, not the Mexicans, nor any other nation of the empire. (P) Father Acosta says that “the Mexicans sacrificed on their children’s ears and genital member, in which way they somewhat imitated the circumcision of the Jews.” But if this author speaks of the true Mexicans, that is, the descendants of the ancient Aztecs who founded the city of Mexico, whose history we are writing, it is absolutely false; for after the most diligent inquiry not the slightest vestige of such a rite could be found among them. If he speaks of the Totonacs, who, having been subjects of the kings of Mexico, are called Mexicans by several authors, it is true that they made such a cut on their children. The foul and biting author of the work entitled Recherches philosophiques sur les Américains adopts Father Acosta’s account, and makes a long discourse on the origin of circumcision, which he believes to have been invented by the Egyptians or the Ethiopians in order to preserve themselves, as he says, from the worms that breed in the uncircumcised of the torrid zone. He asserts that the Hebrews learned it from the Egyptians, and that, being at the beginning nothing but a physical remedy, it was afterwards raised by fanaticism to the status of a religious ceremony. He wishes furthermore to make us believe that the heat of the torrid zone is the cause of such a malady, and that to rid themselves of it the Mexicans and other nations of America used circumcision. But leaving aside the falsity of his principles, his want of respect for the holy books, and his diligence in dwelling minutely on any subject that has some affinity with obscene pleasures, to confine myself to what belongs to my history, I declare that no vestige of circumcision has ever been found either among the Mexicans or among the nations subject to them, except among the Totonacs, nor have I ever had knowledge of such a disease of worms in those countries, though all are situated under the torrid zone, having often visited every sort of patient for more than thirteen years. Besides, if heat is the cause of such a disease, it ought to be more common in that author’s native country than in the inland regions of Mexico, since in these the heat is much more temperate. Nor was the error of M. Mallet, cited by the same author, any less: in his dissertation on circumcision, inserted in the Encyclopédie, not having understood Acosta’s expressions, he believed that the Mexicans entirely cut off the ears and the genital member of all their infants; whence, astonished, he asks whether many could remain alive after so cruel an operation. But if I believed what M. Mallet believed, I should rather ask how there came to be any Mexicans in the world. So that no one, then, may stumble in reading the ancient Spanish historians of America, one must know that where they say that the Mexicans, or other nations, sacrificed the tongue, the ears, or another member of the body, they mean nothing else than that those people made themselves some incision in those members and drew blood from them.

e: In the sixth month, which began on June 6, the third festival of Bk. VI. Tlaloc was celebrated. They carefully strewed the temple with rushes § 33. from the lake of Citlaltepec. The priests who went to fetch them Festivals of months 6, 7, 8, and 9. committed with impunity along the road many hostilities against the travelers whom they met, stripping them of whatever they carried, sometimes to the point of leaving them quite naked, and beating them if they offered any resistance. Such was the impunity of those priests turned brigands that they not only stripped commoners but even took the royal tributes from the collectors, if they happened to fall in with them, neither could private persons lodge a complaint against them, nor the king punish them for such excesses. On the day of the festival all ate a certain porridge called by them Etzalli, whence the month took the name of Etzalcualiztli. They carried to the temple a great quantity of painted paper and of elastic resin, and with it they anointed both the paper and the cheeks of the idols. After so ridiculous a ceremony they sacrificed several prisoners dressed in the same garb as Tlaloc and his companions, and, to complete their cruelty, the priests, accompanied by a great multitude of people, went in boats to a place in the lake where there was a whirlpool, and there they sacrificed to their gods two children of both sexes by drowning them, and with them also the hearts of the prisoners sacrificed at that festival, to obtain from the gods the rain necessary for their fields. On this same occasion they deprived of the priesthood those ministers of the temple who in the course of that year had been negligent in their ministry, or had been caught in some grave crime not otherwise deserving capital punishment, and punished them with a penalty resembling the jest which sailors play on those voyagers who cross the line for the first time; but more severe, since from the repeated immersions in the water they were left so battered that it was necessary to carry them to their houses to be cared for. e: Huixtocihuatl, goddess of salt, was celebrated. A day before the festival there was a great dance of women, who danced in a circle holding on to certain cords of various flowers, [p. 75] and with garlands of wormwood on their heads. In the center of the circle there was a woman prisoner dressed in the same garb as the Bk. VI. idol of that goddess. They accompanied the dance with singing, and in both they were led by two old and authoritative priests. The dance continued all night; and the following morning that of the priests began, and lasted all day, interrupted at times by the sacrifices of the prisoners. The priests danced decently dressed, and carrying in their hands those beautiful yellow flowers which the Mexicans called Cempoalxochitl, and several Europeans Indian carnations. At sunset the sacrifice of the woman prisoner was made, and the festival ended with great banquets. This whole month was one of great rejoicing for the Mexicans. In it they dressed in the best garments they had: dances and amusements in the gardens were frequent: the poems which they sang were all of love, or of other pleasant subjects. The commoners went hunting in the mountains, and the nobles did military exercises, now in the countryside, now on the lake in boats. These rejoicings of the nobility gave this month the name of Tecuilhuitl, festival of the lords, or of Tecuilhuitontli, little festival of the lords, since it was truly small in comparison with that of the following month. In the eighth month, which began on July 16, they held a solemn festival to the goddess Centeotl under the name of Xilonen; for, as we have already noted elsewhere, they changed her name according to the state of the maize. At this festival they called her Xilonen; because the ear of maize, when the grain is still tender, is called xilotl. The festival lasted eight days, during which there was almost continual dancing in the temple of that goddess. The king and the lords gave food and drink to the people on such days. The people were set in rows in the lower court of the temple, and there they were handed the Chianpinolli, which was a certain drink among the most usual among them, the tamalli, that is, certain pastes of maize made in the shape of ravioli, and other foods, of which we shall speak elsewhere. e: K2 [p. 76] invited one another in turn to dinner, and presented one another with Bk. VI. gold, silver, beautiful feathers, and rare animals. They sang the glorious deeds of their ancestors, and boasted of the nobility and antiquity of their houses. At sunset, after the people’s dinner was over, the priests held their dance, which lasted four hours, and for this reason there was a great illumination in the temple. The last day was the dance of the nobles and of the military men, among whom also danced a woman prisoner, who represented that goddess, and after the dance was sacrificed together with other prisoners. Thus both the festival and the month had the name of Hueitecuilhuitl, that is, The great festival of the lords. In the ninth month, the beginning of which was on August 5, the second festival of Huitzilopochtli was celebrated, in which, besides the ordinary ceremonies, they adorned with flowers all the idols, not only those that were venerated in the temples, but even those which they had in their own houses out of private devotion: whence the month was called Tlaxochimaco. The night preceding the festival was spent in preparing the food which they ate with the greatest rejoicing the next day. The nobles of both sexes danced with their arms laid on one another’s shoulders. This dance, which lasted until evening, ended with the sacrifice of some prisoners. Likewise with sacrifices was celebrated in this month the festival of Yacatecuhtli, god of trade. In the tenth month, which began on August 25, the festival of § 34. Xiuhtecuhtli, god of fire, was held. In the preceding month the Festivals of months 10, 11, 12, and 13.

e: (*) The Jauhtli is a plant whose stalk is a cubit long, its leaves similar to those of the willow, but toothed, its flowers yellow, and its root slender. Both the flowers and the other parts of the plant have the same smell and taste as anise. It is very useful in medicine, and the Mexican physicians used it against several diseases; but they also made use of it for certain superstitious purposes. Huitzilopochtli in memory of the inhuman sacrifice which their ancestors made of the princess of Colhuacan; but before presenting it they sacrificed in the common manner four prisoners, to signify, as is to be believed, the four Xochimilcas sacrificed at the time of their captivity in Colhuacan. In this month the review of the troops was held, and the young men were enrolled who were destined for the profession of arms, and who in the future were to go to war whenever there should be need. All, both nobles and commoners, swept the temples, whence this month had the name of Ochpaniztli, which means Sweeping. The streets were cleaned and repaired, and the aqueducts and the houses were mended, works in which superstitious rites were performed. In the twelfth month, which began on October 4, the festival of the Arrival of the Gods was celebrated, and that is what the name Teotleco means, which they gave both to the month and to the festival. On the 16th of this Mexican month they decked with boughs all the temples and the street corners of the city. On the 18th the gods began to arrive, according to what they said, and the first was the great god Tezcatlipoca. They spread before the door of the sanctuary of this god a palm mat, and scattered on it maize flour. The high priest kept watch all the preceding night, and went often to look at the mat; and as soon as he recognized footprints on the flour, doubtless stamped there by some deceitful priest, he began to cry out, Our great god has already arrived. All the other priests with a great crowd of people set out to adore him, and to celebrate his arrival with hymns and dances, which lasted the rest of the night. In the two following days other gods came in succession, and on the twentieth and last day of the month, since all were believed to have arrived, many young men disguised in various shapes of monsters danced around a great fire, and meanwhile they went throwing prisoners into the fire, where they died consumed in holocaust. e: Bk. VI. at which they drank more than usual, believing that the wine with which they filled their bellies was to serve to wash the feet of their gods. To such excesses did the barbarous superstition of those peoples go! No less superstitious was the ceremony which they performed on children to preserve them from the harm which they feared from one of their gods, sticking with turpentine many feathers on their shoulders, arms, and legs. In the thirteenth month, which began on October 24, the fourth festival of the gods of the water and of the mountains was celebrated. The name Tepeilhuitl, by which this month was called, signifies nothing other than the Festival of the mountains. They made certain little mountains of paper, on which they placed some little serpents of wood or of tree roots, and certain little idols, or puppets, called Ehecatotontin, covered with a certain paste. They set both on the altars, and adored them as images of the gods of the mountains, sang hymns to them, and offered them copal and food. The prisoners who were sacrificed at this festival were five, one man and four women, and to each was given a particular name, alluding doubtless to some mystery which we do not know. They dressed them in painted paper smeared with elastic resin, and carried them on litters in procession, which being ended they sacrificed them in the ordinary manner. In the fourteenth month, which began on November 13, the festi‐ § 35. Festivals of the last val of Mixcoatl, goddess of the hunt, was held. It was preceded by five months. four days of rigorous and general fasting, with shedding of blood, in which arrows and darts were made for supplying the armories, and certain little arrows, which together with pine wood and some foods they laid on the sepulchers of their relatives, and after a day burned them. When the fast was ended the Mexicans and the Tlatelolcas went out to a general hunt on one of the neighboring mountains, and all the animals that were taken were carried with the greatest rejoicing to Mexico, where they were sacrificed to Mixcoatl. The king himself took part, not only in the sacrifice, but also in the hunt. They gave this month the name of Quecholli

e: Bk. VI.    Quecholli, because at this time there appeared on the shores of the Mexican lake that beautiful bird which among them had that name, and which many call the flamingo. In the fifteenth month, the beginning of which was on December 3, the third and principal festival of Huitzilopochtli and of his brother was celebrated, in which it seems that the Devil (whom some holy Father calls the Ape of God) sought to imitate in some manner the august mysteries of the Christian religion. On the first day of the month the priests made two statues of those two gods out of several seeds kneaded with the blood of sacrificed children, and set in them, in place of bones, sticks of acacia. They placed them on the principal altar of the temple, and all that night the priests kept vigil. The next day they blessed the statues, and together with them a little water, which was kept in the temple, to sprinkle with it the face of the new king of Mexico and of the general of the armies after their election; but the general, besides being sprinkled, had to drink it. As soon as the statues were consecrated by the blessing, the dance of both sexes began, which throughout that month lasted three or four hours each day. All this month there was great shedding of blood, and for the four days preceding the festival the masters of the prisoners who were to be sacrificed fasted; these were chosen in good time, and wore their bodies painted in various colors. On the morning of the twentieth day, on which the festival was celebrated, they held a great and solemn procession. It was preceded by a priest carrying in his hands a wooden serpent, which they called Ezpamitl, and which was the insignia of the gods of war, and by another carrying one of those standards which they used in their armies. Behind them came another priest, who carried the statue of the god Painalton, vicar of

Quella notte vegliavano i Sacerdoti, e la mattiva seguente portavano la (tatua di pasta di Huitzilopochtli ad una gran fala, che era nel recinto del tempio, e quivi alla «presenza solamente del Re, di quattro Sacerdoti primarj, e di quattro Superiori de' Seminari, il Sacerdote Quertzalcoat] , ch era il capo de’ Tlamacazqui , o Penitenti , tirava un dardo, alla stazua , con cui Îa passava da banda a banda, Dicevano allora, ch’ era già morto il lor Dio . Uno de’ primarj Sacerdoti cavava il cuore alla statua, e davalo a mangiare al Re,Il]cordividevasi in due parti: l'una fi dava a' Tlatelolchi, e L'altra restava per li Messicani, Questa tornava a dividersi in quattro parti per li quattro quartieri della Città, e ciafcuna d' esla in tante minutissime particelle , quanti erano gli pomini del quartiere. Questa cerimonia esprimevano colla Voce T'eocualo, che vale, l'efler Dio mangiato . Le donne non allaggiavano questa sacra pasta , forse perchè a loro non aparteneva il mestier dell'armi . e: Huitzilopochtli. Then came the victims, after the other priests, and finally the people. The procession set out from the great temple for the ward of Teotlachco, where they halted to sacrifice two prisoners of war, and some slaves [p. 81] purchased; thence they proceeded to Tlatelolco, to Popotla, to Chapultepec, from which they returned to the city, and after going Bk. VI. around other wards returned to the temple. In this journey of nine or ten miles they spent the greater part of the day, and in all the places where they halted they sacrificed quails, and perhaps also some prisoners. When they arrived at the temple they placed the statue of Painalton, and the standard, on the altar of Huitzilopochtli: the king incensed the statues of seeds, and then another procession was formed around the temple, at the end of which the prisoners and the remaining slaves were sacrificed. These sacrifices were made at the close of the day. That night the priests kept vigil, and the next morning they carried the paste statue of Huitzilopochtli to a great hall which was in the enclosure of the temple, and there, in the presence only of the king, of four chief priests, and of four superiors of the seminaries, the priest Quetzalcoatl, who was the head of the Tlamacazqui, or Penitents, threw a dart at the statue, with which he pierced it through from side to side. They said then that their god was now dead. One of the chief priests cut out the heart of the statue, and gave it to the king to eat. The body was divided into two parts: one was given to the Tlatelolcas, and the other remained for the Mexicans. This latter was again divided into four parts for the four quarters of the city, and each of these into as many minute particles as there were men in the quarter. This ceremony they expressed by the word Teocualo, which means, the god being eaten. The women did not taste this sacred paste, perhaps because the trade of arms did not belong to them. We do not know whether they made the same use of the statue of Tlacahuepan. The Mexicans gave this month the name of Panquetzaliztli, which signifies the raising of the standard, from what they carried in the aforesaid procession. In this month they were occupied in renewing the boundaries, and in repairing the hedges of their fields.

e: In the sixteenth month, which began on December 23, the fifth and last festival of the gods of the [p. 82] water and of the mountains. They prepared for it with their usual ausBk. VI. terities, and with offerings of copal and of other aromatic resins. They made by vow certain little figures of the mountains, which they consecrated to those gods, and certain little idols of paste of various edible seeds, in which, after having adored them, they opened the breast and cut out the heart with a shuttle, and then cut off their heads, imitating the rites of the sacrifices. The body was divided by each head of family among the members of his household, so that by eating it they might preserve themselves from certain maladies, to which they believed those exposed who were negligent in the worship of those gods. They burned the garments which they had put on the little idols, and scrupulously kept the ashes in their oratories, as also the vessels in which they had made them. Besides these rites customarily performed in the houses, they made some sacrifices of human victims in the temple. The four days preceding the festival there was a rigorous fast accompanied by shedding of blood. They called this month Atemoztli, which means descent of the water, for the reason which we shall give below. The Chevalier Boturini claims that this name is a syncope of Ateomomoztli; but such syncopes were not in use among the Mexicans, besides which the figure of this month, which is that of water running down the steps of an edifice, plainly expresses the descent of the water signified by the word Atemoztli. [p. 83] the rabble amused itself with a game not unlike the Lupercalia of the Bk. VI. Romans; for, running through the streets, they beat with little sacks full of hay all the women whom they met. In the same month was celebrated the festival of Mictlantecuhtli, god of hell, with the nocturnal sacrifice of a prisoner, and the second festival of Yacatecuhtli, god of the merchants. The name Tititl, which they gave to this month, signifies the contraction which the cold causes at that time. (R) In the eighteenth and last month, which began on February 1, the second festival of the god of fire was held. On the 10th of this month all the Mexican youth went out to the hunt, both of wild beasts in the woods and of birds on the lake. On the 16th the fire of the temple and of the houses was put out, and they drew the new fire before the idol of that god, which they adorned for this festival with beautiful feathers and gems. The hunters presented all their game to the priests, of which one part was offered in holocaust to their gods, and the other was sacrificed, and then cooked and seasoned for the nobility and for the priests. The women made offerings of tamalli, which were distributed among the hunters. One of the ceremonies of this festival was that of piercing the ears of all the children of both sexes, in order afterward to put earrings in them. But the most singular thing about this festival was that no human victim was sacrificed. The second festival of the Mother of the Gods was also celebrated in this month, about which we know nothing, except the ridiculous ceremony of lifting children into the air by the ears, believing that in this way they would grow taller. As to the name Izcalli, which they gave to this month, we can affirm nothing. e: Mexican year, the five days Nemontemi began on the 21st, in which no Bk. VI. festival was celebrated, nor any business or lawsuit undertaken, because they were deemed unlucky. A child, moreover, who was born on any of these days, if a boy, had the name of Nemoquichtli, useless man; if a girl, that of Nencihuatl, useless woman. The festivals which were celebrated annually were more solemn in the Teoxihuitl, or divine year, such as were all the years which had the Rabbit for their sign. The sacrifices were then more numerous, the offerings more abundant, and the dances more solemn, especially in Tlaxcala, in Huexotzinco, and in Cholula. Likewise the solemnity of their festivals was greater at the beginning of every period of thirteen years, that is, in the years I Rabbit, I Cane, I Flint, and I House. But the greatest festival, and the most celebrated not only among § 36. the Mexicans, but even among all the nations of that empire, or near Secular festival.

o: Ma la più gran festa, e la più celebrenon solamente presso # Messicani , ma eziand)o presso rutte le Nazioni di quell' Imperio, & ad esso vicine, era quella che fi faceva ogni cinquanta due anni. L' ultima norte del lor Secolo smorzavano il fuoco. di ruit® i temp), e delle case, e rompevano i vali, le pignatte, € tutti gli altri stoviglj: preparandosi così per la fine del mondo, che temevano potere avvenire sul termine di ciascue secolo. Ulcivano del tempio, e della Città i Sacerdoti vestiti di varj abiti, ed insegne de' lor Dei, ed accompagnati d& immensa folla di popolo s' incamminavano verso il monte Huixachtla, preflo alla Città 'd' Iztapalapan, più di sei migli@ discosto- dalla Capitale , Regolavano in maniera il lor viaggi colla. offervazion delle stelle , che potessero arrivare un poc@&_ prima della mezza notte a quel monte , nella cui cim& doveva farsì il nuovo fuoco. Frattanto restava il Popolo is una gran sollecitudine , sperando da un canto assicurare al Mondo: col- nuovo fuoco un nuovo secolo, e. temendo dall! altro canro la total rovina del mondo, se il fuoco per divin@ disposizione non si fosse acceso . Coprivano il viso alle donne gravide i lor mariti con foglie di maguei, e racchiudevanle ne' granai; perchè temevano, che efle convertite ia fiere gli divoraflero . Similmente coprivano il viso a' fanciulli, [p. 85] e non li lasciavano dormire , perché non fossero in sori =trasformati , Gli altri, che non erano andati co' Sacerdoti ,Lis. VL falivano in su’ terrazzi per offervar quindi l' elito di quella gran ceremonia , L’ impiego di cavare il fuoco in questa occasione toccava privativamente ad un Sacerdote di Copolco , una delle contrade della Città . Gli strumenti erano , come altrove diremo , due legni, e il luogo’, dove fi cavava, era il petto di qualche prode prigioniere, che fsacrificavano . Subito che era acceso il fuoco, tutti ad uaa voce gridavano perl allegrezza: faceasi nello-st:ffo monte un gran fuoco , acciocchéè fosse da lontano veduto, e bruciavano in esso la vittima già sacrificata . Tutti a gara andavano a pigliar di quel fuoco sacro, per portarlo colla maggior celerità alle. lor case. I Sacerdoti portavanlo al tempio maggior di Messicos donde fi provvedevano tutti gli abitatori di quella Capitale . N@ tredici giorni seguenti la rinnovazion del fuoco , i quali erano pl intercalari, che si frammettevano tra l’uno, e l altro secolo, per aggiustar l’ anno al corsa solare , s' occupavano nell accomodare, ed imbiancar gli edifizj tanto i pubblici, quanto i privati , e nel procacciarsi nuove stoviglie , e nuove velti: icchè tutto folle , o almeno sembrafle nuovo sul principio del nuovo secolo. Il primo dì di quell’ anno , e di quel secolo , il quale , coma abbiamo già accennato, era alli 25 Febbrajo, a niuno era lecito assaggiare l’ acqua fino al mezzo giorno, Nell' ora stessa cominciavano i facri- \Gz;, il cui numero era corrispondente alla grandezza della a Risfonavano da per rutto le voci di giubilo, e le scam- _ Nevoli congratulazioni pel nuovo. secolo accordato dal Cielo. Le illuminazioni di queste prime notti erano sorprendenti : le gale , i conviti , i balli , ed i giuochi pubblici erano i più solenni . Tra gli altri facevasi fra un immenso concorso di Popolo, @ fra le più singolari dimostrazioni di giubilo , il giuoco de’ Volatori , che altrove descriveremo : nel quale erano quattro 1 volatori, e tredici i giri, che ciascuno faceva nel suo volo, per significare i quattro periodi di tredici anni, di cui éra il secolo composto, Quan:
e: it, was that which was held every fifty-two years. On the last night of their century they put out the fire in all the temples and in the houses, and broke the vessels, the pots, and all the other crockery: preparing themselves thus for the end of the world, which they feared might happen at the close of each century. The priests, dressed in the various garments and insignia of their gods, and accompanied by an immense crowd of people, went out of the temple and of the city and set out toward the mountain Huixachtla, near the city of Iztapalapa, more than six miles distant from the capital. They so regulated their journey by the observation of the stars that they might arrive a little before midnight at that mountain, on whose summit the new fire was to be made. Meanwhile the people remained in great anxiety, hoping on the one hand to secure for the world with the new fire a new century, and fearing on the other the total ruin of the world, if the fire, by divine disposition, should not be kindled. The husbands covered the faces of their pregnant wives with maguei leaves, and shut them up in the granaries, because they feared that, changed into wild beasts, they would devour them. In like manner they covered the faces of the children, [p. 85] and did not let them sleep, lest they be transformed into mice. Those Bk. VI. who had not gone with the priests climbed up on the terraces to observe from there the outcome of that great ceremony. The task of drawing the fire on this occasion belonged exclusively to a priest of Copolco, one of the wards of the city. The instruments were, as we shall say elsewhere, two pieces of wood, and the place where it was drawn was the breast of some brave prisoner whom they sacrificed. As soon as the fire was lit, all cried out with one voice for joy; a great fire was made on the same mountain, so that it might be seen from afar, and they burned on it the victim already sacrificed. All vied with one another to take some of that sacred fire, to carry it with the greatest speed to their houses. The priests carried it to the great temple of Mexico, whence all the inhabitants of that capital were supplied. In the thirteen days following the renewal of the fire, which were the intercalary days inserted between one century and the next in order to adjust the year to the solar course, they were occupied in repairing and whitewashing the buildings, both public and private, and in procuring new crockery and new garments: so that everything might be, or at least seem, new at the beginning of the new century. On the first day of that year and of that century, which, as we have already mentioned, fell on February 26, it was lawful for no one to taste water until noon. In the same hour the sacrifices began, the number of which was proportioned to the greatness of the festival. Voices of jubilation resounded everywhere, and mutual congratulations on the new century granted by Heaven. The illuminations of these first nights were astonishing: the festivities, the banquets, the dances, and the public games were of the most solemn kind. Among the others there was held, amid an immense concourse of people and the most singular demonstrations of jubilation, the game of the flyers, which we shall describe elsewhere: in which there were four flyers, and thirteen the turns that each made in his flight, to signify the four periods of thirteen years of which the century was composed.

e: What we have thus far related concerning the festivals of the Bk. VI. Mexicans shows quite clearly their superstitious character; but this will be seen still more in the account which we are about to give of the rites observed by them at the birth of their children, at their marriages, and at their funerals. As soon as any child came into the light, the midwife, after cutting § 37. the umbilical cord and burying the afterbirth, washed him, saying to Rites at the birth of their children. him these words, Receive the water; for the goddess Chalchiuhcueye is your Mother. May this bath wash away the stains which you bring from your Mother’s womb, cleanse your heart, and give you a good and perfect life. Then, turning her prayer to that goddess, she asked of her the same favor in similar words, and taking the water once more in her right hand she blew upon it, and with it moistened the mouth, the head, and the breast of the child; and then, bathing his whole body, she said, May the invisible God descend upon this water, and cleanse you of every sin and of every impurity, and free you from ill fortune; and turning to the child she spoke to him thus: Darling child, the gods Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl created you in the highest place of Heaven to send you into the world; but be aware that the life which you begin is melancholy, painful, and full of hardships and miseries: nor will you be able to eat bread without toil; may God help you in the many adversities that await you; and she ended this ceremony by congratulating the parents and kinsfolk of the child. If this child was the son of the king, or of some great lord, his principal subjects went to the father to congratulate him, and to wish the infant great happiness. e: celebrated with greater solemnity and superstition. As soon as the son was born, a turkey was sacrificed. The bath was given in some spring or river, where they made offerings of copal, and sacrifices of parrots. The umbilical cord was cut upon an ear of maize, and with a new knife, which was immediately thrown into the river; they sowed the grain of that ear, and watched with the greatest diligence [p. 87] This first bath having been given, the diviners were consulted about the child’s fortune, and for this purpose they were fully in‐ Bk. VI. formed of the day and the hour of his birth. These considered the quality of the sign proper to that day, and of the sign dominant in that period of thirteen days, and if he was born at midnight they compared the two signs, that is, that of the day which was ending and that of the other which was beginning. Having made their observations, they pronounced the good or bad fortune of the infant. If it was bad, and if the fifth day after the birth, on which it was customary to give the second bath or washing, was unlucky, such a ceremony was postponed to another, more favorable day. For this second bath, which was the most solemn, they invited all the relatives and friends, and some boys, and if they were well-to-do they gave lavish dinners, and presented garments to all the guests. If the father of the child was a military man, he prepared for this ceremony a little bow, four little arrows, and a little garment of the same fashion as that which the child was to wear when he was grown. If he was a farmer or an artisan, he prepared some instruments proper to his craft, and proportioned to the body of the infant. If it was a girl, they provided for her a little garment suited to her sex, a little spindle, and some other little weaving instrument. A great number of torches were lighted, and the midwife, taking the infant, carried it through the whole courtyard of the house, and placed it on a heap of iris leaves, beside a basin of water prepared in the middle of the courtyard, and there, stripping it, she said: My son, the gods Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl, lords of Heaven, have sent you to this sad and calamitous world. At other times it was taken from the circumstances attending the birth, just as to one of the four chiefs who governed the republic of Tlaxcala when the Spaniards arrived they gave the [p. 89] name of Citlalpopoca, that is, Smoking Star; because he was born at Bk. VI. the time when a comet was seen in the sky. To one who was born on the day of the renewal of the fire they gave the name of Molpilli if a boy; if a girl, that of Xiuhnenetl, alluding in both cases to the circumstances of the festival. To the boys they gave for the most part names of animals, and to the girls names of flowers; wherein it is to be believed that they had regard both to the dreams of the parents and to the counsels of the diviners. The name that was given to children was for the most part single; but they afterwards used to acquire by their actions a surname, just as to Moctezuma I they gave, because of his prowess, the surnames of Ilhuicamina and Tlacaele. When the religious ceremonies of the bath were ended, banquets were held, at which they tried to do themselves honor according to their means. At such rejoicings it was permitted to drink more than usual, provided that the disorder of drunkenness were kept within the house. The torches were kept lit until they were consumed, and great care was taken to keep up the fire throughout the four days that passed between the first and the second bath, being persuaded that if it should ever fail, the happiness of the infant would fail also. These rejoicings were repeated when they weaned the child, which was done for the most part at three years. (U) As for the marriages of the Mexicans, although in them, as in all § 38. their affairs, there was some superstition, nothing took place in them Nuptial rites. that could offend decency. Every marriage between persons related in the first degree of consanguinity or of affinity was severely forbidden, as we shall say elsewhere, no less by the laws of Mexico than by those of Michoacán, except between brothers- and sisters-in-law. (V) (U) In Guatemala they also held rejoicings when the child began to walk, and for seven years continuously the anniversary of his birth was celebrated.

e: (V) In bk. 4, tit. 2, of the third provincial council of Mexico it is supposed [p. 90] The parents were those who arranged the marriage, and it was never Bk. VI. carried out without their consent. When the son arrived at an age capable of sustaining the offices of the state, which in men was from twenty to twenty-two years, and in women seventeen or eighteen, they sought a wife suitable and proportionate for him; but before undertaking it they consulted the diviners, and these, having considered the day of the birth of the young man and that of the maiden whom they wished to give him, decided on the happiness or unhappiness of the marriage. If from the combination of the signs they declared the alliance unlucky, that maiden was given up, and another was sought. If on the contrary they predicted happiness, the maiden was asked of her parents by means of certain women called by them Cihuatlanque, or solicitors, who were the most elderly and authoritative of the young man’s kinfolk. These went for the first time at midnight to the house of the maiden, carried a present to her parents, and asked for her in a humble and discreet speech. This first request was, according to the custom of that nation, infallibly rejected, however advantageous the marriage might be to the maiden’s parents, and however much it pleased them, some apparent reasons being alleged for such a refusal. After some days those women returned to make the same request, using entreaties and arguments to obtain what they wanted, giving an account of the quality and the property of the young man, and of what he was to give as a dowry to the maiden and that the Gentiles of that New World married their sisters; but it must be known that the zeal of those Fathers was not restricted to the nations of the Mexican empire, among which such marriages were not tolerated, but extended also to the barbarous Chichimecs, to the people of Pánuco, and to other nations more irregular in their customs. There is no doubt that the council was speaking of those barbarians who at that time (in the year 1585) were being reduced to Christianity, not of the Mexicans and of the other nations subject to them, which many years before the council had already been entirely reduced; besides that in the interval of four years which there was between the conquest of the Spaniards and the publication of the Gospel, several abuses were introduced into those nations, never tolerated under their kings, as the apostolic religious who were employed in their conversion bore witness. [p. 91] and informing themselves also of what the maiden might bring. This time the parents answered that before resolving it was necessary to Bk. VI. consult their kinsfolk, and to inquire into the wishes of their daughter. Those women did not return again, since the parents themselves sent the decisive answer by means of other women of their kindred. Having at last obtained a favorable answer, and the day of the wedding having been fixed, after the parents had exhorted their daughter to fidelity and obedience to her husband, and to such a conduct of life as would do honor to her family, they conducted her with a great retinue and with music to the house of the father-in-law, and if she was noble they carried her in a litter. The groom and the parents-in-law received her at the door of the house, with four torches borne by four women. On her arrival the bride and groom incensed one another. The groom, taking her by the hand, led her into the hall or room which they had prepared for the wedding. They both sat down on a new and curious mat which lay in the middle of the room, near the fire which they kept burning. Then a priest tied a corner of the Huepilli, or shirt of the bride, to another of the Tilmatli, or mantle of the groom, and in this ceremony they made the marriage contract essentially consist. The wife then made seven turns around the fire, and, returned to her mat, offered together with her husband copal to their gods, and they presented one another with gifts. The dinner followed. The bride and groom ate on the mat, giving one another the morsels, and the guests in their places. When the guests were warmed with the wine, which on such occasions was drunk in abundance, they went out to dance in the courtyard, the bride and groom remaining in that room, from which for four days they never went out, except for the needs of nature, and to go at midnight to the oratory to incense the idols and make them offerings of foods.
