Their beds on those nights were two new mats of rush covered with little sheets, with certain feathers in the middle, and a chalchihuitl gem. At the four corners of the bed they placed green reeds and maguei thorns, in order to draw blood from the tongue and the ears with them in honor of the gods. The priests themselves were those who arranged the beds to sanctify the marriage; but we do not know the mystery of the gem, the reeds, and the feathers. Until the fourth night the marriage was not consummated, it being believed that it would be unlucky if the consummation were anticipated. The following morning they bathed, and put on new garments, and the guests adorned their heads with white feathers, and their hands and feet with red feathers. The ceremony was concluded with presenting garments to the guests according to the means of the bride and groom, and on the same day the mats, the sheets, the reeds, and the foods presented to the idols were carried to the temple. What we have said concerning the marriages of the Mexicans was not so universal throughout the empire that in some provinces there did not occur some peculiarity. In Ichcatlan, whoever wished to take a wife presented himself to the priests, and they led him up onto the temple, where, before the idol that was adored there, they cut off a part of his hair, and then, pointing him out to the people, began to cry out: This man wishes to marry. Then they made him come down, and take the first free woman who came in his way, as though she were precisely the one whom Heaven destined for him. The woman who did not want him for a husband avoided approaching the temple at that time, so as not to put herself thus under the necessity of marrying him: whence this marriage was not singular, except in the manner of seeking the wife.

e: Before marrying, the Otomis were permitted the use of any unmarried woman. When any of them married, if on the first night he found in his wife something that displeased him, he could on the following day repudiate her [p. 93] but if on that day he showed himself content with having her, he could no longer leave her. The contract being thus ratified, the bride and Bk. VI. groom withdrew to do penance for their past misdeeds for twenty or thirty days, abstaining during that time from many pleasures of the senses, drawing blood from themselves, and bathing often. Among the Mixtecs, besides the ceremony of tying together the ends of the garments of the bride and groom, they cut off a part of their hair, and the husband for a little while carried his wife upon his back. Polygamy was permitted in the Mexican empire. The kings and the lords had very many wives; but it is to be believed that they observed all those ceremonies only with the principal ones, being content, as to the others, with the essential rite of the tying together of the garments. The Spanish theologians and canonists who went over to Mexico immediately after the conquest, being men who were not instructed in the customs of those peoples, raised doubts about their marriages; but having afterward learned their languages, and diligently examined this and other important matters, they recognized those marriages as true and lawful. Pope Paul III and the provincial councils of Mexico ordained, according to the Holy Canons and the usage of the Church, that all those who wished to embrace Christianity should keep the first wife whom they had married and leave all the others. Finally, the Mexicans having been so superstitious in all their actions, § 39. Funeral rites. they surpassed even themselves in their funeral rites. As soon as someone died, certain masters of funeral ceremonies were summoned, who were for the most part elderly men. These, having cut many pieces of paper, dressed the corpse in them, and taking a glass of water they sprinkled it on his head, saying that this was the water used during his life. Then they dressed him in a garment corresponding to his condition, to his means, and to the circumstances of his death. VI. clothed in the garment of Tlaloc; he who was executed for adultery, in that of Tlazolteotl; and the drunkard, in that of Tezcatzoncatl, god of wine. So that, as Gómara well says, they wore more garments after death than when they were alive. They then placed among the garments a jug of water, which was to serve him on the journey to the other world, and they gave him in succession several pieces of paper, indicating the use of each. In handing him the first they said to the dead man: With this you will pass without danger between the two mountains that strike one another. In the second they said: With this you will walk without hindrance along the road guarded by the great serpent. In the third: With this you will go safely through the place where the crocodile Xochitonal is. The fourth was a safe-conduct for the eight deserts, the fifth for the eight hills, and the sixth for passing without injury the sharp wind; for they imagined that one had to pass through a place called Itzehecayan, where there blew a wind so strong that it lifted the stones, and so sharp that it cut like a knife: whence they burned all the garments which he had worn in life, his arms, and some household goods, so that the heat of this fire might defend him from the cold of that terrible wind. One of the principal and most ridiculous ceremonies was that of killing a Techichi, a domestic quadruped, as we have already said, similar to our little dogs, so that it might accompany the deceased on the journey to the other world. They tied a cord to its neck, believing this necessary for crossing the deep river of Chiconahuapan, or of the nine waters. They buried the Techichi, or else burned it together with the corpse of its master, according to the kind of death with which he had ended. While the masters of ceremonies lit the fire in which the corpse was to be burned, the other priests sang in a mournful tone.

This pot they Bk. VI. buried in a deep pit, and for four days they made over it oblations of bread and of wine. These were the funeral rites of the common people; but in the obsequies of the kings, and in proportion in those of the lords and persons of high rank, there occurred certain particulars worthy of being recalled. When the king fell ill, says Gómara, a mask was put on the idol of Huitzilopochtli, and another on that of Tezcatlipoca, and it was not taken off until the king was dead or recovered; but it is certain, as we have said elsewhere, that the idol of Huitzilopochtli always had two masks, not merely one. As soon as the king of Mexico died, his death was published with great pomp, and all the lords were notified, so that they might attend the funeral, both those who were at the court and those who were in places not far from it. Meanwhile they laid the royal corpse upon fine and curious mats, and his household servants kept it company. On the fourth or fifth day, when the lords had already arrived, bringing with them rich garments, beautiful feathers, and slaves to present for the solemnity of the obsequies, they clothed the corpse in fifteen or more very fine cotton garments of various colors, adorned it with gold, silver, and gems, hung from its lower lip an emerald, which was to serve it as a heart, covered the face with a mask, and over the garments put on it the insignia of the god in whose temple or court the ashes were to be buried. They cut off a part of the hair, and together with another lock which had been cut off in his infancy they kept it in a little chest, in order to perpetuate, as they said, the memory of the deceased. The funeral procession was then held, carrying the royal corpse, accompanied by the relatives, by all the nobility, and by the wives of the deceased, who signified their grief by weeping and by other demonstrations of the kind. In those of the rich they placed gold and jewels, and for all they provided food for the long journey that they had to make. The Spanish conquerors, aware of the gold that the sepulchers of the Mexican lords contained, dug up some of them, and found in them considerable sums of that precious metal. Cortés says in his letters that in an incursion which he made into the capital while it was besieged by his army, his soldiers found fifteen hundred castellanos (*), that is, two hundred and forty ounces of gold, in a sepulcher that was in the tower of a temple. The Anonymous Conqueror bears witness that he was present at the opening of another sepulcher, from which they took about three thousand castellanos. The sepulchers of the ancient Chichimecs were the caves of the mountains; but when they became more refined, they adopted, in this as in other matters, the rites and customs of the Acolhuas, which were almost the same as those of the Mexicans. The Mixtecs kept in part the ancient practice of the Chichimecs; but in some things they were singular. When one of their lords fell ill, prayers, vows, and sacrifices were made for his health. If he recovered, great rejoicings were held. If he died, they went on speaking of him as if he were still alive, and led before the corpse one of his slaves, dressed him in the garments of his lord, put a mask on his face, and all that day paid him all the honors that they had been wont to pay to the deceased. Every year they held a festival in honor of their last lord, in which his birth was celebrated, not his death, of which no mention was ever made. The Zapotecs, their neighbors, embalmed the body of the principal lord of their nation. Aromatic preparations for preserving corpses for some time from corruption were also in use among those nations from the time of the first Chichimec kings; but we do not know that they were very frequent. What we have said so far is what we know of the religion of the Mexicans. The vanity of their worship, the superstition of their rites, the cruelty of their sacrifices, and the rigor of their austerities will make plainer to their descendants the incomparable advantages brought to them by the sweet, pure, and holy doctrine of Jesus Christ, and will urge them to give thanks eternally to the Father of mercies for having called them to the wondrous light of his Gospel, having left their ancestors to perish in the darkness of error. VII. those nations and the most enlightened authors. “Nothing,” says Father Acosta, “has caused me more wonder, nor § 1. Education of the seemed to me more worthy of praise and of remembrance, than the Mexican youth. care and the order that the Mexicans had in the education of their children.” In fact, it is hard to find a nation that has employed greater diligence in an article so important to the state. It is true that they vitiated their instruction with superstition; but the zeal that they showed for the education of their children ought to put to shame the negligence of our fathers of families, and many of the precepts that they gave to their youth might serve as lessons to ours as well. All Mexican infants, even the children of kings, were suckled by their own mothers. If the mother was prevented by some illness, they did not entrust the child so readily to a nurse without first informing themselves both of this woman’s condition and of the quality of her milk. From their infancy they accustomed them to bear hunger, heat, and cold. When they reached the age of five years, either they were handed over to the priests, that these might bring them up in the seminaries, as was done with almost all the sons of the nobles, and even with those of the kings themselves; or, if they were to be brought up in their own houses, their parents began from then on to instruct them in the worship of their gods, and to teach them the formulas for praying and for imploring their protection. They often led them to the temples to attach them to religion. They instilled in them a horror of vice, modesty in their actions, respect for their elders, and love of labor. They made them sleep on a mat; they gave them no other food than what the necessity of life required, nor other clothing than what sufficed for the defense of decency. When they reached a certain age, they taught them the use of arms, and if their parents were military men, they took them along to the war, so that they might train themselves in the military art, and drive fear from their minds by growing accustomed to dangers. e: [p. 102] or artisans, they taught them their own trade. They trained the girls Bk. VII. in spinning and weaving, and compelled them to bathe often, so that they might always be clean; and in general they took care that their children should always be occupied. One of the things that they most warmly recommended to their children was truthfulness in their words, and if anyone was ever caught in some lie, they pricked his lips with maguei thorns. They bound the feet of daughters too eager to go out strolling. The disobedient or unruly son was beaten by his father with nettles, or punished with some other penalty of the kind, proportioned, according to their way of thinking, to the fault. § 2.    The system of education that the Mexicans gave to their children, Explanation of seven Mexican paintings on and the extreme care that they had for their actions, can be traced in education. the seven paintings that are in the Mendoza Collection, from the forty-ninth to the fifty-sixth. In them are set forth the quantity and the quality of the food that was given them, the tasks in which they were occupied, and the punishments with which they corrected their faults. In the fiftieth painting there are represented a boy of four years, who is employed by his parents in some easy tasks to accustom him to labor; another of five years, who, carrying a small bundle on his back, accompanies his father to the market; a girl of the same age, who is beginning to learn to spin; and another boy of six years, whom his father employs in gathering the grains of maize and such trifles as were to be found on the ground in the marketplace.

The fifty-fourth shows the youths of the seminaries occupied by their superiors in sweeping the temple, and in bringing branches of trees and herbs for the adornment of the sanctuaries, wood for the braziers, rushes for the making of seats, and stone and lime for the repair of the temple. In this same painting, and in the fifty-fifth, are represented various punishments given to the delinquent youths of the seminaries by their superiors. One of them pricks a youth with maguei thorns for having neglected his duty; two priests throw burning brands on the head of another youth, for having caught him in familiar talk with a girl; another, for the same offense, they prick on the body with sharp pine sticks, and another they punish for disobedience by burning his hair. e: painting is seen a youth who carries the baggage of a priest who goes Bk. VII. to the army to encourage the soldiers and to perform certain superstitious ceremonies. Children were brought up with such great respect toward their parents that even when grown up and married they hardly dared to speak in their presence. The instructions, moreover, and the counsels that they gave them were such that I cannot excuse myself from transcribing here some of the exhortations that they made to them; which the first apostolic religious who employed themselves in their conversion learned from the Mexicans themselves, especially Motolinía, Olmos, and Sahagún, who learned their language perfectly and used the utmost diligence in the investigation of their customs and usages. § 3.    “My son,” his father would say to him, “you who have come into Exhortation of a Mexican to his son. the light from the womb of your mother, like the chick from the egg, and who, growing like it, are preparing yourself to fly through the world, we do not know for how long Heaven will grant us the enjoyment of the precious gem that we have in you; but however that may be, take care to live carefully, praying continually to God to help you. He created you, and He possesses you. He is your Father, and loves you more than I do: place your thought in Him, and direct your sighs to Him by day and by night. Revere and salute your elders, and let no one be scorned by you. With the poor and the afflicted do not be mute; rather, strive to console them with kind words. Honor all, especially your parents, to whom you owe obedience, fear, and service. Beware of imitating the examples of those ill-born children who, like brutes deprived of reason, neither revere their parents, nor listen to their teaching, nor will submit to their correction; for whoever would follow in their footsteps will have an unhappy end, since he will die in despair, or be cast down headlong, or will be killed and eaten by wild beasts.”

e: “Do not mock, my son, the old and the imperfect. Do not scoff at him whom you see fall into some fault or failing, and refrain from reproaching him with it; but be abashed [p. 105] and fear lest that very thing happen to you which offends you in others. Do not go where you are not called, nor meddle in what does not Bk. VII. concern you. In all your actions and words strive to show your good breeding. In conversation do not strike others with the hand, nor talk too much, nor interrupt or disturb the talk of others. If you hear anyone talking foolishly, and it is not your place to correct him, be silent; if it is your place, consider first what you are about to say to him, and do not speak to him with arrogance, so that your correction may be the more welcome. “When someone talks with you, listen to him attentively, and holding yourself in a becoming posture, not playing with your feet, nor taking your mantle in your mouth, nor spitting too much, nor looking here and there, nor rising often, if you are seated; for such actions are signs of levity and of bad breeding. “When you are at table, do not eat hastily, nor show disdain if something does not please you. If someone comes in while you are dining, share with him what you have; and when someone dines with you, do not fix your gaze upon him. “In walking look where you go, that you may not bump into anyone. If you see another coming along the same road, turn aside a little to make room for him. Never pass in front of your elders, unless it be necessary, or they themselves so order you. When you dine with them, do not eat or drink before them, and serve them as is fitting in order to win their favor.

e: “When they give you something, accept it with signs of gratitude. If it is great, do not therefore swagger. If it is small, do not despise it, nor show disdain, nor cause displeasure to him who favors you. If you become rich, do not be insolent, nor scoff at the poor; for those same gods who denied riches to others in order to give them to you, displeased by your pride, will take them from you to give them to others. Sustain yourself by your own labors; for so your food will be more pleasant to you. I, my son, have sustained you [p. 106] until now with my sweat, and in nothing have I failed in the duty of a Bk. VII. father toward you: I have provided you with all that was needful, without having taken it from others. Do you do likewise. “Never lie; for a lie is a great sin. When it is necessary to report to someone what another has told you, give the pure truth, adding nothing. Speak ill of no one. Keep silent about the wrong that you observe in others, if it is not your place to apply the remedy. Do not be a gossip, nor a friend of sowing discord. When you carry some message, if he to whom you bring it grows angry and speaks ill of the one who sent you, do not return to the latter with such an answer, but strive to soften it, and conceal as far as possible what you have heard, so that no displeasures and scandals may arise from it, of which you would afterwards have to repent. “Do not linger in the market longer than is necessary; for in such places there are more occasions of falling into some excess. “When they offer you some office, consider that they do it to test you; so do not accept it at once, even though you recognize yourself as better fitted than others to exercise it; but excuse yourself, until you are compelled to accept it: thus you will be the more esteemed. “Do not be dissolute; for the gods will be angered against you, and will cover you with infamy. Restrain yourself, my son, since you are still young, and wait until that maiden arrives at a good age whom the gods have prepared for you as a wife: leave this to their care, for they will know how to arrange everything as is fitting. When the time comes to marry, do not dare to do it without the consent of your parents; for you will have an unhappy outcome.

e: “Never steal, nor give yourself to gambling; for you will be the disgrace of your parents, when you ought rather to honor them for the education that they have given you. If you are good, your example will put the wicked to shame. No more, my son: this suffices to fulfill the obligations of a father. With such counsels I wish to fortify your heart. Do not reject them, nor [p. 107] forget them; for on them depend your life and all your happiness.” Bk. VII. Such were the instructions that they often suggested and inculcated to their children. The farmers and the merchants gave their children other particular counsels concerning their profession, which I omit so as not to weary the readers; but I cannot excuse myself from transcribing one of the exhortations that the mothers made to their daughters, in order to make their education and their customs better known. § 4. “My daughter,” said the mother, “born of my substance, brought Exhortation of a forth with my pains, and nourished with my milk, I have endeavored Mexican     woman to her daughter. to bring you up with the greatest care, and your father has shaped and polished you like an emerald, that you may appear in the eyes of men as a jewel of virtue. Strive always to be good; for otherwise who will want you for a wife? You will be rejected by all. Life is toilsome, and we must exert all our strength to obtain the goods that the gods wish to send us; and therefore one must not be lazy and negligent, but very diligent in everything. Be clean, and labor to keep your house well ordered. Give water for the hands to your husband, and make bread for the family. Wherever you go, go with modesty and composure, not hastening your step, nor laughing with those whom you meet, nor fixing your gaze on them, nor turning your eyes lightly to one side and the other, lest your reputation suffer from it; but answer courteously whoever greets you or asks anything of you. “Employ yourself diligently in spinning, weaving, sewing, and embroidering; for so you will be esteemed, and will have what is needful to eat and to wear. Do not give yourself to sleep, and shun the shade, going out to the cool, and abandoning yourself to rest; for softness brings with it sloth and other vices. “In doing whatever you do, think not of evil things, but attend only to the service of the gods and to the relief of your parents O2                     If

If your father or mother calls you, do not wait to be called twice; but Bk. VII. go at once to learn what they want, so that your delay may not cause them displeasure. Do not give arrogant answers, nor show reluctance; but if you cannot do what they order you, excuse yourself with humility. If another is called, and does not come at once, come yourself, hear what is commanded, and do it well. Never offer yourself to do what you cannot. Deceive no person; for the gods are watching you. Live in peace with all, and love all honestly and discreetly, that you may be equally loved by all. “Of the goods that you shall have, be not avaricious. If you see something given to another, take no evil suspicion from it; for the gods, to whom all goods belong, distribute them as it pleases them. If you do not wish to receive displeasure from others, let no one receive it from you. “Shun unseemly familiarities with men; nor follow the evil desires of your heart; for you will be the disgrace of your parents, and will stain your soul, as water is stained with mud. Do not keep company with dissolute women, nor with liars, nor with slothful ones; for infallibly they will infect you with their example. Attend to your household, and do not be willing to go out of the house easily, nor let them see you wandering through the streets and the marketplace; for in such places you will find your ruin. Consider that vice, like a poisonous herb, brings death to him who takes it, and that once received into the soul it is all too hard to drive out. If, going along the street, you meet some bold young man, and he smiles at you, do not respond to him; but dissimulate, and pass on. If he says something to you, pay no heed to him nor to his words; and if he follows behind you, do not turn your face to look at him, lest his passion be further inflamed. If you do so, he will tire, and will let you go in peace.

e: “Never enter another’s house without pressing reason; so that nothing may be said or thought against your [p. 109] honor; but if you enter the house of your relatives, greet them with respect, and do not stay there idle; but take up the spindle at once to Bk. VII. spin, or do what is needed. “When you are married, respect your husband, obey him, and do diligently what he commands you. Do not cause him displeasure, nor show yourself disdainful or angry toward him; but receive him lovingly into your bosom, even though, being poor, he lives at your expense. If your husband causes you some displeasure, do not let him know your vexation when he commands something; but for the time dissemble it, and afterwards you will tell him gently what troubles you, so that by your gentleness he may be soothed and avoid vexing you. Do not dishonor him before others; for you too would remain dishonored. If anyone should enter your house to visit your husband, show that you welcome his visit, and render him all the services that you can. If your husband is foolish, be you discreet. If he is wanting in the administration of the goods, admonish him of his failings; but if he is quite useless for caring for the property, take that care upon yourself, attending diligently to the possessions, and never failing to pay the workmen promptly. Beware of letting anything be lost through your negligence. “Embrace, my daughter, the counsels that I give you. I am by now advanced in years, and have sufficient experience of the world. I am your mother; I wish you to live well. Fix these counsels in your inmost heart; for so you will live happily. If through not wishing to listen to me, or through neglecting my instructions, misfortunes befall you, yours will be the fault, and yours the harm. No more, my daughter. May the gods prosper you.” Not content with such instructions, and with domestic education, § 5. Public schools and the Mexicans all sent their children to the public schools, which were seminaries. near the temples, where for three years they were instructed in religion and in good morals. Besides this, almost all, especially the nobles, took care that their children should be brought up in the seminaries attached to the temples, of which there were many in the cities of the Mexican empire

e: [p. 110] for boys, for youths, and for girls. Those of the boys and of the youths Bk. VII. were governed by priests devoted solely to their education; those of the girls were under the direction of matrons respectable both for their age and for their morals. There was no communication between the youths of the one sex and of the other, and any lapse in such a matter was severely punished. There were seminaries distinct for the nobles and for the commoners. The noble youths were employed in the interior services, those nearest to the sanctuary, as in sweeping the upper court of the temple, and in lighting and keeping up the fire of the braziers that stood before the sanctuaries. The others were occupied in carrying the wood needed for the braziers, and the stone and lime for the repair of the sacred buildings, and in other similar employments. Both the one and the other were under superiors and masters, who instructed them in religion, in history, in painting, in music, and in the other arts suited to their condition. The girls swept the lower court of the temples, rose three times in the night to burn copal in the braziers, prepared the food that was offered daily to the idols, and wove several sorts of cloth. They were trained in all the women’s trades; whence, besides avoiding idleness, so dangerous in youthful age, they were growing accustomed to domestic labors. They slept in great halls under the eyes of the matrons who governed them, who zealously required nothing so much of them as modesty and composure in their actions. After having listened for a few moments, with humility and in silence, to the instructions and counsels that his father gave him, he returned to the seminary. There they remained until the time of marriage, which in the youths was, as we have already indicated, from twenty to twenty-two years, and in the [p. 111] girls at eighteen or seventeen. When such a time arrived, either the Bk. VII. youth himself asked permission of the superior to go and marry, or, what happened more often, his parents requested it for the same purpose, first thanking the superior for the care he had taken in instructing him. The superior, in dismissing, as he did at the great festival of Tezcatlipoca, all the youths and girls who had arrived at such an age, made them a discourse exhorting them to perseverance in virtue and to the fulfillment of the obligations of the new state. Virgins brought up in the seminaries were singularly sought as wives, both on account of their morals and for the skill that they had in the arts proper to their sex. The youth who, having reached the age of twenty-two years, did not marry was reputed perpetually consecrated to the service of the temple, and if after such a consecration, repenting of his celibacy, he sought to marry, he made himself infamous forever, and there was no woman who would have him for a husband. In Tlaxcala, those who, when the time for marrying came, refused marriage were shorn, which among them was esteemed a great dishonor. Sons learned for the most part the trade of their fathers, and embraced their profession. Thus the arts were perpetuated in families to the advantage of the state. The youths destined for the magistracy were led by their fathers to the tribunals, where they went on learning both the laws of the kingdom and the practice and the judicial form. In the sixtieth painting of the Mendoza Collection four magistrates are represented examining a case, and behind them four young Teteuctin, or knights, who listen to their deliberation. To the sons of kings and of the principal lords were given tutors, who watched over their conduct, and long before they could enter into possession of the Crown, or of the state, the government of some city or lesser state was for the most part conferred on them, so that they might train themselves in the difficult art of ruling men. This began to be the practice from the very first Chichimec kings; for Nopaltzin, from the time he was crowned king of

Acolhuacan, he put his firstborn Tlotzin in possession of the city of Bk. VII. Texcoco. Cuitláhuac, the penultimate king of the Mexicans, obtained the state of Iztapalapa, and his brother Moctezuma that of Ecatepec, before ascending the throne of Mexico. Upon this foundation of education the Mexicans raised the political system of their kingdom, which we must now set forth. § 6. Mexican law on the       From the time at which the Mexicans, following the example of election of the king. the other neighboring nations, set Acamapichtli at the head of their nation, investing him with the name, the honor, and the royal authority, they established that the Crown should be elective; and accordingly some time afterwards they created four electors, to whose judgment all the suffrages of the nation were entrusted. These were four lords of the first nobility, and for the most part of royal blood, and of as much prudence and probity as so important an office required. Such an office was not perpetual; their electoral voice ended with the first election that they made, and immediately new electors were created, or else those same first ones were elected anew by the votes of the nobility. If before the king’s death one of the electors came to fail, another was elected in his place. From the time of King Itzcoatl two other electors were added, who were the kings of Acolhuacan and of Tacuba; but these had nothing but the honor. They also ratified the election made by the four true electors; but we do not know that they ever took part in any election.

The feudatory lords went before with the proper insignia of their states, then the nobles of the court with the insignia of their dignities and offices; the two allied kings followed, and behind them the king elect, naked, and with no other clothing than the Maxtlatl, that is, that belt or broad band with which they covered their shame. He climbed to the temple supported on the arms of the two principal lords of the court, where one of the high priests awaited him, accompanied by the most considerable personages of the temple. He adored the idol of Huitzilopochtli, touching the earth with his hand, and then carrying it to his mouth. The high priest stained his whole body with a certain ink, and sprinkled him four times with water blessed, according to their rite, at the great festival of Huitzilopochtli, making use for this sprinkling of branches of cedar and of willow, and of leaves of maize; he clothed him in a mantle on which were painted skulls and bones of the dead [p. 114] and covered his head with two other mantles, the one black and the Bk. VII. other blue, on which were represented those same figures; he hung about his neck a little gourd in which was a certain powder, which they esteemed an effective preservative against diseases, witchcraft, and deceits. Very happy would that people be whose king could have such a preservative. He then put into his hands a censer and a little bag of copal, that he might incense the idol. This act of religion completed, during which the king was kept on his knees, the high priest sat down, and made him a discourse, in which, after congratulating him on his exaltation, he reminded him of the obligation in which he stood toward his subjects for having raised him to the throne, and warmly recommended to him zeal for religion and for justice, the protection of the poor, and the defense of the fatherland and of the kingdom. There followed then the harangues of the allied kings and of the nobility, directed to the same end, to which the king replied with thanks, and with offers to strive, as far as lay in his power, for the felicity of the state. Gómara, and other authors who have copied from him, affirm that the high priest made him swear to maintain the ancient religion, to observe the laws of his predecessors, and to make the sun go on its course, the clouds rain, the rivers run, and all the fruits come forth. If it is indeed true that the king made so extravagant an oath, it is to be believed that he wished to bind himself to nothing else than not to forfeit by his conduct such benefits of Heaven. When the harangues were ended, the king descended with all his retinue to the lower court, where the rest of the nobility awaited him to give him obedience, and to render him homage in jewels and garments. Then he was led to a room that was within the enclosure of the temple, called Tlacatecco, where they left him alone for four days, during which he ate only once a day; but he might eat meat and any other food. Every day he bathed twice, and after the bath he drew blood from his ears, and offered it to Huitzilopochtli together with the copal that in his honor [p. 115] burned, making warm and continual prayers to obtain the light that he needed to govern the monarchy wisely. On the fifth day the nobili‐ Bk. VII. ty returned to the temple to lead the new king to his palace, where the feudatories came to be confirmed in the investiture of their fiefs. Then followed the rejoicings of the people, the banquets, the dances, and the illuminations. In order to proceed to the coronation, it was necessary, according § 8. to the law of the kingdom, or rather the custom introduced into it by Coronation,      crown, robes, and royal Moctezuma I, that the king already elected should go out to war to insignia. procure the victims that were to be sacrificed at so great a festival. There were never lacking enemies on whom to make war, now because some province of the kingdom had rebelled, now because some Mexican merchants had been killed, now because some insult had been offered to the royal ambassadors, of which several examples are found in history. The arms and the insignia with which the king went to the war, the apparatus with which his prisoners were conducted to the court, and the circumstances that attended their sacrifice, will be set forth when we come to speak of the militia of the Mexicans; but otherwise we are wholly ignorant of the particular ceremonies of his coronation. The king of Acolhuacan was he who placed the crown on his head. This crown, called by the Mexicans Copilli, was a kind of small miter, whose front part was raised and ended in a point, and the back part lowered and hanging over the neck, in just the manner in which it is seen in the figures of the kings that we shall give below. It was of various materials according to the pleasure of the kings; now of thin plates of gold, now woven of thread and gold, and figured with fine feathers. The garment that he ordinarily wore in the palace was the Xiuhtilmatli, that is, a mantle woven of white and blue. When he went to the temple, he wore a white garment. That in which he clothed himself to attend the council and other public functions was different according to the quality and the circumstances: one for civil cases and another for criminal ones; one for acts of justice, and another for the P2 [p. 116] rejoicings. On all these occasions he always wore the crown. Bk. VII. Whenever he went out, he was accompanied by a great retinue of nobility, and preceded by a noble who carried raised three rods, part of gold and part of gilded wood, thereby warning the people of the presence of their lord. The power and authority of the kings of Mexico varied according § 9. Rights of the king. to the times. At the beginning of the monarchy their power was very limited, and their authority truly paternal, their treatment of their subjects more humane, and the rights that they collected from them very moderate. As their conquests expanded, their wealth, their magnificence, and their pomp increased, and in proportion to their wealth the burdens of their subjects grew also, as for the most part happens. Their pride drove them to overstep the limits that the consent of the nation had prescribed to their authority, until it degenerated into the odious despotism that we have already seen under the reign of Moctezuma II; but in spite of their tyranny the Mexicans always preserved the respect due to the royal character, except in the next-to-last year of the monarchy, in which, no longer able to bear in their king Moctezuma such abasement and cowardice, and so excessive an indulgence toward his enemies, they vilified him and struck him with arrows and stones, as we shall relate below. The pomp to which the Mexican kings attained can well be understood from what we have said in discussing the reign of Moctezuma, and from what we shall say of it in the account of the conquest. The kings of Mexico were rivaled by those of Acolhuacan in magnificence, as these were by the former in polity. The government of the Acolhuas was for the most part the model of that of the Mexicans; but with regard to the right of succession to the crown they were very different; for in the kingdom of Acolhuacan, and the same is to be understood of that of Tacuba, the sons succeeded their fathers, not according to the order of their birth, but according to their rank, since the sons [p. 117] born of the queen or principal wife were always preferred. This was observed from the first Chichimec king Xolotl down to Cacamatzin, Bk. VII. to whom his brother Cuicuitzcatzin succeeded through the intrigues of Moctezuma and of the Conqueror Cortés. The king of Mexico, like the king of Acolhuacan, had three § 10. supreme councils composed of men of the first nobility, in which Royal councils, and officers of the court. were treated all the affairs pertaining to the government of the provinces, to the king’s revenues, and to war; and for the most part the king took no important decision without first having heard the opinion of his councilors. In the history of the conquest we shall see Moctezuma many times deliberate with his councilors on the claims of the Spaniards. We do not know the number of members of each council, nor do the historians furnish us with all the information necessary to clarify this subject. They have preserved for us only the names of some councilors, chiefly of those of Moctezuma II. In the sixty-first painting of the Mendoza Collection are represented the halls of the councils with some of the lords who composed them. Among the many ministers and officers of the court there was a treasurer general, whom they called Hueicalpixqui, or great steward, who received all the tributes that the collectors gathered from the provinces, and kept in paintings the account of income and expenditure, as Bernal Díaz bears witness, who saw them. There was another treasurer for gems and for things of gold, who was at the same time director of the artisans who worked them, and another for the featherwork, whose artisans had their workshops in the royal palace of the birds. There was also a general purveyor of animals, who was called Huejaminqui, and had charge of the royal woods, so that game might never be lacking in them, and of the royal palaces, so that they might be supplied with every species of animal. As to the other royal ministers and officers, we have said enough on the occasion when we spoke of the magnificence of Moctezuma II, and of the government of the kings of Acolhuacan, Techotlala and Nezahualcoyotl.

e: ment made in the fashion of the scapular or “patience” that some of our religious wear, from which hung some tufts of cotton. They wore their hair braided with pretty feathers, with tufts of various colors hanging from it as well. In the right hand they carried an arrow raised with the point downward, in the left a buckler, and hanging from the same arm a net, in which they carried their provisions. In all the places through which they passed they were well received and treated with the distinction that their character required, provided that they did not leave the highway that led to the place where they were sent; for if they strayed from it they lost the immunity and the privileges of ambassadors. When they arrived at the end of their embassy, they halted before entering, and there waited until the nobility of that city came to meet them and conduct them to the house of the community, where they were lodged and well treated. The nobles incensed them and presented them with bouquets of flowers, and after they had rested, led them to the palace of the lord of that state, and introduced them into the audience hall, where the lord himself and his councilors awaited them, all seated on their seats. There, after making a deep bow to the lord, they sat down on their heels in the middle of the hall, and without saying a word or raising their eyes waited until a sign was given them to speak. When the sign had been given, the most distinguished of the ambassadors, after making another bow to the lord, set forth in a low voice his message in a well-composed harangue, which the lord and his councilors listened to attentively, with their heads bowed so low that they almost touched their knees with them. When the harangue was ended, the ambassadors returned to their lodging. In the meantime the lord consulted with his council, [p. 119] and made known his decision to the ambassadors through his ministers; he supplied them abundantly with provisions for the journey, Bk. VII. made them some presents besides, and those very persons who had received them went out to see them on their way beyond the place. If the lord to whom the embassy was addressed was a friend of the Mexicans, it was thought a great dishonor not to accept the presents; but if he was an enemy, the ambassadors could not receive them without the express order of their master. These ceremonies were not always all observed in embassies, nor were all embassies sent to the lord of the city or of the state; for some, as we shall say below, were sent to the body of the nobility, or else to the people. § 12. The couriers, whom the Mexicans often employed, wore different Couriers and posts. insignia according to the nature of the news or of the business for which they were sent. If the news was that the Mexicans had lost some battle, the courier wore his hair loose and disheveled, and, without saying a word to anyone, went straight to the palace and, kneeling before the king, related what had happened. If the news was of some victory won by the Mexican arms, he wore his hair bound with a colored cord and his body girt with a white cotton cloth, carrying in his left hand a buckler and in his right a sword, which he brandished as if in the act of fighting, showing his jubilation by many signs and singing the glorious deeds of the ancient Mexicans. The people, rejoicing at the sight of him, conducted him with such demonstrations to the royal palace. In order that the message might arrive the more promptly, there stood along the highroads of the kingdom certain small towers about six miles apart from one another, where couriers were always ready to set out upon a journey. As soon as the first courier was dispatched, he ran as swiftly as he could to the first post, or little tower, where he communicated the message to another, and handed over to him, if there happened to be any, the paintings that represented the news or the business and served them as letters. As for the nobility of Mexico and of the whole empire, it was diNobility, and rights vided into several classes, which the Spaniards confounded under the of succession. general name of Caziques (*). Each class had its particular privileges and wore its own insignia; so that, although their dress was so plain, the rank of every person was recognized at once. Only nobles might wear ornaments of gold and gems on their garments, and to them exclusively belonged, from the very beginning of the reign of Moctezuma II, all the distinguished offices of the royal household, of the magistracy, and of the militia, at least the more considerable ones. The first degree of nobility in Tlaxcala, in Huexotzinco, and in Cholula was that of Teuctli. To obtain it one had to be of noble birth, to have given proofs of great courage in several battles, to have reached a certain age, and to possess great wealth, for the very heavy expenses that had to be incurred upon taking possession of this dignity. The candidate had besides to undergo a year of rigorous penance, consisting of a perpetual fast, of frequent shedding of blood, and of abstention from all intercourse with women, and he had to endure patiently the insults, the humiliations, and the ill treatment by which his constancy was tested. The Teuctli took precedence over all the others in the senate, both in sitting and in voting, and might have a servant follow them carrying a chair, which was esteemed a privilege of the highest honor. The Mexican nobility was for the most part hereditary. Up to the downfall of the empire very many families descended from those illustrious Aztecs who founded Mexico were preserved in great splendor, and to this day several branches of those most ancient houses survive, but for the most part abased by poverty and mingled with the most obscure rabble. I would set forth here a demonstration of the advantages that would have resulted to both nations, and of the evils that the opposite conduct has caused, if the nature of this History permitted me. In Mexico, and in almost the whole empire, except in the royal house, as we have already said, sons succeeded their fathers in all their rights, and if there were no sons, the brothers, and if these too were lacking, the nephews. The lands of the Mexican empire were apportioned among the § 14. crown, the nobility, the communities, and the temples, and there Division of the lands, were paintings in which what belonged to each was distinctly repreand titles of possession and of property. sented. The crown lands were painted purple, those of the nobility scarlet, and those of the communities a light yellow. In them the extent and the boundaries of the holdings could be recognized at first sight. After the conquest the Spanish magistrates made use of such instruments to decide certain lawsuits that arose among the Indians over the ownership or possession of lands. In the crown lands, called by them Tecpantlalli, the ownership always being reserved to the king, the usufruct was enjoyed by certain lords called Tecpanpouhque or Tecpantlaca, that is, people of the palace. These paid no tribute and gave the king nothing but bunches of flowers and several kinds of birds, which they presented to him as a sign of vassalage every time they visited him; but they were bound to repair and rebuild the royal palaces, whenever necessary, and to cultivate the king's gardens, they contributing their direction, and the commoners of their district their labor. When one of these lords died, his eldest son entered into possession of the lands with all the obligations of his father; but if he went to settle in another place, he lost them, and then the king granted them to another usufructuary, or else left the choice of him to the discretion of the community in whose district the lands were situated. The lands which they called Pillalli, that is, lands of the nobles, were ancient possessions of the nobles, transmitted by inheritance from fathers to sons, or else were grants obtained from the king in reward for services rendered to the crown. The holders of both kinds could for the most part alienate their possessions, but could neither give nor sell them to commoners. I said for the most part, because among these lands there were some granted by the king on condition that they might not be alienated, but must be left by inheritance to their sons. In inheriting the lordships, regard was had to the birth of the sons; but if the eldest was unfit for the administration of the property, the father was entirely free to appoint another of his sons as heir, provided that he secured maintenance for the others. Daughters, at least in Tlaxcala, were not capable of inheriting, lest the lordship should come under the power of some foreigner. The Tlaxcalans were so jealous, even after the conquest by the Spaniards, of preserving the lordships in their families, that they refused to give the investiture of one of the four principalities of the republic to Don Francisco Pimentel, a grandson of Coanacotzin, king of Acolhuacan, (b) married to Doña María Maxixcatzin, a granddaughter of Prince Maxixcatzin, who was, as we shall see below, the foremost of the four lords who governed that republic at the arrival of the Spaniards. e: Fiefs began in that kingdom when King Xolotl divided the land of Bk. VII. Anahuac among the Chichimec lords and the Acolhuas, under the feudal conditions of an inviolable fidelity, of a certain acknowledgment of the supreme dominion, and of the obligation to aid the lord, wherever need might be, with their persons, their goods, and their vassals. Fiefs properly so called were few, as it seems to me, in the Mexican empire, and if we wish to speak with the rigor of the jurists, there was none; for they were neither perpetual by their nature, since every year they needed a new confirmation or investiture, nor were the vassals of the feudatories exempt from the tributes which the other vassals of the crown paid to the king. The lands called Altepetlalli, that is, those of the communities of the cities and of the villages, were divided into as many parts as there were wards in the city, and each ward possessed its part to the complete exclusion of the others and independently of them. These lands could not be alienated in any way. Among them there were some set aside to supply the army with provisions in time of war, which were called Milchimalli or Cacalomilli, according to the kind of provisions they furnished. The Catholic Kings have assigned lands to the towns of the Mexicans (*), and have given the appropriate orders to secure to them the perpetuity of such possessions; but nowadays many villages find themselves deprived of them through the overbearing power of certain private persons, abetted by the iniquity of certain judges. § 15. All the provinces conquered by the Mexicans were tributary to the Tributes and burdens crown, and contributed fruits, animals, and minerals of the country, of the subjects of the crown. according to the tariff prescribed to them; and besides this, all the merchants paid a part of their merchandise, and all the artisans a certain number of their works. e: These excessive contributions, together with the great presents that the governors of the provinces and the [p. 127] feudatory lords made to the king, and the spoils of war, formed that great wealth of the court which caused so much admiration among Bk. VII. the Spanish conquerors, and so much misery to the unfortunate subjects. The tributes, which at the beginning were quite light, later became excessive; for with the conquests the pride and the pomp of the kings increased. It is true that a great part, and perhaps the greatest, of these revenues was spent for the benefit of the subjects themselves, now maintaining a great number of ministers and magistrates for the administration of justice, now rewarding those who had deserved well of the state, now relieving the needy, especially widows, orphans, and the infirm aged, who were the three classes of people that deserved the greatest compassion from the Mexicans, now opening the royal granaries to the people in time of famine; but how many unhappy commoners, of those who could hardly pay the tribute imposed on them, must have been overwhelmed by misery because the royal beneficence did not reach them? To the excessive burdens was added the rigor with which they were collected. He who did not pay the tribute was sold as a slave, in order to draw from his liberty what could not be drawn from his industry. § 16. For the administration of justice the Mexicans had various tri‐ Magistrates of bunals and judges. In the court, and in the larger places of the king‐ Mexico and of Acolhuacan. dom, there was a supreme magistrate called Cihuacoatl, whose authority was so great that from the sentences pronounced by him, whether in civil or in criminal matters, there could be no appeal to another tribunal, nor even to the king himself. It fell to him to appoint the subordinate judges, and to make the collectors of the royal revenues of his district render account. Whoever used his insignia, or usurped his authority, was liable to death. Inferior to this, though quite considerable, was the tribunal of the Tlacatecatl, which was composed of three judges, namely the Tlacatecatl, who was the chief and from whom the tribunal took its name, and two others, whom they called Quauhnochtli and Tlailotlac. They took cognizance of civil and criminal cases in the first and in the second instance, although the sentence

e: [p. 128] was pronounced in the name of the Tlacatecatl alone. Every day they Bk. VII. assembled in a hall of the house of the community, which they called Tlatzontecojan, that is, a place where judgment is given, in which there were doorkeepers and constables. There they listened with great patience to the litigants, examined the cases diligently, and gave sentence according to the laws. If the case was purely civil, there was no appeal; but if it was criminal, one could appeal to the Cihuacoatl. The sentence was published by the Tepojotl, or crier, and carried out by the Quauhnochtli, who was, as we have already said, one of the three judges. Both the crier and the minister who executed justice were held in great esteem among the Mexicans, because they were regarded as images of the king. In every ward of the city there was a Teuctli, lieutenant of the tribunal of the Tlacatecatl, elected annually by the community of that ward. He took cognizance in the first instance of the cases of his district, and went daily to the Cihuacoatl or to the Tlacatecatl to inform him of everything that occurred and to receive his orders. Besides the Teuctli there were in each ward certain commissioners, likewise elected by the community of the ward, and called Centectlapixque; but these, as it seems to us, were not judges, but merely guardians charged with observing the conduct of a certain number of families committed to their care, and with informing the magistrates of whatever occurred among them. Under the orders of the Teuctli were the Tequitlatoqui, that is, the messengers, who carried the notifications of the magistrates and summoned the accused, and the Topilli, or constables, who made the arrests. In the kingdom of Acolhuacan jurisdiction was divided among six principal cities. The judges remained in the tribunals from the break of day until evening. Their dinner was brought to them in the very hall of the tribunal, and in order that they might not be diverted from their duty by attending to the maintenance of their families, nor have any pretext for corrupting the judgments, they had (as likewise in the kingdom of Mexico) their possessions, and peasants to cultivate their fields:

In grave cases they could not pass sentence (at least in the capital) without giving an account to the king. In the court, every Mexican month, or every twenty days, an assembly of all the judges was held before the king to conclude all the pending cases. If, because they were too complicated, they could not then be finished, they were reserved for another general and more solemn assembly, which was held every eighty days and was therefore called Nappapohuallatolli, that is, Conference of the Eighty, in which all the cases were wholly concluded, and there, before the whole assembly, punishment was inflicted on the convicted culprits. The king gave the sentence by making with the point of an arrow a line on the culprit's head, as painted in the record of the trial. In the trials of the Mexicans the parties themselves made their own pleadings; at least we do not know that there were advocates. In criminal cases the plaintiff was not allowed any other proof than that of witnesses; but the accused could clear himself by oath. In disputes over the boundaries of possessions the paintings of the lands were consulted, as authentic documents.

e: All the magistrates had to judge according to the laws of the kingdom, which they had expressed in paintings. Of these I have seen many, and from them I have drawn a part of what I shall say on this subject. The power of making laws in Texcoco always resided in the kings, who rigorously saw to it that those they published were observed. Among the Mexicans the first laws were made, as it seems to us, by the body of the nobility; but afterwards the kings were the lawgivers of the nation, and so long as their authority remained within just limits, they were zealous for the observance of those laws which they or their predecessors had promulgated. In the last years of the monarchy despotism altered them and changed them according to caprice. We shall recall here those that were in force when the Spaniards entered Mexico. In some of them will be seen to stand out a certain prudence, and humanity, [p. 130] and great zeal for good morals; but in others an excessive rigor, which Bk. VII. degenerated into cruelty. The traitor to the king or to the state was torn to pieces, and his § 17. relatives who, being aware of the treason, had not discovered it in Penal laws. time were deprived of liberty. The penalty of death and of confiscation of goods was established against anyone who dared to use in war, or in any public rejoicing, the insignia of the kings of Mexico, of Acolhuacan, and of Tacuba, or those of the Cihuacoatl. Whoever ill-treated an ambassador, or a minister, or a courier of the king was liable to death; but the ambassadors and couriers on their part were not to leave the highroad, on pain of losing their immunity. Likewise liable to death were those who caused any sedition among the people; those who removed or changed the boundaries set in the fields by public authority; and likewise the judges who gave an unjust sentence, or one contrary to the laws, or made to the king, or to the higher magistrate, a false report of some case, or let themselves be corrupted by gifts. He who in war committed some hostility against the enemy without orders from the chiefs, or attacked them before the signal was given, or abandoned the standard, or violated some proclamation published in the army, was beheaded without fail. He who in the market altered the measures established by the magistrates was liable to death, which was inflicted on him without delay in the very square. The murderer paid for his crime with his own life, even if the person killed was a slave. He who killed his wife, even if he had surprised her in adultery, was liable to death; because, as they said, he usurped the authority of the magistrates, whose business it was to take cognizance of misdeeds and to punish the evildoers. Adultery was punished irremissibly with the penalty of death.

e: Adulterers were stoned, or else they crushed their [p. 131] heads between two stones. This law, which prescribed the stoning of Bk. VII. adulterers, is one of those that I have seen represented in the ancient paintings preserved in the library of the Colegio Máximo of the Jesuits in Mexico City. It is seen also in the last painting of the Mendoza Collection, and Gómara, Torquemada, and other authors make mention of it. But the sin of the husband with some free woman, or one not bound by matrimony, was not reckoned adultery, or at least was not punished; so that they did not oblige the husband to as much fidelity as they required of the wife. Throughout the whole empire this crime was punished, but in some places with greater rigor than in others. In Ichcatlan the woman accused of adultery appeared before the judges, and if the proofs of the crime were convincing, the penalty was inflicted on her there without delay, by tearing her to pieces and dividing the pieces among the witnesses. In Itztepec the infidelity of the woman was punished, by sentence of the magistrates, by her husband, who cut off her nose and ears. In some parts of the empire the husband who had union with his wife was punished with the penalty of death, when it was established that she had already failed in fidelity. Repudiation was not lawful without the permission of the magistrates. He who wished to repudiate his wife presented himself in court and set forth his reasons. The judges exhorted him to concord and tried to dissuade him from the separation; but if he persisted in his claim, and the reasons seemed just, they told him to do whatever he judged best, without ever, however, authorizing the repudiation by a formal sentence. If he finally repudiated her, he could never take her back or be united with her again. Those guilty of incest in the first degree of consanguinity or of affinity were hanged, and all marriages between persons related in that degree were severely forbidden by the laws, except that between in-laws; for among the Mexicans, as among the Hebrews, there was the custom that the brothers of a deceased husband married the widowed sisters-in-law;

VII. among the Hebrews such a marriage took place only when the husband had died without issue, whereas among the Mexicans it was required, on the contrary, that the deceased leave children, whose education the brother took charge of, acquiring all the rights of a father. In some places too far distant from the capital the nobles were accustomed to marry their widowed stepmothers, when their fathers had had no children by them; but in the courts of Mexico and of Texcoco, and in the places nearest to them, such marriages were considered incestuous and were punished with severity. He who was guilty of the nefarious sin was hanged, and if he was a priest, they burned him alive. Among all the nations of Anahuac, except the people of Pánuco, this crime was held in abomination, and by all it was punished with rigor. Nevertheless certain malicious men, in order to justify their own excesses, defamed all the American nations with so horrible an excess; but of the falsity of such a calumny, which with too much, and quite blameworthy, readiness several European authors adopted, we are assured by the testimony of many other authors, impartial and better informed. VII. more distinguished the persons whom she served in such a trade, the heavier the penalties imposed on her. By law both the man who dressed as a woman and the woman who dressed as a man were hanged. The thief of trifling things had no other penalty than that of paying back what he had stolen. If the theft was large, the thief was made the slave of him from whom he had stolen. If the stolen thing no longer existed, and the thief had no goods with which to make satisfaction, he was stoned. If he stole gold or gems, after leading him through all the streets of the city, they sacrificed him at the festival which the goldsmiths held for their god Xipe. He who stole a certain number of ears of maize, or pulled up from another's field a certain number of useful plants, was made the slave of the owner of the field; (e) but any poor traveler was permitted to take from the maize plants, or from the fruit trees planted at the edge of the road, as much as sufficed to drive off his present hunger. He who stole in the market was beaten to death with clubs, without delay, in the very square. Likewise condemned to death was anyone who in the army stole from another his arms or his insignia. He who, finding some lost child, made a slave of him by selling him to another as if he were his own, lost as punishment for his crime both his liberty and his goods, half of which was applied to the child for his maintenance, and from the other half the price was paid to the buyer in order to restore the child to his liberty. If the offenders were many, all were subject to the same penalty. The same penalty of servitude and of loss of goods was imposed on anyone who sold the possessions of others that he had taken on lease. (e) The Anonymous Conqueror says that it sufficed to steal three or four ears to incur the penalty. Torquemada adds that it carried the penalty of death; but that was in the kingdom of Acolhuacan, not in that of Mexico.

e: Guardians who did not render a good account of the property of Bk. VII. their wards were hanged without remission. The same penalty awaited the sons who squandered in vices the inheritance they had received from their fathers, because, as they said, it was a great crime to hold in no regard the labors of their parents. He who practiced sorcery was sacrificed to the gods. Drunkenness in the young was a capital crime: the man was beaten to death with clubs in the prison, and the woman was stoned. In older men, although it was not punished with the penalty of death, it was nevertheless chastised with rigor. If he was a nobleman, they deprived him of his office and of his nobility, and he remained infamous; if he was a commoner, they shaved his head (a punishment they felt keenly), and razed his house, saying that he who voluntarily deprived himself of his reason was not worthy to live among men. This law did not forbid drunkenness at weddings, or at other such festivities, at which it was permitted to drink more than usual within the house; nor did it include septuagenarian old men, to whom, out of regard for their age, drinking as much as they pleased was allowed, as is established by painting LXIII of the Mendoza Collection. From him who told some lie that was gravely harmful they cut off a part of the lips, and sometimes the ears as well. § 18.    As for the Mexican law concerning slaves, it is to be noted that Laws concerning slaves. among them there were three sorts of slaves. The first was of prisoners of war, the second of those bought at a price, and the third of certain evildoers who, as punishment for their crimes, were deprived of liberty. Now, prisoners of war were for the most part sacrificed to their gods. Whoever in war took from another his prisoner, or set him at liberty, was liable to death. The sale of a slave was not valid unless it was made before four witnesses of advanced age. Commonly a greater number attended, and this contract was always celebrated with great solemnity.

e: The slave among the Mexicans could have private property, ac‐ Bk. VII. quire possessions, and even buy slaves to serve him, without the master's being able to prevent it, or to make use of such slaves; for slavery was nothing else than the obligation of personal service, and that restricted within certain limits. Neither was slavery hereditary among them. All were born free, even though their mothers were slaves. If a free man got another's slave with child, and she happened to die during her pregnancy, he remained the slave of the slave's master; but if she gave birth happily, both the son and the father remained free. Needy parents could sell some of their children to relieve their necessity, and any free man was permitted to sell himself for the same purpose; but masters could not sell their slaves without their consent, except those of the collar. Slaves who were runaways, contumacious, or vicious were admonished two or three times by their masters, who for their greater justification gave such admonitions before some witnesses. If in spite of this they did not amend, a wooden collar was put on them, and then they could be sold in the market. If after changing two or three masters they persisted in their indocility, they were sold for sacrifices; but this happened rarely. A slave of the collar who, escaping from the prison where his master perchance held him, took refuge in the royal palace remained free; and he who prevented him from taking this asylum lost his liberty as punishment for the attempt, except the master and his sons, who had the right to oppose it. The persons who sold themselves were for the most part gamblers, to stake the price of their liberty at play; those who through their sloth, or through some misfortune, found themselves reduced to misery; and prostitutes, to procure themselves finery to make a show in; since such women among the Mexicans generally sought no other advantage in their disorders

e: [p. 136] than that of their own pleasure. It did not grieve the Mexicans as Bk. VII. much to become slaves as it does other peoples, because the condition of their slavery was not so hard. The labors of slaves were moderate, and the treatment by their masters was for the most part kind, and the masters, when dying, commonly left them free. The ordinary price of a slave was a load of cotton garments. There was also among the Mexicans a kind of slavery which they called Huehuetlatlacolli; and it was when one or two families, because of their poverty, bound themselves to some lord to furnish him perpetually with a slave. They handed over, however, one of their children, and after he had served some years they took him back in order to marry him, or for some other reason, and substituted another. This was done without reluctance on the part of the master; indeed, for the most part he spontaneously gave something for the new slave. In the year 1506, on account of the famine that occurred, many families bound themselves to such servitude; but all were restored to liberty by Nezahualpilli, king of Acolhuacan, because of the inconveniences that were experienced, and, following his example, Moctezuma II did the same in his dominions. The conquerors, who believed themselves put in possession of all the rights of the ancient Mexican lords, had at the beginning many slaves of those nations; but the Catholic Kings, having been informed by learned persons, zealous for the public good and well instructed in the customs of those peoples, declared them all free and forbade, under heavy penalties, any attempt against their liberty, charging with so grave a point the conscience of the viceroys, the supreme tribunals, and the governors. A most just law, and worthy of the Christian zeal of those monarchs; for the first religious who labored in the conversion of the Mexicans, among whom there were men of great learning, declared, after a diligent examination, that among so many slaves not even one had been found of whom it was established that he had been justly deprived of his natural liberty.

e: What we have said so far is all that we know of the legislation of Bk. VII. the Mexicans. A more complete instruction on this subject would be most valuable to us, especially concerning their contracts, their judgments, and their last wills; but the deplorable loss of the greater part of their paintings, and of some precious manuscripts of the first Spaniards, has deprived us of such light. The laws of the capital were not so generally received in all the provinces subject to it that there was not considerable variety; for § 19. just as the Mexicans did not oblige the conquered peoples to speak Laws of other coun‐ tries of Anahuac. the language of the court, so neither did they compel them to adopt all their laws. The legislation of Acolhuacan was more like that of Mexico, but not so much that it was not different in several articles, and far more severe. According to the laws published by the celebrated King Nezahualcoyotl, the thief was dragged through the streets and then hanged. The murderer was beheaded. The active party in sodomy was smothered in a heap of ashes; from the passive party they tore out the entrails and filled the belly with ashes, and then burned him. He who by wicked arts caused discord between two states was burned alive, bound to a tree. He who got drunk to the point of losing his senses, if he was a noble, was hanged at once, and his body was thrown into the lake or into some river; if he was a commoner, he lost his liberty for the first offense and his life for the second; and when someone asked the lawgiver why his law was more severe with regard to nobles, he answered that their crime was so much the graver as their obligation to set a good example was the greater. The same King Nezahualcoyotl prescribed the penalty of death against historians who published any lie in their paintings. (*) He likewise condemned to

The Tlaxcalans adopted for the most part the laws of Acolhuacan. Among them, children who gravely failed in the respect due to their parents were put to death by order of the senate. Those who caused some harm to the public that did not deserve the penalty of death were exiled. Now, speaking generally, among all the civilized nations of Anahuac murder, theft, lying, adultery, and like crimes against continence were severely punished, and everywhere one sees the truth of what we said in speaking of their character, namely, that they were naturally inclined (as they still are) to severity, and more concerned with the punishment of vice than with the reward of virtue. § 20.    Among the punishments prescribed by the Mexican lawgivers Punishments and against evildoers, that of the gallows seems to have been one of the prisons. most infamous. That of exile also carried infamy, since it supposed in the culprit a contagious vice. The lash, however, was not found prescribed by the laws; nor do we know that it was used, except by fathers with their children and masters with their pupils. They had two kinds of prisons: one like our own, which they called Teilpilojan, for debtors who refused to pay their debts and for those culprits who did not deserve the penalty of death; and the other, stricter, which they called Quauhcalli, made like a cage, for the prisoners who were to be sacrificed and for those guilty of capital crimes.

e: Both were always kept under good guard. To those condemned to death very scanty food was given, so that they might begin in advance to taste the bitterness of death. The prisoners, on the contrary, were well fed, so that they might appear with a good complexion at the sacrifice. If through the negligence of the guard some prisoner escaped from the cage, the community of the ward, whose duty it was to provide the prisons with guards, was obliged to pay the master of the fugitive [p. 139] a slave, a load of cotton garments, and a buckler. Bk. VII. Having now spoken enough of the political government of the § 21. Mexicans, it is necessary to say what belongs to the military. There Officers of war, and was among them no profession more esteemed than that of arms. military orders. The god most revered by them was the god of war, whom they venerated as the principal protector of the nation. No prince was elected king unless he had first given in several battles proofs of courage and of military skill, until he had earned the illustrious post of general of the army; and no king was crowned until he had taken with his own hands the enemies who were to be sacrificed at the festivals of his coronation. All the Mexican kings, from Itzcoatl to Cuauhtémoc, who was the last, passed from the command of the army to the government of the kingdom. In the other life, too, the souls they esteemed most happy were those of men who died with arms in hand for their country. Because of the great value in which the profession of arms was held among them, they took care to encourage their children, and to harden them from the most tender age for the hardships of war. So advantageous a conception of the glory of arms was that which formed those heroes whose illustrious deeds we have already touched on; that which made them shake off the yoke of the Tepanecs and raise from so humble a beginning so splendid and so famous a monarchy; that, finally, which extended their dominion from the shores of the lake to the banks of the one sea and of the other. The supreme military dignity was that of general of the army; but there were four different ranks of generals, among which the most notable was that of Tlacochcalcatl (*), and each rank had its own particular insignia.
