(f) After the generals came the captains, each of whom commanded a certain number of soldiers. To reward the services of men of war, and to encourage them still more, the Mexicans invented three military orders, called Achcauhtin, Quauhtin, and Ocelo, that is, Princes, Eagles, and Tigers. The most esteemed were those who in the order of Princes were called Quachictin. These wore their hair bound at the top of the head with a red cord, from which hung as many tassels of cotton as they had performed glorious actions. This honor was held in such esteem among them that even the kings, not to mention the generals, boasted of having it. Moctezuma II belonged to this order, as Father Acosta affirms, and also King Tizoc, as appears from his portraits. The Tigers were distinguished by a certain armor which they wore spotted after the fashion of the skin of those beasts. Such dress was used only in war; at court all the officers of war wore a garment woven of various colors, which they called Tlachquauhjo. All those who went to war for the first time wore no insignia, but went clothed in a white and coarse garment of maguei cloth; and this was observed with such rigor that even the royal princes had to give proofs of their bravery before they could exchange that so ordinary garment for another, more valuable, called Tencaliuhqui. e: (h) Solís claims that the shield was used by none but lords; but the Anonymous Conqueror, who often saw the Mexicans under arms and found himself in many battles against them, says expressly that these arms were common to all. There is no author who speaks more exactly than he of the arms of the Mexicans. [p. 142] of large tortoise shells, trimmed with copper, silver, or gold according Bk. VII. to the rank they held in the militia and their means. These were of a regular size; but there were others so immense that they covered the whole body with them when they pleased; and when there was no need to use them, they shortened them and carried them under the arm, in the manner of our parasols, which may be believed to have been made of the skins of animals, or of cloth waxed with ule, or elastic resin. (*) On the other hand there were other shields, very small, less strong than beautiful, and adorned with beautiful feathers; but these were used not for war but only for the dances which they performed in the fashion of a battle. The defensive arms proper to the officers were certain cuirasses of cotton, a finger and even two fingers thick, which resisted arrows sufficiently well, and for that reason the Spaniards themselves used them in the war against the Mexicans. The name Ichcahuepilli, which the Mexicans gave to this sort of cuirass, was changed by the Spaniards into Escaupil. Over this cuirass, which covered only the trunk, they put on another armor, which, besides the trunk, covered the thighs and half of the arms, as may be seen in our figures of Mexican armor. The lords were accustomed to wear a thick overgarment of feathers over a cuirass composed of several plates of gold or of gilded silver, with which they made themselves impenetrable not only to arrows but also to darts and to our swords, as the Anonymous Conqueror attests. Besides the harness they wore to defend the trunk, the arms, the thighs, and even the legs, they used to wear the head encased in the head of a tiger or of a serpent, made of wood or of other material, with the mouth open and furnished with large teeth, to cause more fear, and so posed that, as the aforesaid author testifies, it seemed to be about to disgorge the soldier. All the officers and the nobles (*) The Anonymous Conqueror, Diego Godoy, and Bernal Díaz, all three of them conquerors, make mention of these large shields.

Erano agilissimi nel tirarle , e destrissimi nell’ imberciare, eflendo in ciò da fanciulli ‘eserci» tati, ed incoraggiti con premj da’ lor maestri, e da’ lor penitori . Le cose ma» ravigliose, che anche a' nostri tempi son vedute farsi da' Taraumarelì, dagli Hiaquelì, e d' altri Popoli di quelle regioni, che ancor conservano l' arco, e la freccia, ci fanno cono» scere ciò , che facevano anticamente i Messicani. e: Mexican armor. [p. 143] nobles wore a fine plume on the head, contriving by such additions to Bk. VII. make their stature appear more imposing. The common soldiers went entirely naked, with no other garment than the Maxtlatl, or girdle, with which they covered their nakedness; but they feigned the clothing they lacked with the various colors with which they painted their bodies. The European historians, who show themselves so amazed at this and at other extravagant customs of the Americans, do not perceive how common such customs were among the ancient nations of Europe itself. The offensive arms of the Mexicans were arrows, slings, clubs, lances, pikes, swords, and darts. Their bows were of an elastic wood, difficult to break, and the string of animal sinews or of spun deer hair. There were some bows so large (as there are even today among some nations of that continent) that they had a string of more than five feet. The arrows were of hard rods armed with a sharpened bone, or with a thick fishbone, or with flint, or with itztli. They were extremely nimble in shooting them and most dexterous in hitting the mark, being trained in this from boyhood and encouraged with prizes by their teachers and their parents. The people of Tehuacán were singularly renowned for their skill in shooting three or four arrows at once. The marvelous things which even in our times are seen to be done by the Tarahumaras, the Yaquis, and other peoples of those regions, who still keep the bow and arrow, make us know what the Mexicans did anciently. (i) No people of the country of Anahuac ever used poisoned arrows; perhaps because they wished to take their enemies alive in order to sacrifice them. (i) The dexterity of those peoples in shooting arrows would not be credible if it were not attested by the deposition of hundreds of eyewitnesses. Several archers, gathering together, throw up an ear of maize and set about shooting at it with such quickness and such dexterity that they do not let it come to the ground until they have taken off all its kernels. They likewise throw a silver coin no larger than a giulio, and by shooting at it keep it in the air as long as they wish.

e: The Maquahuitl, called a sword by the Spaniards, because it was the weapon which they had there equivalent to the sword of the old Bk. VII. continent, was a strong staff about three and a half feet long and four fingers wide, armed on one side and on the other with certain extremely sharp razors of itztli stone, set in and tenaciously fastened to the staff with gum lac; (k) which razors were three fingers long, one or two wide, and as thick as our ancient swords. So cutting was this weapon that, according to Father Acosta, it happened that a horse was completely decapitated with a single blow of it; (l) but only the first blow was to be feared, because the razors soon became blunt. They carried this weapon tied to the arm with a cord, so that it would not slip from them when they delivered their blows. The form of the Maquahuitl is found in several historians, and can be seen in our figures. The pikes of the Mexicans had, instead of iron, a large flint, but others had a copper point. The Chinantecs and some peoples of Chiapas used pikes so immense that they were more than three perches, or eighteen feet, in length, and the conqueror Cortés made use of them against the cavalry of his rival Pánfilo de Narváez. The Tlacochtli, or Mexican dart, was a little lance of otatli, or of some other strong wood, with the point hardened in the fire, or else armed with copper, itztli, or bone, and many had three points in order to inflict three wounds with them at once. They carried the staff of the standard so tightly bound on the back that it was almost impossible to tear it away without cutting to pieces the man who carried it. The Mexicans always carried it in the center of the army. The Tlaxcalans, when their troops marched in time of peace, carried it in the vanguard; but in time of war in the rear guard. Their military music, in which there was more noise than harmony, was composed of small drums, of cornets, and of certain large sea snails, which gave out a very shrill sound. § 25.    To declare war, the cause for undertaking it was first examined in Manner of declaring and of waging war. the council, which was for the most part the rebellion of some city or province, the killing of some Mexican, Acolhua, or Tepanec couriers or merchants, or some grave insult offered to their ambassadors. If the rebellion was that of some chiefs, and not of the peoples, the culprits were brought to the capital to be punished. If the people also were guilty, satisfaction was demanded of them in the name of the king. If they submitted and showed true repentance, their fault was pardoned them and they were exhorted to amend; but if, instead of humbling themselves, they answered with arrogance and persisted in denying the satisfaction demanded, or else committed a new insult against the messengers sent to them, the matter was debated in the council, and when the resolution for war had been taken the appropriate orders were given to the generals. Sometimes the kings, to justify their conduct still further, before undertaking war against some place or state, sent three different embassies: the first to the lord of the guilty state, demanding of him a fitting satisfaction, and prescribing the time within which he must give it, on pain of being treated as an enemy; the second to the nobility, so that they might persuade their lord to escape by submission the punishment that hung over him; and the third to the people, to make them aware of the causes of the war; and sometimes, according to what one historian says, so effective [p. 147] were the reasons proposed by the ambassadors, and so vividly did they exaggerate the advantages of peace and the inconveniences of Bk. VII. war, that some accommodation was arrived at. They were also accustomed to send with the ambassadors the idol of Huitzilopochtli, requiring those who caused the war to give him a place among their gods. If these found themselves with forces sufficient to resist, they rejected the proposal and dismissed the foreign god; but if they did not find themselves in a condition to sustain the war, they received the idol and placed it among their provincial gods, and answered the embassy with a good present of gold, and of gems, or of beautiful feathers, protesting their submission to the sovereign. In case war had to be made, before anything else notice was given to the enemies, so that they might prepare for defense, since they considered it a cowardice, utterly unworthy of courageous men, to assail the unprepared; and for that purpose some shields, which were a token of challenge, and some cotton garments were sent ahead. If one king challenged another, the ceremony was added of anointing him and of fastening feathers to his head by means of the ambassador, as happened in the challenge of King Itzcoatl to the Tyrant Maxtla. Then they dispatched spies, to whom they gave the name of Quimichtin, or mice, so that, disguised, they might go into the enemy's country to observe their movements and the number and quality of the troops that were being made ready. If these men succeeded in their commission, they were well rewarded. Finally, after having made some sacrifices to the god of war and to the tutelary gods of the state or city against which the war was waged, in order to earn their protection, the army marched, not drawn up in wings nor ordered in files, but yet divided into companies, each with its own chief and its own standard. When the army was numerous, it was reckoned by Xiquipilli; and each Xiquipilli was made up of eight thousand men. It is very probable that each of these corps was commanded by a Tlacatecatl or other general. The place where the first battle was commonly given was a field appointed for that purpose in each province, and called T2                Jaotlalli

Jaotlalli, that is, land, or field of battle. The battle was begun with a Bk. VII. frightful noise (much used in ancient Europe, even among the Romans) of the military instruments, of shouts, and of whistles so loud that they frightened anyone not accustomed to hearing them, as the Anonymous Conqueror attests from his own experience. Among the Texcocans, and perhaps among the other peoples as well, the king or the general gave the signal for battle with the sound of a small drum, which he carried hung from his shoulders. Their first onset was furious; but they did not all hurl themselves at once, as several authors have published; for they were accustomed, as is evident from their history, to keep troops in reserve for the greatest need. Sometimes they began the battle with arrows, and sometimes with darts and with stones, and when they had used up the arrows, they employed pikes, clubs, and swords. They took the greatest pains to preserve the union of their ranks, to defend the standard, and to withdraw the dead and the wounded from the sight of their enemies. There were in the army certain men who had no other employment than that of removing from the eyes of the enemies such objects as might have revived their courage and made their pride more insolent.

e: They often used ambushes, hiding among the bushes, or in pits made on purpose, of which the Spaniards had only too much experience; and they frequently feigned flight in order to draw the enemies, engaged in pursuing them, to some dangerous place, or to attack them with fresh troops at their backs. Their greatest effort in battles was not so much to kill as to take prisoners for the sacrifices; nor was a soldier's valor esteemed by the number of the dead he left on the field, but by that of the prisoners whom after the battle he presented to the general, as we have said elsewhere; and this was without doubt one of the principal causes of the preservation of the Spaniards amid so many perils, and above all on that dreadful night in which they came out routed from the capital. When some enemy, already beaten, strove to save himself by flight, they cut [p. 149] his hamstrings, so that he could not escape. When they saw the stan‐ Bk. VII. dard of the army taken by the enemy, or their general dead, they all fled, and then no human force was capable of restraining them. When the battle was over, the victors celebrated the victory with great rejoicings, and rewarded the officers and soldiers who had taken some prisoners. When the king of Mexico took some enemy in person, embassies were sent to him from all the provinces of the kingdom to congratulate him and to present him with some gift. They dressed the prisoner in the finest garments, adorned him with jewels, and carried him in a litter to the court, whence the citizens came out to meet him with music and loud acclamations. When the day of the sacrifice had come, after the king had fasted the day before, as the owners of victims were accustomed to do, they carried the royal prisoner, adorned with the insignia of the Sun, to the common altar of the sacrifices, where he was sacrificed by the high priest. The latter made with his blood an aspersion toward the four principal winds, and sent a vessel full of the same blood to the king, who had it sprinkled upon all the idols that were within the enclosure of the great temple, in thanksgiving for the victory won over the enemies of the state. They skewered the head on a very tall pole, and when the skin of the body had dried, they stuffed it with cotton and hung it in the royal palace, in remembrance of so glorious a deed; in which flattery played no small part. When some city was about to be besieged, the greatest concern of the besieged was to put in safety their children, their women, and the infirm; wherefore they sent them in good time to another city, or else to the mountains. Thus they saved that feeble folk from the fury of the enemies, and prevented the excessive consumption of provisions. § 26. (o) The court of Mexico, strong enough in those times by its situation, had made itself impregnable to its enemies by the industry of its inhabitants. There was no access to the city except by the causeways built on the lake, and to make it still more difficult in time of war, they had constructed many bulwarks on those same causeways and had cut them with several deep ditches, over which they had drawbridges, and to defend the ditches they made good trenches. These ditches were the sepulchers of so many Spaniards and Tlaxcalans on the terrible night of July 1, of which we shall speak later, and they were what so greatly delayed the capture of that great city by an army so numerous and so advantageously armed as the one Cortés employed in the siege; and had it not been for the brigantines, they would have found it harder to take the city, and it would have cost them more blood. To defend the city by water they had many thousands of boats, and often they exercised themselves in this kind of combat. VII. ple, the five armories that were there furnished with every sort of offensive and defensive arms, and the very architecture of the temple, which made the ascent so difficult, make it clearly evident that in such buildings politics had no less interest than religion, and that in constructing them they attended not only to their superstition but also to their defense. We know from history that they fortified themselves in the temples when they could not prevent the enemies from entering the city, and from there harassed them with arrows, darts, and volleys of stones. In the last book of this history we shall see how much the Spaniards struggled to take the great temple, where five hundred Mexican nobles had fortified themselves. The very high esteem in which the things of war were held among the Mexicans did not distract them from the arts of peace. First, agriculture, which is one of the principal occupations of civil life, was practiced from time immemorial by the Mexicans and by almost all the nations of Anahuac. The Toltecs applied themselves diligently to it and taught it to the hunting Chichimecs. Concerning the Mexicans, we know that throughout that long migration which they made from their native land Aztlan to the lake where they founded Mexico, they cultivated the earth in those places where they stayed for some time, and sustained themselves on their harvests. Afterward, overpowered by the Colhuas and the Tepanecs and reduced to the wretched islets of the lake, they ceased for some years to cultivate the § 27. land, because they had none, until, taught by necessity and by indusFloating fields and try, they formed movable and floating fields and gardens on the very gardens on the Mexican lake. waters of the lake. The method they had then of making them, and which they still observe, is quite simple. They make a plaiting of withes, or of the roots of certain marsh plants, or of other light material, but capable nevertheless of holding the earth of the garden together. Upon such a foundation they lay light brushwood of the same plants that float on the lake, and above all the mud which they draw from the bottom of the same lake. Their regular figure is oblong:

e: [p. 153] the length and the breadth vary; but for the most part they are, as it seems to me, about eight perches in length, not more than three in Bk. VII. breadth, and less than a foot in elevation above the surface of the water. These were the first fields which the Mexicans had after the founding of Mexico, in which they cultivated maize, chili pepper, and other plants necessary to their sustenance. In the time that followed, when they had multiplied excessively through the industry of that people, there were also gardens of flowers and of fragrant herbs, which were used for the worship of the gods and for the delight of the lords. At present flowers and every sort of vegetable are cultivated there. Every day of the year at the break of dawn there are seen arriving by the canal at the great square of that capital countless boats laden with many kinds of flowers and herbs cultivated in those gardens. Everything grows there marvelously; for the mud of the lake is most fertile, besides which it has no need of the water of heaven. In the larger gardens there is usually some shrub, and even a hut, for the cultivator to take shelter in and to protect himself from the rain and the sun. When the owner of some garden, or, as they commonly call it, Chinampa, wishes to move to another site, whether to get away from a harmful neighbor or to be nearer his family, he gets into his boat, and by himself, if the garden is small, or helped by others, if it is large, tows it behind him and takes it wherever he wishes, together with the hut and the shrubs. That part of the lake where these gardens and flower gardens are is a place of recreation supremely delightful, where the senses take the sweetest pleasure in the world. After the Mexicans, having shaken off the yoke of the Tepanecs, § 28. began by their conquests to procure arable lands for themselves, they Mannerthe land.

Having neither plow, nor oxen, nor other animals to employ in the cultivation of the land, they made up for it with their own labor and with some very simple instruments. To hoe and dig the earth they made use of the Coatl (today Coa), which is an instrument of copper with a wooden handle, but different from the hoe, and [p. 154] from the spade. To cut trees they used their axe, likewise of copper, Bk. VII. which was of the same shape as ours, except that where ours has its eye, where the handle is put in, theirs, on the contrary, was put inside the eye of the handle. They had also other instruments of agriculture; but the negligence of the ancient writers on this subject has deprived us of the lights necessary for undertaking their description. To irrigate the fields they made use of the waters of the rivers and of the ditches that came down from the mountains, making weirs to hold them back and channels to carry them. In high places, or on the slopes of the mountains, they did not sow every year; but let them lie fallow until there was much brush, which they burned, and with its ashes they restored the salts which the waters had carried off. They surrounded their fields with enclosures of stone, or with hedges of maguei, which are very advantageous, and in the month Panquetzaliztli, which began, as we have already said, on December 3, they repaired them, if need be. The method which they then had, and which they still preserve in some places, of sowing maize is this. The sower makes a little hole in the ground with a stick whose point is hardened in the fire, and throws into it one or two grains of maize from a basket which he keeps hung from his shoulder, and covers it with a little earth, using for this purpose one of his feet; he passes on, and at a certain distance, which varies according to the quality of the soil, makes another hole, and so continues in a straight line to the end of the field, and from there returns forming another line parallel to the first. The lines become as straight as if they had been made with a cord, and the distance between plant and plant as equal everywhere as if it had been taken by measure. This manner of sowing, scarcely used nowadays by some Indians, though slower, (*) is nevertheless more advantageous, since it proportions with greater

Next to the sown fields they used to make certain little towers of timbers and branches, or mats, in which a man, protected from the sun and the rain, kept watch and with a sling drove off the birds that flocked there to damage the crops. The Mexicans were also most devoted to the cultivation of Kitchen gardens, gar‐ kitchen gardens and gardens, in which were planted in fine order fruit dens, and woods. trees, medicinal herbs, and flowers, of which they made great use, no less for the extreme pleasure they took in them than for the custom there was of presenting bouquets of flowers to the kings, the lords, the ambassadors, and other persons of distinction, besides the excessive quantity that was used both in the temples and in private oratories. Among the ancient kitchen gardens and gardens of which some memory remains to us, very famous were the royal gardens of Mexico and of Texcoco, mentioned by us elsewhere, and those of the lords of Iztapalapa and of Oaxtepec. Among the gardens of the vast palace of the lord of Iztapalapa there was one whose size, arrangement, and beauty roused the admiration of the Spanish conquerors. In it were laid out in various beds many kinds of plants, which gave no less pleasure to the sight than to the smell, and among the beds many walks formed, some of fruit trees and others of espaliers of flowers and aromatic herbs. Several canals from the lake watered it, by one of which boats entered. In the center of the garden there was a square fishpond so large that it had sixteen hundred paces in circuit, that is, four hundred on each side, in which lived innumerable water birds, and on each side it had steps for descending to the bottom. This garden, of which Cortés and Díaz make mention as eyewitnesses, was planted, or at least enlarged and improved, by Cuitláhuac, brother and [p. 157] successor to Moctezuma II in the kingdom. He had many foreign Bk. VII. trees transplanted there, as Dr. Hernández attests, who saw them. Much larger and more famous than that of Iztapalapa was the garden of Oaxtepec. This was six miles in circuit and was watered by a fine river that crossed it. Innumerable species of trees and of pleasing plants were planted in it in good order and symmetry, and at proportionate distances from one another were built several pleasure houses. Among the plants there were many foreign ones, brought there even from distant countries. The Spaniards preserved this garden for many years, and cultivated in it every sort of medicinal herbs suited to that climate, for the use of the hospital which they founded there, in which the admirable hermit Gregorio López served for many years. (p) Nor had they less care for the conservation of the woods, for the supply of wood for burning and for building, and of game for the recreation of the king. (q) Among the plants most cultivated by the Mexicans, the principal § 31. ones after maize were those of cotton, cacao, Metl, or maguei, Chia, Plants most cultivated by the Mexicans. and chili pepper, because of the great usefulness they afforded them. The maguei by itself supplied almost everything needed for the life of the poor. Besides making good hedges of it for the sown fields, its trunk was used instead of beams in the roofs of huts, and its leaves instead of tiles. From these leaves they drew paper, thread, needle, clothing, footwear, and cords, and from the very abundant juice it yields they made wine, honey, sugar, and vinegar. From the trunk and the thickest part of the leaves, baked under ground, they drew a not unpleasant dish. In it, finally, they had a powerful medicine for several diseases, and especially for those of the urine. Even today it is one of the most prized plants and one of the most advantageous to the Spaniards, as we shall see below. As for the rearing of animals, which is an accessory occupation to § 32. The rearing of that of agriculture, although among the Mexicans there were no animals. shepherds, since they entirely lacked flocks, there were nevertheless raised in their houses innumerable species of animals unknown in Europe. Private men raised Techichi, quadrupeds resembling, as we have said, our little dogs, turkeys, or American peacocks, quails, geese, ducks, and other species of birds; in the houses of many lords, fish, deer, rabbits, and very many birds; and in the royal houses almost all the species of quadrupeds and flying animals of those countries, and very many aquatic animals and reptiles. It may be said that in this kind of magnificence Moctezuma II surpassed all the kings of the world, and (q) Many places are by now feeling the effects of the pernicious freedom of cutting the woods. The city of Querétaro formerly supplied itself with the timber necessary for its buildings from the wood that was on the neighboring Mount Cimatario. Today it is necessary to bring it from afar, because that mountain is now entirely bare of trees. [p. 159] and that there has never been a nation that could be compared to the Bk. VII. Mexicans in the care of so many species of animals, or in the knowledge of their inclinations, of the food suitable to each, and of all the means for their preservation and for their propagation. Among the animals reared by the Mexicans none is more worthy of being recalled than the Nochiztli, or Mexican cochineal, described by us in the first book. This insect, so prized in Europe for dyeing, and above all for that of scarlet and crimson, being on the one hand so delicate, and on the other so persecuted by a good many enemies, requires far greater care in those who rear it than is needed for silkworms. Rain, cold, and strong wind harm it. Birds, mice, worms, and other animals pursue it furiously and devour it; hence it is necessary to keep always clean the plantations of prickly pear, or nopal, where these insects are reared, to watch continually in order to drive off the pernicious birds, to make for the insects themselves nests of hay or moss in the leaves of the prickly pear, on whose juice they feed, and to take them off the plants together with the leaves, when the season of the rains comes, in order to put them away in the dwellings. Before giving birth the females change their skin, and to remove this husk from them they use the tail of the rabbit, handling it gently so as not to detach them from the leaves or do them any harm. On each leaf they make three nests, and in each nest they put as many as fifteen cochineals. Every year they make three harvests, reserving in each a certain number for the future generation; but the last harvest is less prized, since in it the cochineals are smaller and come mixed with the scrapings of the prickly pear. For the most part they kill the cochineal in hot water. Then the quality of the color that results from it depends chiefly on the manner of drying it. The best cochineal is that which is dried in the sun. Some dry it on the comalli, or griddle, where they bake their maize bread, and others in the temazcalli, or hypocaust, of which we shall speak elsewhere.

The Mexicans could not have gathered so many kinds of animals if Bk. VII. they had not been skilled in the exercise of hunting. For this they § 33. used the bow and arrows, darts, nets, foot-traps, or snares, and blowHunting of the guns. The blowguns used by the kings and the principal lords were cu‐ Mexicans. riously carved, painted, and even mounted with gold or silver. Besides the hunting done by private persons, either to provide themselves with meat or for mere diversion, general hunts were wont to be held, either established by custom to procure a great supply of victims for the sacrifices, or prescribed extraordinarily by the king. For such a hunt a great wood was chosen, which was most often that of Zacatepec, not far from the capital, and there the most suitable place for setting up a great number of snares and nets. Some thousands of hunters made a great circle round the wood of six, eight, or more miles, according to the number of animals they wished to hunt: they set fire everywhere to the hay and the grass, and made at the same time a frightful din of drums, cornets, shouts, and whistles. The animals, frightened by the noise and the fire, fled toward the center of the wood, which was precisely the place where the snares were set. The hunters made their way toward the same spot, and, continuing the noise all the while, kept narrowing the circle, until they left a very small space for the game, and then all hurled themselves against it with their weapons. Of the animals some were killed, and others were taken alive in the snares or in the hands of the hunters. So great was both the multitude and the variety of the animals that were hunted, that the first viceroy of Mexico, having heard it said, and not finding it credible, wished to make the experiment for himself. He assigned as the place of the hunt a great plain which lies in the country of the Otomis between the villages of Xilotepec and San Juan del Río, that is, of the river, and ordered those Indians to make it in the same manner in which they were wont to make it in the time of their heathendom.

e: The same viceroy betook himself with a great retinue of Spaniards to the aforesaid plain, [p. 161] where lodging had been prepared for him in wooden houses built for the purpose. Eleven thousand Otomis formed a circle of more than Bk. VII. fifteen miles, and having done all that we have indicated, there gathered so much game into the plain that the viceroy, full of wonder, commanded that the greater part of it be set at liberty, as in fact was done; nevertheless the animals hunted were so many that it would not be credible, had it not been a public fact, attested by many, and among others by a witness worthy of the highest credit. (*) More than six hundred deer and wild goats were killed, more than a hundred coyotes, and a surprising number of hares, rabbits, and other quadrupeds. That plain still preserves the Spanish name which was then given it, Cazadero, or place of the hunt. Besides the ordinary way of hunting they had others, peculiar and suited to the nature of the animals. To catch monkeys they made a little fire in the wood, and placed among the embers a certain species of stone called by them Cacalotetl (stone of the Raven, or black), which has the property of bursting with great noise when it is well heated. They covered the fire with earth, and scattered a little maize around it. The monkeys, attracted by the grain, ran up, bringing their young with them, and while they were pleasantly eating, the stone burst: they fled in terror, leaving their young in danger, and the hunters, placed in ambush, seized them before the mothers could return to take them back. The way they had, and still have today, of hunting ducks was also curious. There is, both in the lakes of the Valley of Mexico and in others of that kingdom, a prodigious multitude of ducks, geese, and other aquatic birds. The Mexicans left floating on the waters where these birds gathered some hollow gourds, so that, growing accustomed to seeing them, they should approach them without fear. (*) Father Toribio de Benavente, otherwise Motolinía.

They took serpents alive, either snaring them with the utmost dexterity, or approaching them intrepidly and seizing them by the neck with one hand, while with the other they sewed up their mouths. They still practice this kind of hunting, and every day there are seen in the apothecaries’ shops of the capital and of other cities many serpents taken alive in this way. But nothing is more marvelous than their sagacity in tracking wild beasts by their footprints. Although no mark of the beasts appears imprinted, the ground being covered with grass or with dry leaves that fall from the trees, still they follow after them, especially if they are wounded, observing most shrewdly now the drops of blood that they leave on the leaves, now the grass trampled or beaten down by their feet. I hear the same said of the Yucatecans. [p. 163] the manner of performing so bold an action against so terrible a beast. The other method, still used by some, is the very one once em‐ Bk. VII. ployed by the Egyptians against the celebrated crocodiles of the Nile. The fisherman presented himself to the crocodile carrying in his hand a stout stick sharpened at both ends, and when that beast opened its mouth to devour him, he put his armed arm into its jaws, and the crocodile, wishing to close its mouth, was transfixed by both points of the stick. The fisherman waited until it was weakened by the loss of blood, and then killed it. Fishing, hunting, agriculture, and the arts furnished the Mexicans §Trade. 35. with several branches of trade. This was begun by them in the country of Anahuac as soon as they settled on the islets of Lake Texcoco. The fish that they caught there, and the mats that they wove of the rush which the same lake produces, they bartered for the maize, the cotton, and the stone, lime, and timber they needed for their sustenance, their clothing, and their buildings. In proportion to the power which they acquired by their arms, their trade increased and extended; so that, being at the beginning confined to the environs of their city, it afterwards spread to the most remote provinces. There were infinite numbers of Mexican merchants who traveled incessantly, carrying from one city some goods to barter at a profit in another. In all the places of the Mexican empire, and of the whole vast country of Anahuac, there was a market every day; but every five days there was a larger and general one. Places not far from one another held this great market on different days, so as not to harm one another; but in the capital it was held on the days of House, Rabbit, Cane, and Flint, which in the first year of the century were the third, the eighth, the thirteenth, and the eighteenth of each month. The square of Tlatelolco was, according to what the Conqueror Cortés says, twice as large as that of Salamanca, one of the most renowned in Spain, (s) square in form, and surrounded on all sides by porticoes for the convenience of the merchants. Each kind of merchandise had its place assigned by the Judges of Commerce. In one spot there were the goods of gold and silver, and the jewels; in another the manufactures of cotton; in another the featherwork; and so with the other things; and no one was permitted to change his place. But because in that square, however large, not all the merchandise could be accommodated without obstructing the dealers, there was an order to leave in the streets and in the neighboring canals the bulkier goods, such as beams, stones, and the like. The number of merchants who came there daily was, according to what Cortés himself affirms, more than fifty thousand. (t) The things that were sold or bartered there were so many and so various that the historians who saw them, after making a long and prolix enumeration of them, conclude by saying that it was altogether impossible to name them all. I, without departing from their account, shall try to tell them in a few words, in order to spare the readers the tedium. e: (u) Whoever reads the description of the market given by Cortés, by Bernal Díaz, and by the Anonymous Conqueror will see that there is no exaggeration in what I say of the variety of the merchandise. [p. 166] certain small cotton cloths, which they called Patolquachtli, intended almost Bk. VII. solely for the purchase of the merchandise they needed. The third kind was gold in grain, contained inside goose quills, which by their transparency allowed the precious metal they enclosed to be seen, and according to their thickness were of greater or lesser value. The fourth, which came nearest to coined money, consisted of certain pieces of copper in the form of a T, which was used for things of little value. The fifth, of which Cortés makes mention in his last letter to the Emperor Charles V, consisted of certain thin pieces of tin. Goods were sold and bartered by number and by measure; but we do not know that they made use of weight, either because they thought it exposed to frauds, as some authors have said; or because it did not seem necessary to them, as others affirm; or because, although they used it, the Spaniards did not know it. (x) To prevent frauds in contracts and disorders among the dealers, there were § 37. Order in the markets. certain commissaries who went continually through the market observing what took place, and a Tribunal of Commerce composed of twelve judges, residing in a house in the square and charged with deciding all the disputes that arose among the dealers and with taking cognizance of all the crimes committed in the marketplace. On all the goods that were brought into the market a certain duty was paid to the king, who for his part bound himself to do justice to the merchants and to keep their goods and persons unharmed. Seldom was a theft seen in the market, because of the vigilance of the royal ministers and the severity with which it was immediately punished. But what wonder that theft should be punished where minor disorders were not pardoned? The industrious and most truthful Father (x) Gómara believed that the Mexicans did not use weight because they were ignorant of it; but it is not likely that a nation so industrious and so practiced in trade did not know the way of discerning the weight of things, whereas among other American nations less shrewd than the Mexicans there were found, according to what the same author affirms, steelyards for weighing gold. How many things of American antiquity we are ignorant of, because suitable and diligent inquiries have not been made!

e: of Tlaxcala should perhaps be understood of the market held every five days, as we have said of that of Mexico. [p. 168] hand a black, smooth staff, which, according to them, was the image Bk. VII. of their god Yacatecuhtli, and with which they thought themselves safe amid the perils of the journey. As soon as they arrived at some inn they gathered together and tied up all the staffs, and paid them worship, and in the night two or three times drew blood from themselves in honor of that god. All the time that the merchant was absent from his house, his wife and his children did not wash their heads, although they bathed, except once every eighty days, both to show their grief at his absence and to procure the protection of their gods by such a mortification. When any of the merchants died on the journey, the news was sent directly to the oldest merchants of his native place, and these communicated it to his relatives, who immediately made a shapeless statue of pine wood representing the deceased, and performed over it all the funeral ceremonies that they would have performed over the corpse itself. For the convenience of the merchants and of other travelers there § 39. were  public roads, which care was taken to repair every year after the Roads, inns, boats, rainy  season. They also had, on the mountains and in desert places, bridges, etc. houses built expressly for the lodging of the same wayfarers, and on the rivers they had bridges, boats, and other contrivances for crossing them. Their boats were oblong and flat underneath, without keel, masts, sails, or any other device for driving them but oars. Their size varied. The smallest scarcely carried two or three persons, and the largest could carry more than thirty. Many were made of a single hollowed tree trunk. The number of those that went continually on the Mexican lake exceeded, according to what the ancient historians affirm, fifty thousand. Besides boats, for crossing rivers they made use of a particular contrivance called balsa by the Spaniards of America.

e: This was a square platform, about five feet in size, made of otatli, or solid canes, bound tightly upon large gourds, hard and hollow. Four or six [p. 169] passengers at a time; and they were conducted from one bank of the river to the other by one, two, or four swimmers, who, holding a cor‐ Bk. VII. ner of the contrivance with one hand, swam with the other. This contrivance is still in use on some rivers distant from the capital, and I crossed a large river of the Mixteca on it in 1739. It is safe where the course of the water is even and tranquil, but dangerous on rapid and impetuous rivers. Their bridges were of stone or of wood; but those of stone were, as it appears, very few. The most singular was the one to which the Spaniards of those countries gave the name Hamaca. This was a braiding of certain ropes, or natural ligaments of a tree, more pliant than osiers, but thicker still and stronger, called in America Bejucos, whose ends they fastened to the trees on the one bank and the other of the rivers, the braiding, or net, remaining suspended in the air like a swing. (*) Such bridges are still seen on some rivers. The Spaniards dare not cross them; but the Indians cross with as much confidence and fearlessness as if they were walking over a stone bridge, paying no heed to the swaying of the Hamaca or to the depth of the river. But, on the other hand, it may be said that, since the ancient Mexicans were good swimmers, they had no need of bridges, except when, because of the rapidity of the water or the weight of the load they carried, they could not cross by swimming. The historians of Mexico tell us nothing of the maritime trade of the Mexicans. It is to be believed that it was of no importance, and that their boats which were seen coasting along the one sea and the other were for the most part those of fishermen. The place where the greatest traffic by water took place was the Mexican lake. All the stone and timber for buildings and for fuel, the fish, the greater part of the maize, the legumes, fruits, flowers, etc., were carried by water. The trade

VII. cities situated on the lake, was carried on by water, and hence there was that astonishing multi‐ tude of boats of which we have made mention. What was not transported by water was carried on the back, and hence there were infinite numbers of porters, called Tlamama or Tlameme. They were accustomed from childhood to such § 40. an exercise, in which they had to employ their whole lives. The usual load was about sixty Porters. pounds, and the distance they covered each day was fifteen miles; but in this way they made journeys of two and three hundred miles, often walking over crags and rugged mountains. They were subjected to such intolerable toil through the lack of beasts of burden; and even today, although such beasts abound so greatly in those countries, Mexicans are frequently seen making long journeys with a good load on their backs. They carried cotton, maize, and other goods in petlacalli, which were chests made of a certain kind of cane and covered with leather, and which, being light, protected the merchandise sufficiently from the injuries of the sun and of the water. They are still much used today for the journeys of the Spaniards, who call them, corruptly, petacas. The trade of the Mexicans was not hampered by the multitude and variety of the languages § 41. that were spoken in those countries; for the Mexican, which was the dominant language, was unThe Mexican derstood and spoken everywhere. This was the proper and natural language of the Acolhuas and language. of the Aztecs, (z) and, as we have discussed elsewhere, that of the Chichimecs and of the Toltecs as well. Now (z) The Chevalier Boturini says that the excellence of the language which we call Mexican was the reason why the Chichimecs, the Mexicans, and the Teochichimecs adopted it, abandoning their native tongue; but besides that such an opinion is quite opposed to that of all the writers, and of the Indians themselves, there is found in history no trace of such a change. Where has a nation ever been seen to abandon its native idiom in order to adopt another and better one, and especially a nation so tenacious of its primitive language as the Mexican, and all the others of those countries?

e: Now the Mexican language, of which we wish to give the readers Bk. VII. some idea, is entirely lacking in the consonants B, D, F, G, R, and S, and abounds in L, X, T, Z, Tl, and Tz; but although L is so familiar to this language, there is no word at all that begins with that consonant. Nor is there any word of acute ending, except some vocatives. Almost all words have the penultimate syllable long. Its aspirations are moderate and soft, nor is it ever necessary to use the nose in pronunciation. In spite of the lack of those six consonants it is a most copious language, very polished and extremely expressive: whence it has been singularly prized and extolled by all those Europeans who have learned it, to the point of being esteemed by many superior to Latin, and even to Greek; (A) but although I recognize the singular merits of the Mexican language, I would never dare to compare it with Greek. Of the copiousness of this language we have a good proof in the Natural History of Dr. Hernández; for, since there are described in it twelve hundred plants of the country of Anahuac, two hundred and more species of birds, and a great number of quadrupeds, reptiles, insects, and minerals, scarcely will anything be found that has not its proper name. But what wonder that it abounds in words signifying material objects, when almost none is lacking to it of those that are needed to express spiritual things? The loftiest mysteries of our Religion are found well explained in Mexican, without it ever having been necessary to make use of foreign words. Father Acosta wonders that the Mexicans, having had knowledge of a supreme Being, Creator of heaven and earth, should not likewise have had in their language a word to express it, equivalent to the Dios of the Spaniards, the Deus of the Latins, the Theos of the Greeks, the El of the Hebrews, and the Alà of the Arabs: whence the preachers have been obliged to Y2                       make

e: (A) Among the praisers of the Mexican language there have been some French and Flemings, and many Germans, Italians, and Spaniards. [p. 172] make use of the Spanish name. But if this author had had any acBk. VII. quaintance with the Mexican language, he would have known that the Teotl of the Mexicans means the same as the Theos of the Greeks, and that there was no other reason for introducing the Spanish word Dios there than the excessive scrupulousness of the first preachers, who, just as they burned the historical paintings of the Mexicans because they suspected some superstition in them (of which the same Acosta rightly complains), so rejected the Mexican name Teotl because it had been used to signify the false gods that they worshiped. But would it not have been better to follow in the footsteps of St. Paul, who, finding in Greece the name Theos used to signify certain wicked deities more abominable than those of the Mexicans, did not compel the Greeks to adopt the El or the Adonai of the Hebrews, but made use of the same Greek name, causing it from then on to be used to signify a supreme, eternal, and infinitely perfect Being? In fact, many wise men who have since written in Mexican have made use of the name Teotl without any scruple, just as all make use of Ipalnemoani, Tloque Nahuaque, and other names significant of the supreme Being, which the Mexicans gave to their invisible God. In one of our Dissertations we shall give a list of the authors who have written in Mexican on religion and on Christian morality, another of the numeral names of that language, and another of the words significant of metaphysical and moral things, in order to confound the ignorance and the insolence of the Researcher (**), who had the audacity to publish that the Mexicans had no words for counting beyond three, nor for expressing metaphysical and moral ideas, and that because of the hardness of the Mexican language there has never been any Spaniard who could pronounce it. e: (**) The author of the work entitled Recherches philosophiques sur les Américains. [p. 173] show how common this language has been among the Spaniards, and Bk. VII. how well those have known it who have written in it. The Mexican language also lacks, like Hebrew and French, superlative nouns, and, like Hebrew and most of the living languages of Europe, comparative nouns, and it makes up for them with certain particles equivalent to those that are used in such languages. It abounds, more than Tuscan, in diminutives and augmentatives, and more than English, and any other language known to us, in verbal nouns and abstract nouns; for there is almost no verb from which many different verbal nouns are not formed, and scarcely any noun, whether substantive or adjective, from which abstracts are not formed. The copiousness of verbs is no less than that of nouns; for from each verb several others of different signification are derived. Chihua is to make; Chichihua, to make diligently or often; Chihuilia, to make for another; Chihualtia, to cause to make; Chihuatiuh, to go to make; Chihuaco, to come to make; Chiuhtiuh, to go on making, etc. We could say a great deal on this subject, if we were permitted to go beyond the limits of History. The manner of speaking in Mexican varies according to the condition of the persons to whom one speaks, or of whom one speaks, certain particles denoting respect being added to nouns, verbs, prepositions, and adverbs. Tatli means father; Amota, your father; Amotatzin, your lordly father. Tleco is to go up: now if I command a servant of mine to go up to some place, I say to him only Xitleco; but if I request some person of consequence, I shall say Ximotlecahui, and if I wish to show him a greater submission and respect, Maximotlecahuitzino. This variety, which makes the language so courteous, does not however make it difficult to speak; for it is subject to fixed and easy rules, nor is there a language, as far as I know, more methodical and regular. The Mexicans have, like the Greeks and other nations, the advantage of composing one word out of two, three, or four simple ones; but they do it with greater economy than the Greeks;

e: [p. 174] for whereas the latter use in composition almost entire words, the Bk. VII. Mexicans truncate them, dropping syllables, or at least some letters. Tlazotli means esteemed or beloved, Mahuiztic honored or revered, Teopixqui priest, a word likewise composed of Teotl, God, and the verb pia, which means to hold, to guard, or to keep; Tatli is father, as we have said. Now, to unite these five words into one, they drop eight consonants and four vowels, and say, for example, Notlazomahuizteopixcatatzin, that is: My esteemed lord father and revered priest, prefixing No, which corresponds to the pronoun my, and adding tzin, which is a reverential particle. Such a word is very familiar to the Indians in speaking to priests, and especially in confessing, and, large as it is, it is not even among the longest; for there are some which, by reason of the many words of which they are composed, have as many as fifteen or sixteen syllables. Of such compositions they made use in order to give in a single word the definition or description of anything whatever. This can be seen in the names of the animals and plants found in the natural history of Hernández, and in the names of places which are often read in our history. Almost all the names given by them to places of the Mexican empire are compounds, and express the situation or the quality of the places, or else some memorable action that took place there. There are many locutions so expressive that they are so many hypotyposes of things, and particularly on the subject of love. Finally, all those who have learned this language, and see its copiousness, its regularity, and its most beautiful expressions, are of the opinion that such a language cannot have been that of a barbarous people. § 42. Oratory and poetry.     Among a nation that possessed so beautiful a language, orators and poets could not fail to be found. In fact, these two arts were much practiced by the Mexicans, although they were very far from knowing all their merits. Those who were destined to be orators were from childhood instructed [p. 175] in speaking well, and learned by heart the most famous harangues of Bk. VII. their ancestors, handed down from fathers to sons. Their eloquence was employed chiefly in embassies, in councils, and in the congratulatory harangues that were made to new kings. Although their most celebrated haranguers are not to be compared with the orators of the civilized nations of Europe, it cannot, however, be denied that their speeches were weighty, solid, and elegant, as can be seen from the remains of their eloquence that survive. Even today, when they find themselves reduced to such humiliation and stripped of their ancient training, they deliver in their assemblies speeches so just and so well conceived that they cause wonder in those who hear them. The number of their haranguers was surpassed by that of their poets. In their verses they attended to meter and to cadence. In the remains that survive of their poetry there are some verses in which, among the significant words, certain interjections or syllables devoid of all meaning are seen interposed, used only, as it appears, to fit the meter; but this perhaps was an abuse of their poetasters. The language of their poetry was pure, pleasant, brilliant, figurative, and adorned with frequent comparisons drawn from the most agreeable things of nature, such as flowers, trees, brooks, etc. It was in poetry that they most made use of the composition of words, which often became so long that a single word made up one of their longest verses. The subject of their poetic compositions was varied. They composed hymns in praise of their gods, and to obtain from them the goods they needed, which they sang in the temples and in their sacred dances. Others were historical poems containing the events of the nation and the glorious actions of their heroes, which they sang in their profane dances. Others were odes containing some moral or some teaching useful to life. Others, finally, were love poems, or poems on some other pleasing subject, such as hunting, which they sang at the public rejoicings of the seventh month.

e: The composers were for the most part the priests, who taught them to the Bk. VII. children, so that when they had reached a greater age they might sing them. We have made mention elsewhere of the poetic compositions of the celebrated King Nezahualcoyotl. The esteem in which this king held poetry spurred his subjects to cultivate it, and multiplied poets at his court. Of one of these poets it is related in the annals of that kingdom that, having been condemned to death for some crime or other, he made in prison a composition in which he took leave of the world, so tender and so pathetic that the palace musicians, who were his friends, took counsel together to sing it to the king: he heard it, and was so moved that he granted the culprit his life. A rare event in the history of Acolhuacan, in which only examples of the greatest severity are read. We should like to have here some fragments of those which we have seen of the poetry of those nations, in order the better to satisfy the curiosity of the readers. (*) Not only lyric poetry was prized among the Mexicans, but dramatic poetry § 43. as well. Their theater, in which such compositions were represented, was a The Mexican theater. square platform in the open air, situated in the market square or in the lower court of some temple, and suitably high, so that the actors might be seen and heard by all. VII. used in them, I shall never be able to believe that their comedies were conducted according to the rules of the drama, or worthy of the magnificent praises of that Chevalier. Much more worthy of credit, and more in keeping with the character of those nations, is the description of their theater and of their performances that Father Acosta has left us, where he recalls those which were given at Cholula at the great festival of the god Quetzalcoatl: “There was, he says, in the court of the temple of this god a small theater thirty feet square, curiously whitened, which they adorned with branches and arranged with the greatest neatness, surrounding it with arches made of flowers and feathers, and hanging up in it many birds, rabbits, and other pleasing things, (B) where, after dining, all the people assembled. The actors appeared and gave their burlesque performances, pretending to be deaf, to have colds, to be lame, blind, and crippled, and presenting themselves to ask the idol for health: the deaf answering beside the point, those with colds coughing, and the lame limping, they recounted their ills and miseries, whereby they made the people laugh a great deal. Others appeared in the name of several little animals, some disguised as beetles, some as toads, some as lizards, and meeting one another they set forth by turns their occupations, each boasting over the other: which greatly pleased the hearers; for they did it with the greatest wit. There also appeared several boys of the temple disguised as butterflies and as birds of various colors, and climbing the trees planted there for the purpose, the priests shot at them with balls of clay from blowguns, with ridiculous turns in favor of some and against others. Then all the actors performed a great dance, and with it the festival ended. This was done (B) The Indians still use such arches and bowers adorned with many kinds of flow‐ ers, fruits, and animals. Those which I saw for the procession of Corpus Christi in the village of Jamiltepec, capital of the province of Jicayán, were among the most beautiful and curious things I have ever seen. [p. 178] at the principal festivals.” (*) This description of Father Acosta reminds us of Bk. VII. the first scenes of the Greeks, and we do not doubt that if the Mexican empire had lasted some centuries longer, their theater would have been brought to a better form, just as that of the Greeks improved little by little. The first religious who announced the Gospel to those peoples, seeing them so inclined to song and to poetry, and perceiving that in their compositions, already in use in paganism, there was some superstition, composed in Mexican many canticles in praise of the true God. The industrious Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún composed in pure and elegant Mexican, and printed in Mexico City, three hundred and sixty-five canticles, one for each day of the year, full of the most devout and tender sentiments of religion, (C) and many in praise of the true God were also composed by the Indians themselves. The Chevalier Boturini makes mention of the compositions of Don Francisco Plácido, governor of Azcapotzalco, in praise of the Blessed Mother of God, and sung by him in the sacred dances which he performed with other Mexican nobles before the famous image of Our Lady of Guadalupe. Those zealous Franciscans also made several dramatic compositions in Mexican on the mysteries of the Christian Religion. Among others, that on the Last Judgment was celebrated, which the indefatigable missionary Andrés de Olmos composed, and had performed in the church of Tlatelolco, in the presence of the first viceroy and the first archbishop of Mexico, with a great concourse of the Mexican nobility and people. All their music was reduced to the Huehuetl, the Teponaztli, horns, sea conches, and certain little flutes of a shrill sound. e: Form of the great dance. Plan of the ball court. [p. 179] or Mexican drum, was a cylinder of wood, more than three feet high, Bk. VII. curiously carved and painted on the outside, covered on the top with a well-tanned and stretched deerskin, which they tightened or slackened in order to make the sound sharper or deeper. It was played only with the fingers, and required great skill in the player. The Teponaztli, which is still in use among the Indians today, is also cylindrical and hollow, but entirely of wood and without any skin, nor has it any other opening than two longish slits in the middle, parallel and a little apart from one another. It is played by beating the interval between the two slits with two little sticks like those of our drums, but covered for the most part at their ends with ule, or elastic resin, in order to make the sound softer. The size of this instrument varies: there are small ones, which are carried hung from the neck, middle-sized ones, and large ones, which are more than five feet long. The sound it gives is melancholy, and that of the largest is so loud that it is heard at a distance of two miles and more. To the sound of such instruments, whose form we present here to the readers, the Mexicans intoned their songs. Their singing was harsh and wearisome to European ears; but they took so much pleasure in it that at their festivals they used to spend the whole day singing. This, finally, was the art in which the Mexicans succeeded least. But although their music was so imperfect, their dances were most § 45. beautiful, and in them they exercised themselves from childhood un‐ Dances. der the direction of the priests. They were of various sorts, and were called by several names signifying either the quality of the dance or the circumstances of the festival in which it was held. They danced sometimes in a circle and sometimes in rows. In some dances only the men danced, and in others the women also. For the dance the nobles dressed in the most sumptuous garments, adorned themselves with bracelets, earrings, and several pendants of gold, jewels, and beautiful feathers, and carried in one hand a shield covered with the finest feathers, or a fan, likewise of feathers, and in the other an Ajacaxtli,

VII. bling a little gourd, round or oval, with many small holes, and containing a good number of little pebbles, which they shook, accompanying with this sound, which is not unpleasant, that of the instruments. The commoners disguised themselves in various figures of animals, in costumes made of paper and of feathers, or of skins. The small dance, which was held in the palaces for the amusement of the lords, or in the temples out of particular devotion, or in the houses when weddings were celebrated or there was some other such domestic rejoicing, was composed of few dancers, who, forming for the most part two straight and parallel lines, danced now with the face turned toward one of the ends of their line, now each looking at his counterpart in the other line, now those of one line crossing with those of the other, now one from each line detaching himself and dancing alone in the space between the two lines, the others meanwhile ceasing. The great dance, which was held in the great squares or in the court of the great temple, differed from the small one in order, in form, and in the number of dancers. It was so large that some hundreds of persons used to dance together. The music occupied the center of the court or square: near it the lords danced, forming two, three, or more circles according to the number that took part. A little apart from them other circles of less distinguished dancers were formed, and after another small interval, other circles, much larger, composed of young men. e: Huehuetl and the Teponaztli. In the diagram which we give of the order and arrangement of this dance, it is represented in the manner of a wheel, in which the points denote the dancers and the circles indicate the figure that they described in their dance. The spokes of the wheel are as many as there are persons who dance in the smaller circle near the music. All in the dance described a circle, and no one left his spoke, or line. Those who danced near [p. 181] the music moved with slowness and gravity, since the circuit they had Bk. VII. to make was smaller, and therefore that was the place of the lords and of the nobles more advanced in age; but those who occupied the position farthest from the music moved very swiftly, so as not to lose the straightness of the line, nor fall behind the measure of the lords. The dance was almost always accompanied by singing; but both the singing and all the movements of the dancers were adjusted to the beat of the instruments. In the singing two intoned a verse, and all answered them. The music began for the most part in a grave tone, and the singers in a low voice. The longer the dance continued, the more the music was enlivened in a gayer tone, they raised their voices higher, their movements were swifter, and the subject of their song gayer still. In the interval that remained between the lines of the dancers, some buffoons danced, imitating in their dress other nations, or disguised as wild beasts and other animals, trying to make the people laugh with their buffoonery. When one company of dancers grew tired, another took its place, and so a dance was commonly continued for six and even eight hours. This was the form of the ordinary dance; but there were others quite different, in which they represented now some mystery of their religion, now some event of their history, now war, now hunting, now agriculture. Not only the lords, the priests, and the girls of the colleges danced, but also the kings, in the temple as a ceremony of their religion, or for recreation in their palaces, who even in such an exercise had a distinguished place out of regard for their rank. Among the other dances there was one quite curious, which is still in use today among the Yucatecans. They planted in the ground a pole fifteen or twenty feet high, from whose top they suspended twenty or more cords, according to the number of the dancers, long, and all of different colors. Each took his cord by the end, and they began to dance to the sound of the musical instruments, crossing one another

e: [p. 182] with great skill, until they formed around the pole a pretty braiding Bk. VII. of the cords, in which the colors were seen arranged in checks and in fine order. Since, because of the braiding, the cords became so short that they could scarcely hold them with the hand raised, they undid the braid with fresh crossings. There is likewise in use among all the Indians of Mexico an ancient dance, commonly called Tocotin, which is quite beautiful, and so decent and grave that it has become a sacred dance, which is performed at certain festivals in our temples. The theater and the dance were not the only amusements of the § 46. Mexicans. They also had games, both public, established for certain Games. times and occasions, and private, for the solace of individuals. Among the public games was that of running, in which they exercised themselves from childhood. In the second month, and perhaps at other times too, there were military games, in which the men of war represented a pitched battle to the people. These were games truly useful to the state; since besides the innocent pleasure that the people took in them, they made themselves more agile, and accustomed themselves to the fatigues of war. Less useful, but far more celebrated than all, was the game of the flyers (Volatori), which was played at some great festivals, and especially at the secular ones. They sought in the forest a very tall, strong, and straight tree, and after stripping it of its branches and bark, they carried it to the city and set it in the center of a great square. They fitted the tip of the tree into a cylindrical piece of wood, which was called by the Spaniards, from some resemblance, a mortar. From this piece of wood hung four strong cords, which served to support a small square frame. In the interval between the cylinder and the frame they attached four other thick cords, and made of them as many windings around the tree as there were turns that the flyers were to make. These cords were threaded through four holes made in the middle of the four boards of which the frame consisted. The four principal flyers, disguised as eagles, as herons

e: The game of the flyers. [p. 183] herons, and as other birds, climbed with great agility up the tree by a Bk. VII. rope fastened to it from its foot as far as the frame. From the frame they mounted one by one onto the cylinder, and after dancing there a little, and entertaining the immense multitude of people who gathered there, they tied themselves with the ends of the cords threaded through the holes of the frame, and, launching themselves with force, began their flight with wings outspread. The force of their bodies set the frame and the cylinder in motion: the frame with its turnings unwound the cords from which the flyers hung; so that as the cords lengthened, the circles that they made in their flight were larger still. Meanwhile, while these four flew, another danced on the cylinder, playing a tambourine or waving a small flag, without showing any fear of the danger in which he found himself of falling from so great a height. The others who were on the frame (for as many as ten or twelve used to climb up), as soon as they saw the flyers in the last turn, let themselves down by the same cords in order to arrive on the ground together with them, amid the acclamations of the people. Those who let themselves down by the cords used, in order to make their agility appear the more, to pass from one cord to another in that part where, because of the smallness of the distance, they could do so. The most essential point of this game consisted in so proportioning the height of the tree and the cords that with thirteen turns the four flyers should arrive exactly on the ground, in order to represent in that number their century of fifty-two years, composed, as we have already said, of four periods of thirteen years. This celebrated game is still in use in that kingdom; but without any more regard for the number of turns, or for that of the flyers, nor conforming in everything to the form of the ancients; for the frame is wont to be hexagonal or octagonal, and the flyers six or eight. In some places they put a kind of guard on the frame to prevent the too frequent accidents since the conquest; for since drunkenness is so common among the Indians, they are wont to climb the tree

Among the private games of the Mexicans the most common, and the most prized by them, was that of the ball. The place where it was played, which they called Tlachco, was, according to the description given of it by Torquemada, a level, oblong space, which was about eighteen perches in length, and of proportionate width, enclosed between four walls thicker below than above, the lateral ones being higher than the others, well whitened and polished, and crowned all around with battlements, and with two idols upon the lower walls, which were set up at midnight with several superstitious ceremonies; and before playing there for the first time, the place was blessed by the priests with such superstitions. Thus Torquemada describes it; but in four or more Mexican paintings that I have seen, the plan of this game is represented just as we give it among our figures, which is altogether different from that of Torquemada. It may be believed that there were different forms of the same game. The idols set on the walls were those of the gods of the game, whose names we do not know; but we suspect that one of them was that of Omacatl, god of rejoicing. The ball was of ule, or elastic resin, three or four inches in diameter, which, although heavy, bounces higher than one filled with air. They played matches of two against two, or three against three. The players went entirely naked, with no other garment than the maxtlatl, that is, a wide band to cover the privy parts. It was an essential condition of the game not to touch the ball except with the joint of the thigh, or of the arm, or of the elbow, and whoever touched it with the hand, or with the foot, or with any other part of the body, lost a point by it. The player who drove the ball as far as the opposite wall, or made it bounce over it, won a point. The poor staked ears of maize, or else, if they had nothing else, gambled their liberty; others a certain number of garments [p. 185] of cotton, and the rich things of gold, precious feathers, and jewels. There were in the space between the players two great stones resem‐ Bk. VII. bling in shape our millstones, each with a hole in the middle a little larger than the ball. Whoever made the ball pass through the hole, which seldom happened, not only won the match; but by a law established in the game made himself master of the garments of all those who were present, and such a throw was celebrated as an immortal deed. Such a game was in great esteem among the Mexicans and the other nations of that kingdom, and as common as may be seen from the surprising number of balls which every year Tochtepec, Otatitlan, and other places paid as tribute to the crown of Mexico, which, as we have said elsewhere, was not less than sixteen thousand. The kings themselves often played, and challenged one another, as Moctezuma II and Nezahualpilli did. Today it is no longer in use among the nations of the Mexican empire; but it is among the Nayarits, the Opatas, the Tarahumaras, and other peoples of the north. All the Spaniards who have seen them play have marveled at their prodigious agility. The Mexicans also took delight in another game, called by some writers Patolli. (*) They drew on a fine palm mat a square, inside which they drew two diagonal lines and two transverse ones. They threw, in place of dice, large beans marked with certain little dots. According to the point which the dice gave, they put or removed certain little pebbles at the meeting of the lines, and whoever first had three pebbles in a row won. Bernal Díaz makes mention of another game, with which King Moctezuma used to amuse himself with the Conqueror Cortés during the time of his imprisonment, and which, according to him, was called Totoloque. There were among the Mexicans men very skillful in games of hands and feet. A man would lie on his back on the ground, and raising his feet would take on them a beam, or a thick piece of wood, round and about eight feet long. He tossed it to a suitable height, and as it fell he tossed it again with the soles of his feet; then, taking it between his feet, he whirled it most violently, and what is more, he did this, as I have seen done sometimes, with two men seated astride on the two ends of the wood. This game was played at Rome by two Mexicans sent by Cortés before Pope Clement VII and many Roman princes, to the singular satisfaction of that court. Also common among them was that game which in some countries is called the feats of Hercules. A man would set himself to dance; another, standing upright on his shoulders, accompanied him with some movements; and a third, standing on the head of the second, danced and gave other proofs of his agility. They also raised a beam on the shoulders of two dancers, and another danced on the end of the beam. The first Spaniards who saw these and other such games of the Mexicans were so amazed at their agility that they suspected, as they themselves attest, that the Devil was involved in them, not considering what human intelligence can do when seconded by application and by toil. But games, dances, and music served pleasure more than utility; § 47.
