e: Various Mexican games. [p. 187] of Anahuac. The Chichimecs and the Otomis, who abandoned the Bk. VII. savage life, learned it from the Acolhuas and the Toltecs. Among the paintings of the Mexicans, and of all these nations, there were many that were mere images, or portraits of their gods, their kings, their illustrious men, their animals, and their plants, with which the royal palaces of Mexico and Texcoco were filled. Others were historical, containing the accounts of their events, such as the first thirteen paintings of the Mendoza Collection, and that of the journey of the Aztecs, which is found in the work of the traveler Gemelli. Others were mythological, containing the mysteries of their religion, and of this kind is the volume that is preserved in the great library of the Institute of Bologna. Others were codices, in which their laws, their rites, their customs, and their duties or tributes were compiled, and such are all those of the aforesaid Mendoza Collection from the fourteenth to the sixty-third. Others were chronological, astronomical, or astrological, in which were represented their calendar, the positions of the stars, the aspects of the moon, the eclipses, and the forecasts of changes in the air. This sort of painting was called by them Tonalamatl. Dr. Sigüenza makes mention (*) of a painting of such forecasts, which he inserted in his Ciclografía mexicana. Father Acosta relates “that in the province of Yucatán there were certain volumes, folded in their fashion, in which the Indian sages kept the distribution of their times, the knowledge of the planets, of the animals, and of other natural things, and their antiquities, all of them extremely curious and diligently described,” which, according to the same author, perished through the indiscreet zeal of a parish priest, who, thinking them full of superstition, burned them, to the weeping of the Indians and the great displeasure of the curious Spaniards. e: (*) In his work entitled Libra astronómica, printed in Mexico. [p. 188] or chorographical, which served not only to represent the extent and Bk. VII. the boundaries of possessions, but also the situation of places, the direction of the coasts, and the course of the rivers. Cortés says in his first letter to Charles V that, wishing to know whether there was in the Gulf of Mexico any safe harbor for ships, King Moctezuma presented him with the whole coast painted on a sheet of paper, from the port of Chalchiuhcuecan, where Veracruz now stands, as far as the river Coatzacoalco. Bernal Díaz relates that the same Cortés made use, on the long and difficult journey which he made to the province of Honduras, of a map presented to him by the lords of Coatzacoalco, on which were marked all the places and all the rivers of the coast from Coatzacoalco as far as Huejacallan. The Mexican empire was full of all these sorts of paintings; for the painters were innumerable, and there was nothing that they did not paint. Had they been preserved, nothing would be left to be desired in the history of Mexico; but the first preachers of the Gospel, suspecting that there was superstition in such paintings, persecuted them with fury. Of all that they could obtain in Texcoco, where the principal school of painting was, they made so great a heap in the market square that it looked like a mountain, and they set fire to it, and the memory of many notable events was buried in those ashes. The loss of so many monuments of their antiquity was inexpressibly lamentable to the Indians, and it grieved the authors of the fire themselves, after they perceived what they had done; but they strove to remedy the harm, now by informing themselves by word of mouth from the Indians, now by collecting, as an aid to history, the paintings that had escaped their search; and although they collected many, they did not collect as many as were needed; for from that time forward the possessors of paintings became so jealous in guarding them, and in concealing them from the Spaniards, that it is far too difficult to obtain one from them.

e: The canvas on which they painted was of thread of maguei, or [p. 189] of the palm Icxotl (D), or of tanned skins, or even of paper. They made the paper from the leaves of a certain species of maguei, macer‐ Bk. VII. ated in the manner of hemp, and then washed, stretched, and § 48. smoothed. They made it also from the palm icxotl, from thin barks of Canvas and colors. other trees joined together and prepared with a certain gum, from silk, and finally from cotton, although we are ignorant of the manner of making it. I have had in my hands several sheets of this Mexican paper. In thickness it resembles European pasteboard, but it is softer and smoother, and one can write on it comfortably. For the most part they made the paper in excessively long sheets, which they kept rolled up like the ancient parchment rolls of Europe, or else folded in the manner of our bed screens. The volume of Mexican paintings that is preserved in the library of the Institute of Bologna is a thick, badly tanned skin, made of several pieces, painted all over, and folded in this way. The very beautiful colors which they employed both in their paintings and in their dyes they drew from the wood, the leaves, and the flowers of several plants, and from various mineral earths. They drew white from the mineral stone Chimaltizatl, which, when calcined, resembles fine gypsum, or from the Tizatlalli, which is a mineral earth that, after being made into a paste, kneaded like clay, and formed into little balls, takes on in the fire a white very like Spanish white. They made black from another mineral earth, foul-smelling, which for that reason they called Tlalijac, or from the soot of Ocotl, a certain species of very fragrant pine, collected in earthen vessels. Blue and azure they drew from the flower of the Matlalxihuitl and of the Xiuhquilitl pitzahuac, which is the indigo plant (E), although the (D) The coarse canvas on which the most renowned image of Our Lady of Guadalupe is painted is of palm icxotl.

VII. They put the broken foliage of that plant into vessels of hot, or rather lukewarm, water, and after stirring it sufficiently with a paddle, they passed the water, now dyed, into certain jars or basins, where they let it rest until, the solid parts of the dye having settled to the bottom, they slowly poured off all the water. These dregs, or sediment, were dried in the sun, and then put between two plates over the fire, so that it hardened. The Mexicans had another plant of the same name, from which they also drew the azure, but of inferior quality. They drew red from the seeds of the Achiote, or Rocou, boiled in water, and violet and purple from the Nochiztli, or cochineal. They drew yellow from the Tecozahuitl, or ochre, and from the Xochipalli, a plant whose leaves resemble those of the artemisia. The beautiful flowers of this plant, boiled in water with niter, yielded them a beautiful orange color. Just as they used niter for this color, so for others they made use of alum. After grinding the aluminous earth, called by them Tlalxocotl, and tempering it in water, they cooked it over the fire in earthen vessels; then they drew off by distillation the pure alum, white and transparent, and before it was entirely hardened they divided it into pieces to sell in the market. To fix the colors still more firmly they made use of the glutinous juice of the Tzauhtli (F), or of the excellent oil of Chian. But this is one of the many blunders of that philosopher. We know from the testimony of Don Ferdinand Columbus, in ch. 61 of the Life of his famous father, Don Christopher Columbus, that one of the plants native to the island of Hispaniola was that of indigo. We know also from the testimony of the historians of Mexico, and in particular of Dr. Hernández, that the ancient Mexicans made use of indigo. Among so many historians of Mexico seen by me I have not found even one who has believed that plant to be foreign. (F) The Tzauhtli is a quite common plant in that country. Its leaves are like those of the leek, its stalk is upright and knotty, its flowers are tinged a lively yellow, and its root is white and fibrous. e: The figures of mountains, rivers, buildings, plants, and animals, and above all those of men, which are seen in the paintings that re‐ Bk. VII. main from the ancient Mexicans, are for the most part out of proportion and deformed; which ought, as it seems to me, to be ascribed not so much to their ignorance of the proportions of objects, or to their slight skill, as to their haste in painting, to which the Spanish conquerors bear witness: so that, attending only to the faithful representation of things, they did not care about the perfection of their images, and therefore often contented themselves with outlines. § 49. Nevertheless I have seen among many ancient paintings certain por‐ Character       of their painting, and manner traits of the kings of Mexico in which, besides the singular beauty of of representing objects. the colors, the proportions were seen to be exactly observed; yet, speaking in general, we shall not deny that the Mexican painters lacked far too much to reach perfection in drawing and in chiaroscuro. The Mexicans made use in their paintings not only of simple images of objects, as some writers have claimed, but also of hieroglyphics and of characters. (*) They represented material things by their own figures, and, to abbreviate, and to save labor, paper, and colors, they were content to represent a part of the thing sufficient to make it known to those who understood; for just as we cannot understand the writings of others unless we first learn to read, so those Americans needed first to be instructed in the manner of representing objects in order to understand the paintings, which served them in place of writings. (H) To represent a person they painted a man, or else a human head, and above it a figure expressing the meaning of his name, as is seen in the figures of the Mexican kings. To express a city or village they painted in the same way a figure expressive of what its name signified. To form their histories, or annals, they painted along the edge of the canvas, or paper, the figures of the years in as many little squares, and beside each little square the event or events corresponding to that year; and if, because the years whose history they wished to express were many, they could not all stand on one canvas, they continued on another. As for the order of representing the years and the events, the historian was free to begin them from any corner of the canvas he pleased; but with this rule, constantly observed in all the paintings I have seen, that if the painter began from the upper right-hand corner, he continued toward the left hand. If he began, and this was the more usual, from the upper corner at the left hand, he went on perpendicularly downward. If he painted the first year in the lower corner at the left hand, he continued toward the right, and if he began in the lower right-hand (H) With regard to the numeral characters, it is to be noted that they painted as many points as there were units up to twenty. This number has its own character. From there this character was repeated up to twenty times twenty, that is, four hundred. The character of 400 was similarly repeated up to twenty times four hundred, that is, eight thousand. Then the character of eight thousand began to be repeated. With these three characters, and the points, they expressed any quantity whatever, at least up to twenty times eight thousand, or a hundred and sixty thousand. It is to be believed, although we do not know it, that for this number they had another character.

VII. left hand to the right, nor ever in the lower part from the right to the left; nor did they advance upward along the left side, nor downward along the right. Once this method of the Mexicans is known, it is easy to recognize at first sight where the beginning is, and where the end, of any historical painting. It cannot be denied that such a way of signifying things was imperfect, confused, and equivocal; but the endeavor of those peoples to perpetuate the memory of events is worthy of praise, and so is their industry in supplying, however imperfectly, the lack of letters, which they would perhaps have discovered, considering their progress in civilization, had their empire not been so short-lived; at the least they would have considerably abbreviated and facilitated their paintings by the multiplication of characters. Their paintings, moreover, ought not to be considered so much as an orderly and complete history as monuments and supports of tradition. The care that the fathers and teachers took to instruct their sons and their pupils in the history of the nation cannot be told sufficiently. They made them learn the harangues and speeches which they could not express with the brush; they put into verse the events of their ancestors, and taught them to sing them. This tradition cleared up the doubts and removed the equivocations that the paintings by themselves might have caused, and, seconded by such monuments, it immortalized the memory of their heroes, the examples of virtue, their mythology, and their rites, laws, and customs. Nor did those peoples make use only of tradition, paintings, and songs to preserve the memory of events, but also of threads of various colors, variously knotted, called by the Peruvians Quipu, and by the Mexicans Nepohualtzitzin. This rare way of representing things, so much used in Peru, does not appear to have been employed in the countries of Anahuac except in the most remote centuries; for

Boturini says that after the most diligent search he was barely able to find one, in a place in Tlaxcala, whose threads were already spoiled and almost consumed by time. If the settlers of South America ever passed through the country of Anahuac, they could have left that art there, which was then perhaps abandoned in favor of the use of painting, which the Toltecs, or some other nation more ancient than they, introduced. After they had learned from the Spaniards the use of our letters, several skillful Mexicans, Texcocans, and Tlaxcalans wrote their histories, partly in Spanish and partly in elegant Mexican speech, which writings are still preserved in some libraries of Mexico, as we have noted elsewhere. More fortunate than in painting were the Mexicans in sculpture, § 50. Sculpture. and in cast-metal and mosaic work. They expressed the images of their heroes and of the works of nature better in stone, wood, gold, silver, and feathers than on paper, either because the greater difficulty of such works caused them to be undertaken with greater diligence, or because the very high esteem in which they were held among those peoples awakened talent and quickened industry. Sculpture was one of the arts practiced by the ancient Toltecs. Down to the time of the Spaniards there were preserved several stone statues worked by the artisans of that nation, such as the idol of Tlaloc placed on the mountain of the same name, which had so much worship and veneration among the Chichimecs and the Acolhuas, and the gigantic statues erected in the two celebrated temples of Teotihuacan. The Mexicans already had sculptors when they left their homeland Aztlan, since we know that the idol of Huitzilopochtli, which they carried with them on their long migration, was made by them at that time.

e: The common material of their statues was stone and wood. They worked stone without iron, or steel, or any other instrument than a chisel of flint. There was need [p. 195] of their incomparable composure and constancy in labor to overcome so great a difficulty, and to bear the slowness of such works; but they Bk. VII. succeeded in spite of such crude instruments. They knew how to express in their statues all the attitudes and postures of which the body is capable, they observed the proportions exactly, and they made, where it was required, the most minute and delicate carvings. Not only did they make whole statues, but they also carved on stones figures in low relief, such as those of Moctezuma II and of one of his sons, carved on a stone of the mountain of Chapultepec, mentioned and celebrated by Father Acosta. They also made statues of clay and of wood, using for these a copper chisel. The surprising number of their statues may be conjectured from that of their idols, which we mentioned in the preceding book. We have, moreover, to complain in this matter of the zeal of the first bishop of Mexico and of the first preachers of the Gospel; for, in order not to leave their neophytes any incentive to idolatry, they deprived us of many valuable monuments of Mexican sculpture. The foundations of the first church that was built in Mexico were of idols, and statues were counted by the thousands that were broken, to such a degree that, that kingdom having been the most abundant in works of this kind, nowadays scarcely a few can be found after the most diligent search. The conduct of those blessed religious was very praiseworthy, both for its motive and for its effects; but we could wish that the innocent statues of those peoples had not been subjected to the same condemnation as the superstitious simulacra, and that even of these some had been preserved in some place where they would not have been a stumbling block to the neophytes. Cast-metal works were held by the Mexicans in far greater esteem than all the works of sculpture, both for the greater value of the ma‐ § 51. terial and for the excellence of the workmanship itself. The marvels Cast-metal work. of such an art would not be credible if, besides the testimony of all who saw them, such rarities had not been sent to Europe in great abundance. e: The works of gold and silver sent as a present to Charles V by the Bk. VII. conqueror Cortés filled the goldsmiths of Europe with amazement; and these, according to the testimony of several writers of that time, (*) declared them quite inimitable. The Mexican founders made, in gold as well as in silver, the most perfect images of natural things. They cast in metal a fish whose scales were alternately one of gold and the next of silver; a parrot with movable head, tongue, and wings; and a monkey with movable head and feet, and with a spindle in its hand in the attitude of spinning. They set gems in gold and in silver, and made most curious jewels of great value. Finally, such were these works that even those Spanish soldiers who felt themselves tormented by the accursed hunger for gold prized in them the art more than the material. This marvelous art, already practiced by the Toltecs, whose invention or perfection they ascribed to the god Quetzalcoatl, has been utterly lost through the abasement of the Indians and the negligence of our Spaniards. I do not know that any remnant of those so valuable works has remained; at the least it will be easier to find one in some cabinet of Europe than in all New Spain. Without doubt the desire to profit by their material prevailed over the curiosity to preserve them. The Mexicans also worked with the hammer, but little in comparison with what they made by casting, and not comparably to the works of the European goldsmiths; for they had no other instruments for beating metals than stones. Nevertheless it is known that they worked copper well, and that their axes and their pikes pleased the Spaniards greatly. The Mexican casters and goldsmiths made up a respectable body. They rendered a particular worship to Xipe, their tutelary god, and in his honor they held a great festival in the second month with the most inhuman sacrifices. e: But nothing was so prized by the Mexicans as the works of mosaic Bk. VII. which they made of the most delicate and beautiful feathers of birds. They therefore raised many species of very beautiful birds, with § 52. which that country abounds, not only in the palaces of the kings, Mosaic work. where there was, as we have already said, every sort of animal, but also in private houses, and at a certain time they plucked their feathers to use them in this kind of work, or to sell them in the market. They held in great esteem the feathers of those marvelous little birds which they call Huitzitzilin, and the Spaniards Picaflores, or flower-peckers, both for their delicacy and for the fineness and variety of their colors. In these and other very beautiful birds Nature supplied them with as many colors as Art knows how to employ, and some besides which she is not capable of imitating. For each work of mosaic several artisans were gathered, and after making the design and taking the measurements and the proportions, each one was charged with a part of the image; and he applied himself to it with such diligence and patience that he would often spend a whole day in matching a single feather, trying now one, now another, and examining it now from one side, now from another, until he found the one that completed the idea of perfection which he had proposed to himself. When the part that fell to each was finished, they gathered again to form the whole image. If some part was found to be out of order, they went back to work on it until they gave it its final perfection. They took the feathers with certain thin tweezers so as not to damage them, and attached them to the canvas with the tzauhtli, or with some other glutinous material; then they joined all the parts upon a little board, or upon a sheet of copper, and smoothed them gently until the surface of the image was left so even and so smooth that it seemed to have been made with the brush. e: [p. 198] justly prized, causing wonder how works so fine and so even could be Bk. VII. made of the feathers of birds that they seem made with the brush; and what neither the brush nor the colors of painting can produce, a certain appearance which they have when looked at slantwise, so beautiful, so lively, and so cheerful that it delights marvelously. Some Indians, excellent artisans, portray with feathers so perfectly what they see painted with the brush that they yield not to the best painters of Spain. To the Prince of Spain, Don Philip, his teacher presented three very tiny images, to put as markers in his diurnal, and His Highness showed them to the king Don Philip (the second of that name), his father; and His Majesty, having considered them, said that he had never seen a more excellent work in figures so small. Having also presented to Pope Sixtus V another, larger picture of St. Francis, and telling him that it was the work of Indians, made of feathers, His Holiness wished to test, by rubbing his fingers a little over the picture, whether it was really feather, since it seemed to him a marvelous thing that it should be so well adjusted and flattened that the eyes could not discern whether they were natural colors of feathers or artificial ones of the brush. The appearance which the green makes, and a color of orange as if gilded, and other fine colors, are exceedingly beautiful, and when the image is looked at in another light these same colors seem faded.” (*) Such works of feathers were so esteemed by the Mexicans that they prized them more than gold. Cortés, Bernal Díaz, Gómara, Torquemada, and all the other historians who saw them find no expressions with which to extol their perfection sufficiently. e: Not long ago there lived in Pátzcuaro, formerly the capital of the kingdom of Michoacán, where more than elsewhere such an art flour‐ Bk. VII. ished after the conquest, the last mosaic artisan who remained there, and with him an art so precious will already have come to an end, or will soon end, although it is now more than two centuries since they worked any longer with the perfection of the ancients. Several works of this kind are still preserved in the museums of Europe, and many in Mexico, but few, as it seems to me, of the sixteenth century, and none, so far as I know, made before the conquest. The mosaic which they made of broken shells was also very curious, an art which down to our own days has been preserved in Guatemala. In imitation of such skilled artisans there were others who with various flowers and leaves formed on mats several most beautiful works to be used at certain festivals. After the reception of the faith of Jesus Christ they made such works for the adornment of our temples, which were sought after in rivalry by the Spanish nobility for the singular beauty of the workmanship. Nowadays there are many artisans in that kingdom who employ themselves in counterfeiting with silk the images of feathers; but their works are in no way comparable with those of the ancients. e: [p. 200] edifices in those places where they stayed for some years; whose reBk. VII. mains still exist, as we have already said, on the banks of the river Gila, in the Pimería, and near the city of Zacatecas. Reduced afterward to the greatest misery on the little islands of Lake Texcoco, they built humble huts of reeds and mud until, by the trade in fish, they procured better materials. In proportion as their power and wealth increased, their buildings kept increasing and improving; so that when the conquerors arrived, their eyes found much to admire, and their hands no less to destroy. The houses of the poor were of reeds, or of unbaked bricks, or of stone and mud, and the roof of a certain long and coarse hay, which is very common in the countryside, particularly in the hot countries, or of leaves of maguei laid on like tiles, which they somewhat resemble both in thickness and in shape. One of the columns, or supports, of such edifices was usually a tree of suitable thickness, in which, besides the pleasure they took in its foliage, they saved some labor and expense. Such houses had for the most part only one room, where the family lived with its animals, its hearth, and all its household goods. If the family was not so poor, it had, in addition to two or three rooms, an Ajauhcalli, or oratory, a Temazcalli, or bath, and a small granary. The houses of the lords and of the well-to-do were of stone and lime, and of two stories, with their halls and rooms well arranged, and large courtyards: the flat roof of good timber, well worked, with its terrace: the walls so well whitewashed, burnished, and shining that to the first of the Spaniards who saw them from afar they appeared to be of silver: the floor of cement was perfectly level and smooth. Many of these houses were crowned with battlements, and had their towers, and a garden attached, with its fishponds and its paths laid out with symmetry. The great houses of the capital had for the most part two doors, the principal one on the street, and [p. 201] the other on the canal. In their doorways they had no wooden doors, thinking, perhaps, that their dwellings were secure enough through Bk. VII. the severity of the laws against thieves; but to defend them from the view of passers-by they covered the doorways with reed mats, hanging on them some strings of potsherds, or pieces of broken crockery, or some other thing capable of rousing with its noise the attention of the servants whenever anyone lifted the mat in order to enter. No one was permitted to enter without the consent of the master. When necessity, or courtesy, or the claim of kinship did not justify the entrance of him who arrived at the door, he was heard there and promptly dismissed. The Mexicans knew how to build arches and vaults (L), as is clear from their baths, from the remains of the royal palaces of Texcoco and of other buildings saved from the fury of the conquerors, and also from many of their paintings. Cornices and other particular ornaments of architecture were in use among them. They delighted in making ornaments of stone in the form of knots around their doors and windows, and in some edifices there was a great serpent of stone in the attitude of biting its tail above the main doorway, after winding its body about all the windows of the house. The walls of their edifices were straight and perpendicular, they using for this the plumb level, or some other equivalent instrument; for through the negligence of the historians we are ignorant of the instruments which they used for their buildings, as of several other things belonging to this and to other arts. e: (L) Torquemada says that when the Spaniards removed the centerings from a vault built in the first church of Mexico, the Mexicans, terrified, did not dare to enter the church, expecting every moment to see the vault fall. But if they felt any amazement, it was certainly not caused by seeing the vault, which, as we have said, was in use among them, but perhaps by seeing the centerings removed too soon, or by some other circumstance involved that deserved their admiration. [p. 202] to such a degree that the walls, until the building was finished, reBk. VII. mained entirely covered and buried: so that the masons had no need of scaffolds or planks. But although this manner of building seems to have been in use among the Mixtecs and other nations of the Mexican kingdom, we do not believe that the Mexicans employed it, considering the extreme brevity with which they finished their buildings. Their columns were cylindrical, or square; but we do not know that they had either bases or capitals. Nothing did they seek in them more eagerly than to make them of a single piece, adorning them at times with figures in low relief. The foundations of the great houses of the capital were laid, on account of the little solidity of that ground, upon a platform of thick cedar stakes driven into the earth, whose example the Spaniards have imitated. The roof of such houses was either of cedar, or of fir, or of cypress, or of pine, or of Ojametl: the columns were of ordinary stone; but in the royal palaces they were of marble, and some even of alabaster, which certain Spaniards took for jasper. Before the reign of Ahuitzotl the walls of the houses were of common stone; but the quarries of Tetzontli stone having been discovered under that king on the shores of the Mexican lake, it began to be used as the most suitable for the buildings of the capital; for it is hard, light, and porous like a sponge, so that lime adheres to it strongly. For such advantages, and for its color, which is a blood red, it is even today prized above every other stone for buildings. The pavements of their courtyards and of the temples were for the most part of Tenayuca stone; but there were some made in checkerboards of slabs of marble and of other valuable stones. The Mexicans also constructed, for the convenience of inhabited § 54. Aqueducts, and places, many good aqueducts. Those of the capital, for conducting causeways on the the water from Chapultepec, two miles distant, were two, made of lake. stone and cement, five feet high and two paces wide, constructed on a causeway built on purpose upon the lake, through which the water was conducted to the beginning of the city, and from there was divided by other, smaller conduits to supply several fountains, and chiefly those of the royal palaces. Although the aqueducts were two, the water flowed through only one at a time, and meanwhile they cleaned the other, in order always to have the water clear. There is still to be seen at Tetzcotzinco, once a pleasure place of the kings of Texcoco, the aqueduct by which the water was conducted to the royal gardens. The aforesaid causeway of Chapultepec, as well as the others built on the lake and often mentioned by us, are incontestable monuments of the industry of the Mexicans; but it is shown still more plainly in the very ground of their city; for whereas other architects have nothing else to do but lay the foundations in the earth and raise the edifices, the Mexicans had in addition to make the ground itself on which to build, by joining with embankments some separate little islands. Besides this great labor, they had also that of constructing dikes and sluices in several places of the city to render their buildings more secure. But if in such works the industry of the Mexicans is discerned, in others their magnificence is displayed. But neither this nor any other building of all those that remain to Remains of ancient buildings. us of Mexican antiquity can be compared with the famous aqueduct of Cempoala. This great work, worthy to rival the greatest of Europe, was made toward the middle of the sixteenth century. It was directed, without his even knowing the principles of architecture, by the apostolic Franciscan Francisco de Tembleque, and it was executed with the greatest perfection by the people of Cempoala. Moved to pity by the scarcity of water which his neophytes suffered, since what they formerly gathered in ditches was consumed by the herds of the Spaniards, that distinguished religious undertook to relieve at all costs the need of those peoples. The water was too far away, and the ground over which it had to be conducted was all mountainous and broken; but everything was overcome by the active zeal of the missionary, and by the industry and labor of the neophytes. They made, then, an aqueduct of stone and lime more than thirty-two miles long, (*) on account of the windings that had to be made in the mountains. The greatest difficulty consisted in surmounting three great ravines lying in the way; these too were overcome with three bridges, the first of forty-seven arches, the second of thirteen, and the third, which is the largest and the most surprising, of sixty-seven arches. The greatest arch, which is the one in the middle, situated at the greatest depth of the ravine, is 110 geometric feet high and 61 wide, so that a great ship could pass under it. They labored on it five years, and on the whole aqueduct seventeen. The description of this superb structure did not seem to me out of place in my History; for although it was undertaken by a Spaniard after the Conquest, it was nevertheless carried out by the people of Cempoala, who survived the ruin of their empire. The ignorant Researcher denies to the Mexicans the knowledge and the use of lime; but it is evident from the testimony of all the historians of Mexico, from the register of tributes, and above all from the ancient edifices still standing, that all those nations made the same use of lime as the Europeans do. The common people of that kingdom believe that the Mexicans mixed eggs with the lime to make it more tenacious; but this is an error, caused perhaps by seeing the ancient walls yellowish. It is likewise evident from the testimony of the first historians that baked bricks were in use among the Mexicans, and that they were sold, like all other things, in the markets. The stonecutters, who cut and worked the stone for edifices, did not § 56. use picks, nor chisels of iron, but only certain instruments of flint; nev‐ Stonecutters, jewel‐ ers, and potters. ertheless they made fine works and carvings in the stone. But more than such works done without iron, one wonders at the stones of stupendous size and weight that were found in the capital and elsewhere, carried from afar and placed in lofty positions without the aid of the machines which Mechanics has invented. Besides common stone, they also worked marble, jasper, alabaster, Itztli, and other valuable stones. Of Itztli they made fine mirrors mounted in gold, and those very sharp razors which they used in their swords, and of which their barbers also made use. They made such razors with such speed that a single artisan produced more than a hundred in an hour. e: The Mexican jewelers not only had knowledge of gems, but also knew how Bk. VII. to polish them, to work them, and to engrave them, forming on them as many figures as they wished. The historians affirm that these works were done with a certain sand; but it is certain that they could not have been done without some instrument of flint or of hard copper, such as exists in that country. The gems most in use among the Mexicans were emeralds, amethysts, carnelians, turquoises, and others unknown in Europe. Emeralds were so common that there was no lord who did not have some, and none of them died from whose corpse they did not hang an emerald at the lip, so that it might serve him, as they said, in place of a heart. Those that were sent to the court of Spain in the first years after the conquest were likewise beyond counting. When Cortés returned to Spain for the first time, he brought with him, among other inestimable jewels, five emeralds, which, as Gómara, who was then living, testifies, were valued at a hundred thousand ducats, and for one of them certain Genoese merchants wished to give forty thousand in order to resell it to the Grand Turk; (N) and besides these, two vessels, likewise of emerald, valued, according to the celebrated Father Mariana, (*) at three hundred thousand ducats, which vessels Cortés lost in the shipwreck that he suffered in the unfortunate expedition of Charles V against Algiers. Today such gems are no longer worked, nor is the place known of the mines from which they dug (N) As for Cortés’s emeralds, the first was made in the form of a rose, the second like a little horn, the third like a fish with eyes of gold, the fourth was a little bell with a fine pearl for a clapper, and on it this Spanish inscription in gold letters, Bendito quien te crió, that is, Blessed be he who created you. The fifth, which was the most valuable, and for which the Genoese would have given 40,000 ducats, was a small cup with a foot of gold, and with four little chains, also of gold, which were joined together in a pearl in the manner of a button. The rim of the cup was encircled by a ring of gold, on which was engraved this Latin inscription: Among those born of women there hath not risen a greater. These five emeralds, worked by the Mexicans by order of Cortés, were presented by him to his second wife, the noble lady Doña Juana Ramírez de Arellano y Zúñiga, daughter of the Count of Aguilar: Jewels, says Gómara, who saw them, better than any lady in Spain ever had.

The potters made of clay not only the vessels necessary for the use of houses, but also other works of mere curiosity, which they adorned with various colors; but they did not know, as it appears, the art of glazing them. The most famous potters were formerly the Cholulans, whose vessels were much § 57. prized by the Spaniards; today the potters of Cuauhtitlan are celebrated.      Carpenters, weavers, The carpenters worked several kinds of wood well with their copper tools, etc. some of which are to be seen even today. The manufacture of various kinds of cloth was common everywhere, and this was one of the arts that nearly everyone learned. They had neither wool, nor common silk, nor flax, nor hemp; but they supplied the place of wool with cotton, of silk with feathers and with the hair of the rabbit and the hare, and of flax and hemp with the Icxotl, or mountain palm, with the Quetzalichtli, with the Pati, and with other species of maguei. Of cotton they made both coarse cloths and cloths as fine and delicate as those of Holland, which were rightly prized in Europe. A few years after the Conquest a priestly vestment of the Mexicans was carried to Rome, which, as the Chevalier Boturini affirms, made that court marvel at its fineness and excellence. They wove these cloths with several figures and colors, representing on them various animals and flowers. Of feathers woven in with cotton they made mantles, bedcovers, tapestries, coats, and other things no less soft than beautiful. I have seen some handsome mantles of this kind, which some lords still preserve, and are accustomed to wear on certain extraordinary festivals, such as that of the coronation of the King of Spain. From the leaves of the Pati and of the Quetzalichtli (kinds of maguei) they drew a fine thread for making cloths equivalent to those of linen, and from the leaves of other species of maguei, as from those of the mountain palm, they drew a coarser thread, similar to hemp. The manner they had of preparing these materials was the same that Europeans have for flax and hemp. They macerated the leaves in water, and then cleaned them, put them in the sun, and beat them, until they put them in a condition to be spun. Of the same leaves of the mountain palm, as also of those of the Izhuatl (another species of palm), they made very fine mats of various colors. Others, coarser, they made of the rush that grows in abundance in that lake. Of the thread of the maguei they also made ropes, and shoes, and other articles. They tanned very well the skins of animals, both those of quadrupeds and those of birds, leaving on some the hair or the feather, and removing it from others, according to the use they wished to make of them. Finally, in order to give some idea of the taste of the Mexicans in the arts, it seemed to me appropriate to transcribe here the list of the first things that Cortés sent from Mexico to Charles V a few days after arriving in that country. e: (P) Dr. Hernández, being physician to Philip II, King of Spain, and very renowned for his works published on the Natural History of Pliny, was sent by that monarch to Mexico to make researches into the natural things of that kingdom. He was employed there, together with other learned naturalists, for several years, availing himself of the instruction of the Mexican physicians. His work, worthy of the 60,000 ducats spent on it, consisted of 24 books of history and eleven volumes of excellent pictures of plants and animals; but the King, thinking it too voluminous, ordered his physician Nardo Antonio Recchi, a Neapolitan, to make a compendium of it. This compendium was published in the Spanish language at Mexico by Francisco Ximénez, a Dominican, in 1615, and then in Latin at Rome in 1651 by the Lincean Academicians, with learned notes and dissertations, but too long and tedious. Hernández's manuscripts were kept in the library of the Escorial, whence Father Nieremberg took a great part of what he wrote in his Natural History, as he himself avows. Father Claude Clement, a French Jesuit, speaking of Hernández's manuscripts, says thus: If all these books and commentaries were as perfect and finished as they were begun, Philip II and Francisco Hernández would in no way yield to Alexander and Aristotle in this respect. From this most valuable, though imperfect, history there could be formed a body of practical medicine for that kingdom, as indeed Dr. Farfán did in his book of Cures, and so did the admirable anchorite Gregorio López and other celebrated physicians. And if from that time on the study of natural history had not been neglected, nor the prejudice in favor of everything from overseas been so great, the inhabitants of New Spain would have been spared a great part of the expense incurred in acquiring the drugs of Europe and of Asia, and would have drawn greater advantage from the products of their own country. To the Mexican physicians Europe owes tobacco, American balsam, gum copal, liquidambar, sarsaparilla, tacamahaca, jalap, barley, and purging nuts, and other simples which have been of great use in medicine; but infinite are those of which Europe is deprived through the ignorance or the negligence of merchants. Among the purgatives used by the Mexican physicians, besides jalap, the purging nuts, and the small bean, there was very common among them the Mechoacan, so well known in Europe, (Q) as well as the Izticpatli, so celebrated by Dr. Hernández, and the Amamaxtla, commonly called friars’ rhubarb. Among several emetics they used the Mexochitl and the Neixcotlapatli, and among the diuretics the Axixpatli and the Axixtlacotl, which is highly praised by the aforesaid Hernández. Among their antidotes the famous contrahierba was justly prized, called by them, from its figure, Coanenepilli (serpent’s tongue), and from its effects Coapatli, that is, remedy against serpents. The Mexican physicians made use of infusions, decoctions, plas‐ Oils, ointments, infusions, etc. ters, ointments, and oils, and all these things were sold in the market, as Cortés and Bernal Díaz, eyewitnesses, attest. The oils most in use among them were those of ule, or elastic resin, of Tlapatl, a tree resembling the fig, of Chilli, that is, chili pepper, of Chian, and of Ocotl, a species of pine. This last they drew by distillation, and the others by decoction. That of Chian served painters more than physicians. They also drew from the Huitziloxitl, as we have mentioned elsewhere, those two sorts of balsam mentioned by Pliny and other ancient naturalists, namely the opobalsam, or balsam distilled from the tree, and the xylobalsam, obtained by the decoction of the branches. From the bark of the Huaconex, macerated four days continuously in water, they drew another liquor equivalent to balsam. From the plant called by the Spaniards Maripenda (a name, as it appears, taken from the Tarascan language), they likewise drew a liquor resembling balsam, both in its good odor and in its marvelous effects, by putting the tender stalks with the fruit of the plant to boil in water until the water became so thick

Bloodletting was very common among the Mexicans and the other Bloodletting and nations of Anahuac, and their physicians performed it with skill and baths. safety with lancets of itztli. The country people were accustomed to draw blood from themselves, as they still do, with maguei thorns, without availing themselves of any other hand, or interrupting the work in which they are engaged. They also used, in place of leeches, the spines of the Huitztlacuatzin, or Mexican porcupine, which are thick and have a small hole at the point. Among the means which they employed for the preservation of their health, that of baths was much used. They bathed very frequently, and many of them daily, in the natural water of rivers, lakes, ditches, and ponds. Anahuac, was the bath of the Temazcalli, which, being in all its circumstances worthy of particular mention in the history of Mexico, there has not been even one among the historians of that kingdom who has described it, while they often dwell on descriptions and accounts of little importance: so that if that bath had not been preserved to this day, its memory would have perished altogether. The Temazcalli, or Mexican hypocaust, is built for the most part of unbaked bricks. Its form is very like that of the ovens for baking bread; but with this difference, that the floor of the Temazcalli is a little convex, and lower than the surface of the ground, whereas that of our ovens is flat, and raised for the greater convenience of the bakers. Its greatest diameter is about eight feet, and its greatest height six. Its door, which is also like the mouth of an oven, is wide enough for a man to enter comfortably on all fours. The part where the furnace is joined to the hypocaust, which measures about two and a half feet square, is closed with a dry stone of tetzontli, or of another as porous as that. In the upper part of the vault there is another hole, or vent, like that of the furnace. This is the common structure of the Temazcalli, as shown in the accompanying figure; but there are others which have neither vault nor furnace, and are reduced to small oblong chambers, otherwise well covered and protected from the air. When someone wishes to bathe, he has put inside the temazcalli first a mat, (*) a basin of water, and a bunch of herbs or of maize leaves. Then a fire is made in the furnace, and kept burning until the stones that lie between the temazcalli and the furnace are quite red-hot. He who wishes to bathe enters, for the most part naked, and often, either because of illness or for his greater convenience, is accompanied by one of his servants. As soon as he enters, he shuts the door tightly, leaving open for a little while the vent which is in the roof of the temazcalli, so that the smoke introduced through the cracks of the stones may go out; and after it has all gone out, he stops up the vent also. Then he throws water on the heated stones, from which a dense vapor at once rises, and goes to occupy the upper part of the Temazcalli. Meanwhile, as the sick man lies on the mat, his servant (if he cannot do it for himself) begins to draw the vapor down, and to beat the sick man gently, especially on the aching part, with the bunch of herbs somewhat dipped in the now warm water of the basin. The sick man at once falls into a gentle and copious sweat, which is increased as one wishes, or diminished in proportion to need. Once the desired evacuation is obtained, freedom is given to

The Temazcalli has always been used in several diseases, especially in fevers caused by some obstruction. The Indian women commonly use it after childbirth, and also those who have been bitten or wounded by some venomous animal. It is without doubt an effective remedy for all who need to evacuate thick and tenacious humors, and I do not doubt that it would be most useful in Italy, where rheumatisms are so frequent and so severe. When a more copious sweat is desired, they lift the sick man and bring him near the vapor; for he sweats the more, the nearer he approaches it. So common is the Temazcalli even now that there is no place inhabited by Indians where there are not many of them. § 63. It is a wonder that the Mexicans, and especially the poor, were not Foods  of the Mexicans. subject to many diseases, considering the quality of their foods. This is an article in which they had some singular things; for having been reduced, for so many years after the founding of Mexico, to the most wretched life on the little islands of the lake, they were compelled by their necessity to feed on whatever they could find in those waters. In a time so calamitous they learned to eat not only the roots of marsh plants and the aquatic serpents which abound there, the Axolotl, the Atetepiz, the Atopinan, and other such little animals of the water, but also ants, marsh flies, and the eggs of those same flies. Of these flies, which they called Axajacatl, they caught so great a quantity that they had enough to eat, to feed several species of birds, and to sell in the market. They pounded them, and made little balls of that mass, which, wrapped in maize leaves, they put to cook in water with niter. Such a dish did not displease some historians, who tasted it. From the eggs which these flies lay in the greatest abundance on the rushes of the lake they drew, as we have mentioned, that singular kind of caviar which was called by them Ahuauhtli. Not content with feeding on living things, they also ate a certain slimy substance which floats on the waters of the lake, which they dried in the sun and preserved for use, like cheese, which it resembles in taste. They gave this substance the name of Tecuitlatl, that is, excrement of stones. (R) Among their edibles the first place belongs to maize, which they called Tlaolli, a grain granted by Providence to that part of the world in place of the wheat of Europe, the rice of Asia, and the millet of Africa, with some advantages over them; for besides being wholesome and tasty, it is more nutritious, multiplies more, grows equally well in warm climates and in cold, does not require so much cultivation, is not so delicate as wheat, nor needs, like rice, a damp soil harmful to the health of the cultivators. They had many kinds of maize differing in size, in color, and in quality. Of maize they made their bread, altogether different from the bread of Europe, no less in taste and in shape than in the manner of making it, which they had anciently, and preserve to this day. They put the grain to cook in water with a little lime. When it is somewhat soft, they rub it between the hands to take off the skin. Then they grind it on the Metlatl, (*) take a little of that paste, and, spreading it with reciprocal clapping of the hands, form the bread, and then give it its final cooking on the Comalli. The shape of such loaves is round and flat, their diameter is about eight fingers, and their thickness more than a line; but they also make them smaller and thinner, and for the lords they made them as thin as our thickest paper. They were accustomed to mix some other thing into the maize, to render the bread more wholesome or more delicious. This is the bread that the Mexicans, and all the other nations of those vast countries, have always used down to our own days, rejecting in comparison with it the best wheat bread. Their example has been imitated by very many Spaniards; but, to tell the truth, this bread, although it is very wholesome and substantial, and when freshly made has a good taste, is nevertheless somewhat unpleasant when it grows cold. The making of bread, like the preparing and seasoning of every sort of food, has always been among those nations a trade proper to women. They were the ones who made it for their families, and the ones who sold it in the market. Not only bread, but also very many foods and drinks they made of maize, with various ingredients and preparations. The Atolli is a gruel, or polenta, made of the paste of cooked maize, well ground, diluted in water, and strained. They put that liquid, strained through the sieve, on the fire, and give it a fresh cooking until it takes on the proper thickness. It is tasteless to the palate of the Spaniards; yet they commonly give it to their sick, as a wholesome nourishment, sweetening it with a little sugar in place of the honey formerly used by the Indians. To these, however, it is so agreeable that they cannot do without it. It was formerly, and is even today, their breakfast, and with it they bear the labors of agriculture and of the other servile occupations in which they are engaged. Dr. Hernández distinguishes seventeen species of Atolli, differing as much in the seasoning as in the manner of preparing it. After maize, the seeds most used were those of cacao, of chia, and of kidney beans. Of cacao they made several usual drinks, and among others that called by them Chocolatl. Clothing. Their ordinary garb was very simple, being reduced altogether, for men, to the Maxtlatl and the Tilmatli, and for women to the Cueitl and the Huepilli. The Maxtlatl was a band, or broad girdle, with the two ends hanging in front and behind to cover the private parts. The Tilmatli was a square mantle, about four feet long; its two ends were knotted on the breast, or over one shoulder, as may be seen in our figures. The Cueitl, or Mexican skirt, was a piece of cloth, also square, with which the women wrapped themselves from the waist down to the middle of the leg. The Huepilli was a woman’s little shirt, or jacket without sleeves. The clothing of the poor people was of maguei thread, or of mountain palm, or at best of coarse cotton cloth; but that of the well-to-do was of fine cotton adorned with various colors, and with various figures of animals, or of flowers, or even of cotton interwoven with beautiful feathers, or with fine rabbit fur, and decorated with several little gold figures, and with handsome tassels, especially on the girdle, or Maxtlatl. The men were accustomed to wear two or three mantles, and the women three or four little shirts and as many skirts, putting the longest ones underneath, so that some part of each might be seen. The lords dressed in winter in jackets of cotton interwoven with soft feathers, or with rabbit fur. The ladies wore, besides the huepilli, an overgarment somewhat like the surplice of our ecclesiastics, but broader, and with longer sleeves. (*) Their shoes were nothing but soles of leather, or of coarse cloth of maguei, tied with laces in such a manner that they covered only the soles of the feet. The kings and the lords adorned the laces with rich ribbons of gold, and with gems. All (*) We have spoken elsewhere of the royal, the priestly, and the military dress.

e: All the Mexicans wore their hair long, and held it a dishonor to be Bk. VII. shorn, except the virgins who were consecrated to the service of the § 67. temple. The women wore it loose, and the men tied it in various Their ornaments. ways, and adorned the head with beautiful plumes, no less when they danced than when they went to war. It is difficult to find another nation that joined with such simplicity in dress so much vanity and luxury in the adornment of their bodies. Besides the feathers and the jewels with which they used to decorate their garments, they used ear-rings, pendants in the lower lip, and many also in the nose, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and even certain rings in the manner of collars on the legs. The ear-rings and other pendants of the poor people were of shells, of crystal, of amber, or of some little glittering stone in the manner of a gem; but the rich wore them of pearls, of emeralds, of amethysts, or of other gems set in gold. But their household goods did not correspond to such vanity. § 68. The pillow of the poor was a stone or a piece of wood, and that of the well-to-do was perhaps of cotton. The common people covered themselves in bed with nothing but the tilmatli itself, or mantle; but the rich and the nobles used coverlets of cotton and of feathers. The Comalli was, and still is (for it is as much used as the metlatl), a round, somewhat concave earthen dish, a finger in thickness and about fifteen inches in diameter. The drinking vessels of the Mexicans were made of certain fruits resembling gourds, which grow in the hot countries on trees of moderate size. Some are large and perfectly round, and these they call Xicalli (X); the others are smaller and cylindrical, and to these they give the name of Tecomatl. Both kinds of fruit are solid and heavy: their rind is hard, woody, and of a dark green color, and their seeds are like those of gourds. The Xicalli is about eight inches in diameter, and the Tecomatl a little less in length and about four fingers in thickness. Each fruit, divided in half, yielded two equal vessels: they hollowed out all the seeds, and gave them, with certain mineral earths, a permanent varnish of a pleasant odor and of various colors, above all a beautiful red. Nowadays they are accustomed also to silver and gild them. e: (X) The Spaniards of Mexico called the Xicalli Xicara. The Spaniards of Europe adopted this name to signify the little cup for taking chocolate, and from it arose the Italian chicchera. M. de Bomare mentions the tree of the Xicalli under the name of Calebasse d’Amérique, and says that in New Spain it is known by the names of Choyne, Cujete, and Hyguero; but this is not true. The name Hibuero (not Hyguero) was the one that the Indians of the island of Hispaniola gave to this tree: the conquering Spaniards formerly used it; but no one else afterwards made use of it in New Spain. The other names I have never heard in those countries. [p. 226] of wax from the honeycombs, they either did not wish to, or did not Bk. VII. know how to, derive from it the advantage of light. In the maritime countries they used for this purpose the cucui, or luminous beetles; but in general they made use of torches, or brands, of Ocotl, which, although they gave a fine light and a good odor, smoked and blackened the dwelling with soot. One of the European customs that they most prized upon the arrival of the Spaniards was that of candles; but to tell the truth, those peoples had little need of candles, since they devoted to rest almost all the hours of the night, after having employed all those of the day in labor or in affairs. The men worked at their arts or trades, and the women at sewing, weaving, embroidering, making bread, preparing food, and cleaning the house. All of them daily offered prayers to their gods, and burned copal in their honor, and therefore there was no house, however poor, that did not have its little idols and its censers. The manner that the Mexicans and the other American nations had of getting fire was the same that the ancient shepherds of Europe used (Y), that is, by the violent rubbing together of certain pieces of wood. The Mexicans made use for the most part of achiote, which is the roucou of the French. The Chevalier Boturini asserts that they got it also from flint. In the morning, after some hours of work, they took their breakfast, which was for the most part atolli, or polenta of maize, and their dinner after midday; but among so many historians of Mexico I have not found even one who makes mention of their supper. They ate little; but they drank often, now their wine of maguei or of maize, now chia, now some drink of cacao, and now natural water. After (Y) Warm woods are the mulberry, the laurel, the ivy, and all those from which fire-sticks are made. Scouts found this use in camps, and shepherds as well, since for striking fire there is not always an occasion for a stone. Wood is therefore rubbed against wood, and conceives fire by the friction, the fire being very easily caught by a receiving material of dry tinder, fungus, or leaves. Pliny, Natural History, bk. 16, ch. 40. The same may be seen in bk. 2 of Seneca’s Natural Questions, and in other ancient authors.

e: After dinner the lords were accustomed to induce sleep with the smoke of tobacco. (Z) This plant was in great use among the Bk. VII. Mexicans. They used it in several plasters, and took it both in smoke § 69. by the mouth and in powder through the nose. For smoking, they put Use of tobacco. into a tube, or little channel, of wood, or of cane, or of some other more noble material, the leaf of the tobacco with the resin of the liquidambar and with other hot and fragrant herbs. They received the smoke by pressing the little channel with the mouth and stopping the nostrils with the fingers, so that it might more easily pass with the breath as far as the lung. Who would ever have believed that the use of tobacco, which the necessity of those phlegmatic nations invented, should be in the future a vice or a fashion general among almost all the peoples of the world; and that so humble a plant, of which the Europeans spoke and wrote so unfavorably, should become one of the greatest revenues of the kingdoms of Europe? But what ought to cause greater wonder, the use of tobacco being now so common among those very nations that censured it, is that it is yet so rare among its inventors, that there are very few today (I speak of the Indians of New Spain) who take it in smoke, and none who take it in powder. Just as the Mexicans lacked the use of candles for giving themselves light, so too they lacked the use of soap for washing, although §Plants 70. used in place there were animals from which it could be got; (aa) but they made up of soap. well for such a lack with a fruit and with Ff2                              a (Z) Tabaco is a name taken from the Haitian language. The Mexicans had two kinds of tobacco, very different in the size of the plant and of the leaves, in the shape of the flower, and in the color of the seed. The smaller, which is the common one, they called Picietl, and the larger Quaujetl. This grows as tall as a tree of moderate size. Its flower is not divided into five parts like that of the Picietl, but only distinguished into six or seven angles. These plants vary greatly by reason of the climate, not only in the quality of the tobacco but also in the size of the leaves and in other accidents; whence several authors have multiplied the species.

e: (aa) I have heard it said that from the Epatl, or zorriglio, an excellent soap is extracted. [p. 228] a root. The fruit was that of the Copalxocotl, a tree of moderate size, Bk. VII. which grows in Michoacán, in Yucatán, in the Mixteca, and elsewhere. (bb) The pulp under the rind of the fruit, which is white, viscous, and very bitter, turns water white, foams, and serves like soap to wash and clean linen. The root is that of the Amolli, a small plant, very common in that country, to which the name of Saponaria americana is more justly suited, because it is less unlike the soapwort of the old continent; but the Amolli is more used nowadays in washing the body, and particularly the head, than clothes. (cc) What we have set forth thus far concerning the political and economic government of the Mexicans is all that we have found worthy of belief and of being brought to public light. Such were their public and private customs, their government, their laws, and their arts, when the Spaniards arrived in the country of Anahuac, whose war and memorable events we wish to relate in the following books. End of Volume II. of the History of Mexico. Additions (bb) Dr. Hernández mentions it under the name of Copalxocotl, but says nothing of its detergent virtue. Vetancurt speaks of it under the name of Soap Tree, by which it is known to the Spaniards, and M. Valmont de Bomare describes it under the name of Savonnier and of Saponaria americana. The root of this tree is also used in place of soap; but it is not as good as the fruit. (cc) There is a species of Amolli whose root dyes the hair the color of gold. I saw this singular effect for some days in a man of mature years who, having been blond in his youth, was by now white-haired.

Delle figure del Secolo Me fficano : -TElla ruota dal secolo Messicano sono quattro figuré tredici volte replicate, per significare, siccome abbiam già detto, i quattro periodi ( da alcuni Storici appellati indizioni ) di tredici anni, di cui fi componeva il loro seco. lo. Le quattro figure sono 1. una testa di coniglio esprimente questo quadrup:do, 2. una canna, 3. un coltello , o fia una punta di lancia rappreseatante il selce, o pietra focaja , 4: un pezzo d' edifizio fignificante la casa , Cominciano a contarsi gli anni del secolo dalla piegatura superiore della serpe discendendo verso la man finistrca . La I. figara con un puntino denota I Coniglio, la 2. con due figaifaca IL Canna, la 3. con tre puntini significa III. Selce, la 4. con quattro puntini IV. Casa, la 5. con cinque puntini V. Comiglio, @ così si continua sin’ alla piegatura della man finistca; là onde comincia il 2, periodo colla figura della canna, € termina nella piegatura inferiore: ed indi comincia il terza periodo ec. 2. Delle figure dell anno. La i. figura è quella dell’ acqua distesa sopra un edifizio p2r denotare il primo mese , il cui nome Acabualco , o lia Atlacabuaico, fignifica la ceflazione dell'acqua, poichè nel mesedi Mar» zo ceflanno le pioggie dell’ Inverno ne’ paesi settentrionali, donde ebbs origine il Calendario Messicano, o fia Tolteco, Chiamavanlo ancora Quabuirlebua, ciò che significa il germogliamento degli alberi, che accade a questo tempo ne’ paesi freddi. I Tlascalleli appella vano questo mele X ilomanilizeli, cioè , Obliazione di pannocchie di frumentone; perchè in esso offerivanoa' loro Dei quelle dall’ anno scorso per secondare la seminatura , che per questo tempo cominciavano a fare ne' luoghi alti. e: E X P L A N AT I O N 1. Of the Figures of the Mexican Century. In the wheel of the Mexican century there are four figures, repeated thirteen times, to signify, as we have already said, the four periods (called by some historians indictions) of thirteen years, of which their century was composed. The four figures are: 1. the head of a rabbit, expressing that quadruped; 2. a cane; 3. a knife, or rather a lance point, representing the flint, or firestone; 4. a piece of building, signifying the house. The years of the century begin to be counted from the upper coil of the serpent, descending toward the left hand. The first figure, with one dot, denotes I Rabbit; the second, with two, signifies II Cane; the third, with three dots, signifies III Flint; the fourth, with four dots, IV House; the fifth, with five dots, V Rabbit; and so it continues as far as the coil of the left hand: there the second period begins with the figure of the cane, and ends at the lower coil: and from there the third period begins, etc. 2. Of the Figures of the Year. The first figure is that of water spread over a building, to denote the first month, whose name, Acahualco, or Atlacahualco, signifies the ceasing of the water; for in the month of March the rains of winter cease in the northern countries, whence the Mexican calendar, or Toltec calendar, took its origin. They also called it Quahuitlehua, which signifies the budding of the trees, which happens at this season in cold countries. The Tlaxcalans called this month Xilomaniliztli, that is, offering of ears of maize; because in it they offered to their gods those of the past year, to promote the sowing, which at this time they began to do in the high places.

o: La figura del mese secondo sembra a prima vista un padiglione ; ma io credo , che fia piuttosto una pelle umana mal disegnata per esprimere ciò, che significa il nome Til caxipebualizzli , che davano a questo mele , cioè , Scorticamento d' uomini per cagione del barbaro rito di scorticar le vittime umane nella festa del Dio degli Orefici . I Tlascallesi appellavano questo mese Couilbuitl, @ fia Festa penerale , e lo rappresentavano nella figura d’ una serpe aggirata attorno ad un ventaglio, e ad un Afacaxzli, Il ventaglio, e l'Ajacaxtli denotano i balli, che allora fi facevano, e la serpe aggirata significa la loro generalità. La figura del mese terzo è quella d' un uccello sopra una lancetta, La lancetta significa lo spargimento di sangue, che facevano nelle notti- di questo mese; ma non sappiamo, che uccello fia quello, che vi si vede , nè che fignifichi . Il mese quarto fi rappresenta nella figura d' un piccolo . edifizio, sopra il quale si vedono alcune foglie di giunco per fignificar la ceremonia, che in questo mese facevano, di metrer sulle porte delle case del giunco, del ghiaggiuolo, e d' altre erbe bagnate nel sangue, che si cavavano ad onor de’ loro Dii. I Tlascallesi rappresentavano il mese terzo con una lancetta per fignificar sì) fatta penitenza, ed il mese quarto con una lancetta più grande per denotare, ch’ era anche in eflo maggior la penitenza, La figura del mese quinto è quella d' una testa umana con una collana sotto, per rappresentar quelle flze di frumentone abbrustolito , che fi mettevano al collo, e delle quali fregiavano ancora !' idolo di Tezcatlipoca , onde il mese prese il nome Toxcarl , secondo ciò che abbiamo detto nel lib. VI. , Il mese sesto fi rappresenta in una pignatta, ovvero orciuolo, per fignificar certa polenta , che allora prendevano, ed appellavano Eezalli, dalla quale ebbe il mese il nome d' Erizalqualizali . e: The figure of the second month seems at first sight a pavilion; but I believe that it is rather a human skin badly drawn, to express what is signified by the name Tlacaxipehualiztli, which they gave to this month, that is, Flaying of men, because of the barbarous rite of flaying the human victims at the festival of the god of the goldsmiths. The Tlaxcalans called this month Coailhuitl, or General festival, and represented it in the figure of a serpent coiled around a fan and an Ajacaxtli. The fan and the Ajacaxtli denote the dances that were then performed, and the coiled serpent signifies their generality. The figure of the third month is that of a bird above a lancet. The lancet signifies the shedding of blood which they practiced during the nights of this month; but we do not know what bird it is that is seen there, or what it signifies. The fourth month is represented in the figure of a small building, above which are seen some rush leaves, to signify the ceremony which they performed in this month, of placing on the doors of the houses rushes, iris, and other herbs bathed in the blood which they drew from themselves in honor of their gods. The Tlaxcalans represented the third month with a lancet to signify penance of this kind, and the fourth month with a larger lancet to denote that the penance was greater in it also. The figure of the fifth month is that of a human head with a necklace beneath, to represent those strings of toasted maize which were hung about the neck, and with which they also adorned the idol of Tezcatlipoca, whence the month took the name Toxcatl, according to what we have said in bk. VI. The sixth month is represented by a pot, or little jar, to signify a certain polenta which they then took, and called Etzalli, from which the month took the name of Etzalqualiztli. The two figures of the seventh and eighth months seem to have been invented

Preflo. alle suddette figure fi vedono delle lancette per denotare l' austerità , con' cui fi preparavano a quelle feste. I Tlascallesi rappreseatavano questi due mesi in due teste di Signori, quella del mese Tecuilbuirontli, o fia Felta piccola de' Signori pare, che sia d' un giovane, e quella del mese Hucitecuilbuizl , cio, Festa grande de' Signori , sembra d' un vecchio. Le figure de’ mesi nono, e decimo sono fenz' altro . fignificative del bruno, che fi vestivano, e del duolo, che facevano pe' lor morti, il che fece appellare il mese nono Miccailbuitl , cioè , Festa de' morti, ed il mese decimo Hueimiccailhuir!, o Felta grande de' morti ; ma perch’ era più grande il duolo del mese decimo , è anche più grofla la fi+ gura che lo rappresenta. I Tlascallesi dipingevano in ciascuno de' suddetti mesi un teschio con due osla; ma il teschia del mese decimo più grande. La figura del mese undecimo è una scopa, nella quale vien fignificata la ceremonia dello spazzamento de' tempj, che in questo mese sì faceva da tutti ; onde ebbe il nome. Ocbpanizzli . I Tlascallesi dipingevano una mano impugnati do la scopa. La figura de’ mesi dodecimo, e decimoterzo, è quella d’ una pianta parasita , Appellata da' Messicani Pacbili , che viene în questo tempo sulle quercie, ed indi prese nome il mese dodecimo. Or perchè nel mese seguente questa pianta è cresciuta, la sua figura è più grofla, ed il mese ha il nome d' Hucipacheli . Questi nomi, benchè più usari prefso i Tilascallel , eran pure in uso presso i Messicani ; ma noi adoperiamo nella Storia i nomi di Teorleco, e di Tepeilhuil, perchè gli troviamo più comunemente usati da” Metflicani- La figura del mese decimoquarto è molto somigliante a quella del mese secondo; ma non sappiamo, che significhi, I Tlascallelsi rappresentavano questo mese nella figura. di quell' uccello, che da noi è appellato Fiammingo , e da' Meslli-
