Ii [p. 250] to signify the dances that were performed in them, and because the dances of the eighth month were greater, the figure that represents it is also greater. Beside the aforesaid figures are seen lancets, to denote the austerity with which they prepared for those festivals. The Tlaxcalans represented these two months in two heads of lords: that of the month Tecuilhuitontli, or Small festival of the lords, seems to be that of a young man, and that of the month Hueitecuilhuitl, that is, Great festival of the lords, appears to be that of an old man. The figures of the ninth and tenth months are undoubtedly significant of the mourning dress which they wore, and of the grief which they made for their dead, which caused the ninth month to be called Miccailhuitl, that is, Festival of the dead, and the tenth month Hueimiccailhuitl, or Great festival of the dead; but because the grief of the tenth month was greater, the figure that represents it is also larger. The Tlaxcalans painted in each of the aforesaid months a skull with two bones; but the skull of the tenth month larger. The figure of the eleventh month is a broom, in which is signified the ceremony of sweeping the temples, which in this month was performed by everyone; whence it took the name Ochpaniztli. The Tlaxcalans painted a hand grasping the broom. The figure of the twelfth and thirteenth months is that of a parasitic plant, called by the Mexicans Pachtli, which grows at this season on the oaks, and from it the twelfth month took its name. Now because in the following month this plant has grown, its figure is larger, and the month has the name Hueipachtli. These names, though more used among the Tlaxcalans, were also in use among the Mexicans; but in the History we employ the names Teotleco and Tepeilhuitl, because we find them more commonly used by the Mexicans. The figure of the fourteenth month is very similar to that of the second month; but we do not know what it signifies. The Tlaxcalans represented this month in the figure of that bird which is called by us the Flamingo, and by the

o: Messicani . Quecholli , il qual nome imposero ancora al mese i Messicani; perchè appunto per questo tempo arrivano sì fatti uccelli al lago di Meslico . La figura del mese decimoquinto è quella d' un pezza di stendardo melslicano per fignificar quello, che fi portava nella solennisslima processione d' Huitzilopochili, che lì facevain questo mese . Il nome Panquetzalizili , con cui era appellato, non altro fignifica, secondo che abbiamo detto altrove , che l' inalberare lo stendardo, La figura del mese decimosesto è quella dell’ acqua sopra una scala per fignificar la discesa dell' acqua, e ciò sigoifica il nome Aremozzli, che. davano a quelto mese, o perchè questo tempo ne’ paesi settentrionali è quello delle pioggie , o perchè in questo mese fi faceva la festa agli Dei de' monti, e dell’ acqua, per ottenere la pioggia opportuna, La figura del mese decimosettimo è quella di due, o tre legni legati con una corda, ed una mano, che tirando fortemente la corda stringe i legni, per fignificar lo strignimento, che cagiona in questo tempo il freddo , ciò che è fignificaro nel nome Tiris . I Tlascallesi dipingevano due ba- {toni incaflati , e bene aggiustati in un' afle . La figura del mess diciottesimo è quella della testa d’ un quadrupedo sopra un altare per significare i facrifizj d’ animali, che si facevano in questo mese al Dio del fuoco . I Tlascallesi lo rappresentavano nella figura d’ un uomo sostenendo un bambino per la testa: ciò che rende verifimile l' interpretazione del nome lzcalli , che si trova presso alcuni Autori, mentre dicono, che coral nome fignifica , Risuscita+ to 54 © nuova creazione», La figura della Luna, che è nel centro della ruota, o circolo dell’ Anno, è stata copiata da una dipintura messicana, nella quale fi scorge , che quegli antichi Indiani {apevano bene, che la Luna ha la sua luce dal-Sole. In alcune ruote dell' Anno messicano da me vedute, dopo le figure de' diciotto mesi, v’ erano cìnque punti groffi denotanti i cinque giorni Nemontemi, I 1 2 3. Del-
e: Mexicans Quecholli, which name the Mexicans also gave to the month; for it is precisely at this season that such birds arrive at the lake of Mexico. The figure of the fifteenth month is that of a piece of a Mexican standard, to signify the one that was carried in the most solemn procession of Huitzilopochtli, which was held in this month. The name Panquetzaliztli, by which it was called, signifies nothing other, as we have said elsewhere, than the raising of the standard. The figure of the sixteenth month is that of water above a staircase, to signify the descent of the water, and this is what is signified by the name Atemoztli, which they gave to this month, either because this season in the northern countries is that of the rains, or because in this month the festival was held to the gods of the mountains and of water, to obtain the opportune rain. The figure of the seventeenth month is that of two or three pieces of wood bound with a cord, and a hand which, pulling the cord tight, draws the wood together, to signify the constriction which the cold causes at this season, which is signified in the name Tititl. The Tlaxcalans painted two sticks inserted and well fitted into a board. The figure of the eighteenth month is that of the head of a quadruped above an altar, to signify the sacrifices of animals which were made in this month to the god of fire. The Tlaxcalans represented it in the figure of a man holding a child up by the head: which makes plausible the interpretation of the name Izcalli that is found in some authors, when they say that this name signifies Resuscitated, or new creation. The figure of the Moon, which is in the center of the wheel, or circle, of the Year, has been copied from a Mexican painting, in which it is seen that those ancient Indians knew well that the Moon has its light from the Sun. In some wheels of the Mexican Year that I have seen, after the figures of the eighteen months there were five large dots denoting the five Nemontemi days. Ii2                       3.

o: V' è una gran varietà presso gli Autori intorno afla fignificazione di Cipacrli , nome del primo giorno . Secondo Boturini fignifica una serpe, preflo Torquemada il pesce Spada, e preflo Betancurt il Tiburone, Nell' unica ruota del mese messicano finora pubblicata, la quale è quella del Valadéès , la figura rapresentante il primo giorno è quasi in tutto simile a quella della Lucertola, che si vede nel giorno quarto, Noi pertanto non sapendo che cola fia, abbiamo messo la testa d’ un Tiburone secondo l' interpretazione di Retancur:. Il giorno fecondo s' appella Ebecazl , cioè Vento, e fi rappresenta in una testa umana soffiando colla bocca, Il giorno terzo s' appella Calli,, cioè Casa, e fi rappresenta in un piccolo edifizio. IL nome del giorno quarto è Cuerzpalin , cioè Lucertola, e la figura quella del suddetto animale. Il nome del giorno quinto è Coarzl, cioè Serpe , e la figura quella dello stesso animale. Il nome del giorno sesto è Miquizzli, cioè , morte, è vien rappresentato in un teschio . Il giorno settimo s' appella Mazaz! , o sia Cervo, e fi rap» presenta nella testa'di tal quadrupede , siccome il giorno ottavo in quella del Coniglio , Tocheli, e così è appellato . Il Homé;del giorno nono è Al, cioè, Acqua, e fi rappresenta “ella figura di quest' elemento, Il giorno decimo è quello dell’ Irzcuineli , cioè certo quadrupede Messicano somigliante ad un cagnuolo, e la fi gura è quella di tal animale. IL gioeo undecimo s' appellava Ozomarli, 0 fia Scimia, € fi rappresenta nella figura di tzl animale, Il giorno dodecimo s' appellava Malinalli , nome di certa pianta della quale facevano granate , e fi rapprelenta tal mese mella figura della stessa pianta, Il giorno decimoterzo è Acarl, o Canna, € fi rappre. senta in una canna, Il
e: There is a great variety among the authors concerning the signification of Cipactli, the name of the first day. According to Boturini it signifies a serpent; according to Torquemada the swordfish; and according to Vetancurt the shark. In the only wheel of the Mexican month published up to now, which is that of Valadés, the figure representing the first day is almost wholly similar to that of the Lizard, which is seen on the fourth day. We, therefore, not knowing what it is, have put the head of a shark, following the interpretation of Vetancurt. The second day is called Ehecatl, that is, Wind, and is represented in a human head blowing with the mouth. The third day is called Calli, that is, House, and is represented in a small building. The name of the fourth day is Cuetzpalin, that is, Lizard, and the figure is that of the aforesaid animal. The name of the fifth day is Coatl, that is, Serpent, and the figure is that of the same animal. The name of the sixth day is Miquiztli, that is, death, and it is represented in a skull. The seventh day is called Mazatl, or Deer, and is represented in the head of that quadruped, just as the eighth day is in that of the Rabbit, Tochtli, and is so called. The name of the ninth day is Atl, that is, Water, and it is represented in the figure of that element. The tenth day is that of the Itzcuintli, that is, a certain Mexican quadruped resembling a little dog, and the figure is that of such an animal. The eleventh day was called Ozomatli, or Monkey, and is represented in the figure of such an animal. The twelfth day was called Malinalli, the name of a certain plant from which they made brooms, and this day is represented in the figure of the same plant. The thirteenth day is Acatl, or Cane, and is represented in a cane.

o: Il giorno decimoquarto è Ocelo:!, Tigre, ed il decimoquinto Quaubrli , Aquila , e fi rappresentano nelle teste degli stessi animali. Il giorno decimosesto è Cozcaquaubrli , nome d' ua uccello messicano da noi descritto nel libro I, della Storia, e fi rappresenta nella figura, benchè imperfetta, d' eflo. Il giorno decimosettimo è Olin ronatiub, cioè, Moto del Sole, e la figura è quella dello stesso Pianeta, Il giorno diciottesimo è Tecparl, cioè Selce , e la figura è la punta d’ una lancia, la quale soleva efler di selce. Il giorno decimonono è Quiabuirl, Pioggia , è fi rappresenta in una nube piovendo . Il giorno ventesimo è Xochil, Fiore, e la figura quella d' up fiore. Nel centro di questa ruota abbiamo messo la figura del mele decimoquinto per ridurla ad un mese determinato . 4. Delle figure di Cirrà . La prima figura è quella d' una opunzia, o fia Nopal, sopra una pietra, simbolo della Città di Tenochtitlax , o Meslico. Tenochtizlan vuol dire, il luogo, dov' è l’ opunzia nella pietra , alludendo a quello che abbiamo detto intorno alla fondazione di questa gran Città, La figura seconda è quella, colla quale figoificavano la gemma . Il nome Chalcho vale, Nella gemma . (*) La figura terza è quella della parte deretana d'un uomo presso ad una pianta di giunco, ea quarta è quella della medesima parte deretana presso ad un fiore, per significar le Città di Tollantzinco, e di Xochitzinco , i nomi delle quali fignificano, Nel fine della giuncaja, e nel fine de' fiori, o fia del campo fiorito - € quasi tutti i nomi de’ luoghi , che hanno la ter-
e: The fourteenth day is Ocelotl, Tiger, and the fifteenth Quauhtli, Eagle, and they are represented in the heads of those same animals. The sixteenth day is Cozcaquauhtli, the name of a Mexican bird described by us in Book I of the History, and it is represented in a figure of it, though an imperfect one. The seventeenth day is Olin Tonatiuh, that is, Movement of the Sun, and the figure is that of the same planet. The eighteenth day is Tecpatl, that is, Flint, and the figure is the point of a lance, which used to be made of flint. The nineteenth day is Quiahuitl, Rain, and it is represented in a cloud raining. The twentieth day is Xochitl, Flower, and the figure is that of a flower. In the center of this wheel we have placed the figure of the fifteenth month, in order to reduce it to a determinate month. 4. Of the Figures of Cities. The first figure is that of a prickly pear, or Nopal, on a stone, the symbol of the city of Tenochtitlan, or Mexico. Tenochtitlan means, The place where the prickly pear is on the stone, alluding to what we have said concerning the founding of this great city. The second figure is that by which they signified the gem. The name Chalco means, In the gem. The fifth figure is that of a little branch of the tree Huaxin on a nose, to represent the city of Huaxyacac, a name composed of Huaxin and of jacatl, and meaning, At the point or extremity of the grove of Huaxin; for although jacatl properly means the nose, it is used to signify any point whatever. Thus Tepeyacac, the name of two places, means On the point of the mountain. In our figure that little branch is seen not on the nose, as it should be, but on the forehead, through a mistake of the engraver. In the sixth figure is seen a pot on three stones, just as the Indians used to place it, and still place it today, to hold it over the fire, and in the mouth of the pot the figure of water, to represent the city of Atotonilco (*), whose name signifies, In the hot water, or place of the hot springs. The seventh figure is that of water, in which is seen a man with arms spread as a sign of joy, to represent the city of Ahuilizapan (called Orizaba by the Spaniards), whose name means, In the water of pleasure, or in the joyful river. The eighth figure is likewise that of water in a mouth, to represent the city of Atenco. (**) This name is composed of Atl, Water, of Tentli, Lip, and metaphorically bank, shore, brim, etc., and of the preposition co, which means in: so that Atenco means, On the bank, on the shore, or on the brim of the water, and all the places that have such a name are situated on the shore of some lake or river. The ninth figure is that of a Mexican mirror, to represent the city of Tehuiloyocan, whose name means, Place of mirrors. The (*) There were, and there still are, many places called Atotonilco; but the chief one has always been that which lies to the north of Mexico, toward Tollantzinco. e: The tenth figure is that of a hand in the attitude of counting on the fingers, to represent the village of Nepohualco, whose name means, Place where one counts, or place of counting. The eleventh figure is that of an arm taking a fish, to represent the city of Michmaloyan, whose name signifies, Place where fish are caught, or place of fishing. The twelfth figure is that of a piece of a building with an eagle’s head inside it, to represent the city of Cuauhtinchan, which name signifies, House of the eagles. The thirteenth figure is that of a mountain such as the Mexicans depicted it in their paintings, and somewhat above it a knife, to represent the city of Tlacotepec, whose name means, Cut mountain. The fourteenth figure is that of a flower, and beneath it five of those dots which they used to signify the numbers from one to twenty. With this figure they represented the place called Macuilxochitl, whose name means, Five flowers. This name is also used to signify a day of the year, and it may be believed that the founding of that place having begun on such a day, it received this name. The fifteenth figure is that of a ball game, to represent the city of Tlachco (called Tasco by the Spaniards), whose name signifies the place where such a game is played. Those two little round figures seen in the middle are the two millstones pierced in the middle which were used in that game, so that the ball might be passed through one of the holes. There were at least two cities or villages so called. The sixteenth figure represents the place of Tecozauhtla, whose name means, Place abounding in ochre. 5. Of the Figures of the Mexican Kings.

e: These figures are not portraits of the kings, but symbols signifying [p. 256] their names. In all of them is seen a head crowned in the Mexican fashion, and each has its own mark to signify the name of the king represented in it. Acamapichtli, name of the first king of Mexico, means, He who has reeds in his fist, and this is seen represented in his figure. Huitzilihuitl, name of the second king, means, Feather of the hummingbird, and therefore the head of such a little bird with a feather in its beak is represented, though badly. Chimalpopoca, name of the third king, means, Smoking shield, and this is represented in his figure. Itzcoatl, name of the fourth king, means, Serpent of Itztli, that is, armed with lancets, or with razors of Itztli stone, and this is meant to be represented in the fourth figure. Ilhuicamina, surname of Moctezuma I, fifth king of Mexico, means, He who shoots at the sky, and therefore there is represented an arrow shot at that figure with which the Mexicans represented the sky. Axayacatl, name of the sixth king, is also that of a marsh fly, and signifies, Face, or visage of water, and therefore it is represented in a face, above which is the figure of water. Tizoc, name of the seventh king, means, Pierced, and therefore it is represented in a pierced leg; but the engraver, instead of small holes, made large wounds in our figure. Ahuitzotl, name of the eighth king, is also that of an amphibious quadruped, of which we made mention in Book I., and therefore the figure, though imperfect, of such a quadruped is represented, and to signify that this animal lives in the water, there is seen on its back and on its tail the figure of that element. Moctezuma, name of the ninth king, means, Angry lord; but we have not been able to understand the figure. We lack the figures of the last two kings, Cuitláhuac and Cuauhtémoc; but we do not doubt that that of Cuauhtémoc is a descending eagle, since such is the meaning of that name. 6. Of

Ì L' acqua fignifica il Diluvio + quella testa umana, e quell' uccello , che fì vedono nell’ acqua, significano l’annegamento degli'uomini, e degli animali . La barca con un uomo sopra denota quella, nella quale fecondo la loro tradizione fi salvarono un uomo, ed una donna, per conservar la spezie umana sulla terra . Quella figura , che fi veda in un cantone, è quella del monte Colhuacan , preffo al quale, secondo che egli diceano, sbarcarono l' uomo, e la donna, che scamparono dal Diluvio. In tutte quelle dipinture messicane, nelle quali fi fa menzione di quel monte, lì vede rappresentato in sì fatta figura. L' uccello sull' albero rappresenta una colomba, la quale al dir loro comunicò la favella agli uomini, mentre tutti erano nati mutoli dopo il Diluvio. Quelle virgole, ch’ escono dal becco della colomba verso gli uomini sono figure de’ lioguaggj . Ogni volta che nelle pitture messicane occorre far menzione di lingue, o di voci, s'adoperano rali virgole . La loro moltitudine nella nostra dipintura denota la moltitudine delle lingue comunicate. Quei quindici uomini, che ricevono dalla colomba le lingue rappresentano altrettante famiglie dal resto degli uomini separa» te, dalle quali al dir loro discendevano le Nazioni d’ Ana- Huac, Szjoria del Messico Tomo 11. e: Water signifies the Flood; that human head and that bird, which are seen in the water, signify the drowning of men and of animals. The boat with a man on it denotes that in which, according to their tradition, a man and a woman were saved, to preserve the human species on the earth. That figure which is seen in a corner is that of Mount Colhuacan, near which, as they said, the man and the woman who escaped from the Flood landed. In all those Mexican paintings in which mention is made of that mountain, it is seen represented in such a figure. The bird on the tree represents a dove, which, according to them, imparted speech to men, all of them having been born mute after the Flood. Those little strokes that issue from the dove’s beak toward the men are figures of languages. Whenever in the Mexican paintings it is necessary to make mention of tongues or of voices, such strokes are used. Their multitude in our painting denotes the multitude of the languages imparted. Those fifteen men who receive the languages from the dove represent as many families separated from the rest of men, from which, as they said, the nations of Anahuac descended. From Your Lordship’s work . . . I understand with the greatest regret how deplorable is the loss of those documents which served the celebrated Dr. Sigüenza in composing his Ciclografía, and the Chevalier Boturini in publishing his Idea de una nueva historia general; and at the same time I am confirmed the more in my opinion that the use of the solar year is contemporary with the Flood, or even anterior to it, as I intend to prove in vol. XI of my work, where the Ecstatic Journey to the Planetary World is set forth, in which I propose on the Mexican calendar some reflections that I wish here to insinuate and to submit to your censure. The year and the century have been regulated among the Mexicans from time immemorial with an intelligence greater than corresponds to their arts and sciences. In these they were without doubt inferior to the Greeks and the Romans; but the talent that is discerned in the calendar does not yield to that of the most cultivated nations. Hence we must conjecture that this calendar was not the work of the Mexicans, but of another, more enlightened nation; and since in America

e: [p. 259] it has not been found, we must seek it elsewhere, as in Asia or in Egypt. This supposition is confirmed by what you affirm, namely, that the Mexicans had their calendar from the Toltecs (who came from Asia), who, according to Boturini, had their year exactly adjusted to the solar course more than 100 years before the Christian era; and by seeing that other nations, such as the Chiapanecs, used the same Mexican calendar with no other difference than that of the symbols. The Mexican year began on February 26, a day famous in the era of Nabonassar, which was fixed by the Egyptian priests 747 years before the Christian era; for at noon of that day there corresponded among them the beginning of the month Thoth. Now if those priests also fixed this day for the epoch because it was (a) famous in Egypt, we have in that case the Mexican calendar in conformity with the Egyptian. But leaving this aside, it cannot otherwise be doubted that the Mexican calendar agreed closely with the Egyptian. Of this Herodotus says, (b) that it was first regulated by the Egyptians by giving the year 12 months of 30 days and adding five days to each year, so that the circle of the year might return upon its own tracks: that the principal gods of Egypt were twelve, and that each month was under the tutelage and patronage of one of these gods. The Mexicans also added five days in every year, which were called by them Nemontemi, that is, useless, because in them they did nothing. Plutarch says (c) that on such days the Egyptians celebrated the festival of the birth of their gods. It is, however, certain that the Mexicans divided their year into 18 months, not into 12 as the Egyptians did; but since they called the month meztli, that is, Moon, as Your Lordship observes, it seems undeniable that their ancient month was lunar like that of the Egyptians and of the Chinese, thus verifying Kk2                        in (a) On February 26 of that year the year properly began according to the meridian of Alexandria, which was built three centuries afterward. So that the Mexicans, having perhaps received the lunar month from their ancestors, will afterward have instituted the other species of months for other ends. You affirm in your history, on the faith of Boturini, that the Mixtecs had the year of 13 months, which number was sacred in the Mexican calendar out of regard for their 13 principal gods, in the same manner as in Egypt the number 12 was consecrated to their twelve greater gods. Admirable indeed is the use, in the Mexican calendar, of symbols and of periods of years, of months, and of days. As for the periods, it seems to me that that of five days might be called their civil week, and that of thirteen their religious week. Similarly the period of twenty days will have been their civil month; that of twenty-six days the religious month; and that of thirty the lunar and astronomical month. In the century it may be believed that the period of four years was the civil one, and that of thirteen the religious one. By the multiplication of these two periods they had their century of fifty-two years, and from the doubling of the century they had their age of a hundred and four years. In all these periods is discerned an art no less marvelous than that of our indictions, cycles, etc. The period of civil weeks was contained perfectly in the civil month and in the astronomical; the latter had six of them, and the former four, and the year contained seventy-three complete weeks: in which our method is exceeded by the Mexican; for our weeks are not contained perfectly in the month, nor even in the year. The period of religious weeks was contained twice in their religious month, and twenty-eight times in the year; but in this a day was left over, just as one is left over in our weeks. The period of civil months multiplied by the number of days (that is, 18 multiplied by 20) and the period of lunar months multiplied by the number of days (that is, 12 multiplied by 30) give the same product, or number, 360: a number indeed no less immemorial, and in use among the Mexicans, than among the most ancient nations; and a number which from time immemorial rules in geometry and astronomy, and is most important for its relation to the circle, which is divided into 360 parts, or degrees. We have among no nation of the world anything similar to this clear and admirable method of calendar. From the small period of four years multiplied by the aforesaid cycle of 260 years there came another marvelous cycle of 1040 years. The Mexicans combined the small period of 4 years with the period above mentioned, the week of 13 years; whence there resulted their well-known cycle, or century, of 52 years; and so with the four figures indicating the period of 4 years they had, as we have with the dominical letters, a period which, to tell the truth, exceeded ours: for ours is of 28 years, and the Mexican is of 52 years: this was perpetual, and ours in the Gregorian years is not perpetual. Such variety and simplicity of periods of weeks, months, years, and cycles cannot fail to be admired: all the more so as there is discovered at once the well-known relation which the said periods have to many different ends, which Boturini indicates, saying, “the Mexican calendar was of four kinds: namely, natural for agriculture, chronological for history, ritual for the festivals, and astronomical for the course of the stars, and the year was luni-solar.” This year, unless we place it at the end of three Mexican ages, after several calculations made I do not find. e: [p. 262] difficult, since, the eclipses being noted in the Mexican paintings, there is no doubt that from them can be derived the true epoch of the chronology, just as Father Souciet derives the Chinese from the solar eclipse which he fixed in the year 2155 before the Christian era. A well-circumstanced eclipse, as Father Briga (a) Romagnoli proves at length, can give light to fix the epoch of the chronology within a space of 20 thousand years: and although in the Mexican paintings not all the circumstances of the eclipses are described, the defect of these is remedied by the many eclipses that are noted in them. Hence the Mexican gentlemen, who still preserve a great number of paintings, could by the study of them bring great advantage to chronology. As regards the symbols of the months and of the Mexican year, ideas are discovered totally conformable to those of the ancient Egyptians. These (as is seen in their monuments) distinguished each month, or part of the zodiac where the Sun stood, with characteristic figures of what happened in each season of the year. Thus we see the signs of Aries, of Taurus, and of the two kids (which are now the two Twins) to be in the months of the birth of these animals: the signs of Cancer, of Leo, and of Virgo with the ear of grain in those months in which the Sun retrogrades, like a crab, in which there is greater heat, and in which the harvest is gathered: the signs of Scorpio (which in the Egyptian sphere occupied the space which Libra now occupies) and that of Sagittarius in the months of venomous illnesses and of the chase: and lastly the signs of Capricorn, of Aquarius, and of Pisces in those months in which the Sun returns to climb toward us, in which it rains much, and in which the abundant fishing begins. Somewhat similar to these are the ideas which the Mexicans adapted to their climate. They called their first month, which began on February 26, Acahualco, that is, cessation of the waters; and they symbolized this month with a house and the figure of water above it. They also gave to the said month the (a) Scientiæ eclipsium ex Europa in Sinas, pt. 3, ch. 2, § 20. [p. 263] the name of Quahuitlehua, that is, the budding, or moving, of the trees. The Mexicans, then, distinguished their first month by two names, of which the first, namely Acahualco, or cessation of the waters, did not suit their climate, where the waters cease in October; but it suits the fields of Sennaar, and the northern climes of America, in which their progenitors had been: and from this it is clearly gathered that the origin of the said name is most ancient. The second name, namely Quahuitlehua, or budding of the trees, agrees much with the word Kimah used by Job to signify the Pleiades, (a) which in his time announced the spring, in which the trees put forth. The symbol of the second Mexican month was a pavilion; which served to denote the great heat that is felt in Mexico in April before the rains of May begin. The symbol of the third month was a bird, which at that time would be seen. The twelfth and thirteenth months had for symbol the plant pachtli, which in the said months springs up and grows. The symbol of the seventeenth month was expressed with certain pieces of wood bound with a cord, and a hand that was pulling it; the intention being thereby to signify how much the cold constricts in that month, namely in January: and to this same end the name Tititl, which was given to the said month, clearly alludes. The constellation Kesil, of which Job speaks to signify winter, in the Arabic root (which is Kesal) signifies to be cold and drowsy: and in the text of Job it reads thus, “Will you be able to break the cords, or bonds, of Kesil?” And here, setting aside the clear conformity which the Mexican symbols and expressions for spring and winter have with those of Job, who in my opinion flourished a short time after the Flood (as I say in my vol. XI), it must be noted how the said symbols, which are truly excellent for keeping the year invariable, demonstrate the use of intercalary days among the Mexicans: otherwise it would be seen that in two centuries the symbol of the month of cold would come to fall in (a) Job, ch. 9, v. 9, and ch. 38, 31. [p. 264] in the month of heat. Thus, if from the Mexican paintings it is gathered that in them the conquest of Mexico was noted in their ninth month, called Tlaxochimaco, it would be inferred from this that intercalary days had been in use. The same would be deduced from seeing that the Mexicans at the entrance of the Spaniards preserved that order of months which, according to the signification of their names, suited the seasons of the year and the products of the earth. Further, to find out how the Mexicans regulated their leap years, and whether their year was exact, a precise examination and comparison should be made of some event known to us which could be seen to be noted by the Mexicans. You, for example, fix the death of Moctezuma on June 29, 1520: if this were found in the Mexican paintings on the day VII Cuetzpalin of the seventh month, it would be inferred that their year was exact, and that the leap days had been interspersed every four years: if it corresponded to the day IV Cipactli, it was a sign that their year was exact, and that the leap days were counted after the century: if it corresponded to the VII Ozomatli, then it was inferred that their leap days were placed after the century, and that their year was as much in error as ours was at that time. The proposed example rests upon the calendar which you put at the end of vol. II: this I have done for the sake of greater clarity: but if it were a question of making the calculation exactly, it should be borne in mind that your Calendar corresponds to the year I of the Mexican century, and that the year 1520 was the year XIV of that century: whence the names of the days would have a different order from that which has been proposed for the sake of greater clarity. Lastly, most respected Friend, the symbol which you put to signify the Mexican century convinces us evidently that it is the very one which the ancient Egyptians and Chaldeans had. There is seen in the Mexican symbol the sun, as if eclipsed by the moon, and surrounded by a serpent, which makes four knots, and embraces the four periods of thirteen years. This very same idea of the serpent with the sun is immemorial in the world to signify the periodic, or annual, course of the sun. We [p. 265] have in astronomy that the points where eclipses occur are called (as Father Briga (a) Romagnoli noted) from time immemorial head and tail of the dragon. The Chinese, with false ideas, but conformable to this immemorial allusion, believe that in eclipses a dragon is in the act of swallowing the sun. The Egyptians agree more particularly with the Mexicans; for to symbolize the sun they used a circle with one or two serpents: still more did the ancient Persians agree, among whom their Mithras (who certainly was the sun), worshiped by the Greeks and by the Romans, was symbolized (b) with the sun and with a serpent; and from Father Montfaucon (c) we have in his Antiquities a monument of a serpent, which, encircling the signs of the zodiac, cuts them in various ways by coiling around them. In view of these undeniable examples the following reflection is most convincing, namely: there is no doubt that the symbol of the serpent is a totally arbitrary thing to signify the sun, with which it has no physical relation: why then, I ask, have so many dispersed nations, some of which did not deal with one another except in the first centuries after the Flood, why have they agreed in using one and the same symbol, so arbitrary, and wished to signify by it one and the same object? The finding of the word sack in the Hebrew, Greek, Teutonic, Latin, etc. languages obliges us to believe that it belongs to the primitive language of men after the Flood; and will not the seeing used by the Mexicans, by the Chinese, by the ancient Egyptians, and by the Persians one and the same arbitrary symbol to signify the sun, and its course, oblige us to recognize in the said symbol its true origin in the time of Noah, or of the first men after the Flood? e: Bishop of Chiapa, in the Proem to his Synodal Constitutions) put as the first symbol, or name, of the first year of the century a Votan, grandson, they say, of the one who built a wall up to heaven and gave to men the languages that are now spoken. Behold here the Mexican calendar with a fact clearly related to the building of the tower of Babel and to the confusion of tongues. Many other similar reflections might be made on the fine documents which you exhibit to us in your history: I, however, heartily wish you health, etc. Cesena, July 31, 1780. = So far the letter of Abbé Hervás. But whatever may be said of the use of the solar year among those first men, in which dispute I do not wish to become entangled, I cannot persuade myself that the Mexicans, or rather the Toltecs, were indebted to any of the nations of the old continent for their calendar and for their method of reckoning time. From whom did the Toltecs learn their age of 104 years, the century of 52, the year of 18 months, the months of 20 days, the periods of thirteen years and of thirteen days, the cycle of 260 days, and above all the thirteen intercalary days at the end of the century to adjust the year to the solar course? The Egyptians were the ablest astronomers of those remote times, and yet they used no intercalary correction to remedy the annual retardation of the Sun of about six hours. Now if the Toltecs by themselves perceived that retardation, it is no wonder that they perceived other things, which did not require such minute and such prolix astronomical observations. The very Chevalier Boturini, on whose testimony Abbé Hervás relies, says expressly, on the faith of the Toltec Annals seen by him, that the Toltec astronomers, having observed in their ancient homeland Huehuetlapallan (a northern country of America) the excess of about six hours of the solar year over the civil year which was in use among them, corrected this by the use of intercalary days a hundred and more years before the Christian era. As for the analogy between the Mexicans and the Egyptians, we shall speak of it in the dissertations. THE

e: T H E AU T H O R’ S N O T I C E O N T H E WO R K E N T I T L E D : Some of the reflections of Abbé Hervás are made also by the learned author of the Lettere americane, a most recent work, full of erudition, published in the Magazzino letterario of Florence, and which reached me when the last sheets of this second volume were being printed. The author, in refuting the absurdities of M. de Pauw, gives a true, though incomplete, idea of the civilization of the Mexicans: he reasons for the most part well of their customs, their usages, their arts, and above all of their astronomical knowledge: he sets out their calendar and their cycles, and in all this compares them with the ancient Egyptians, as the most learned Mexican Sigüenza did in the last century, to prove their conformity and the antiquity of the peopling of America. In running through these letters I have had the pleasure of seeing promoted and illustrated some of my views set forth in my dissertations; but on the other hand I am sorry to have found in them some mistakes, besides certain passages too injurious to the Spanish nation and unbecoming in an honest and impartial man of letters. Almost all the Mexican names are read altered, and some so disfigured that not even I, who am so familiar with the language and history of Mexico, can recognize them. Sometimes a king is mistaken for a city, as where, mention being made of painting IV of the Mendoza Collection, published by Purchas and by Thévenot, there is spoken of the city of Chimalpopoca, this being the name of a Mexican king, and not of any city, etc. In letter IX of the second part, in which he speaks of the Mexican year, this author cites Gemelli, and unjustly charges him with an error. e: Ll2 [p. 268] at the beginning of their century began on April 10; but that every four years it advanced a day, on account of our leap day: so that after four years it began on the 9th of that month, after eight years it began on the 8th, and thus it went on advancing a day every four years to the end of the Mexican century, in which, by the interposition of the thirteen intercalary days, omitted in the course of the century, the year returned to begin on April 10. This, adds the author of the Letters, is a contradiction of fact, since the year after four years ought to begin on the eleventh, and not on the ninth, and thus for every four years a day ought to be added, and in that case the correction of the thirteen days after the 52 years became superfluous, or, a retrogression of a day being admitted every four years, the difference of the sidereal year at the end of the cycle would have been double, that is, of 26 days. I am amazed that a man of letters who shows himself to be a good calculator should err in so simple and so clear a calculation. The year 1506 was secular among the Mexicans. Now, for greater clarity, let us suppose that their year began, like ours, on the 1st of January. This first year of the Mexican century, composed, like ours, of 365 days, ended just like ours on December 31, and similarly the second year, corresponding to 1507; but in 1508 the Mexican year had to end a day before ours; because ours, being a leap year, had 366 days, whereas the Mexican had no more than 365. Therefore the fourth year of that Mexican century, corresponding to 1509, had to begin a day before ours, that is, on December 31, 1508. Likewise the eighth year, corresponding to 1513, had to begin on December 30, 1512, for the same reason of that year having been a leap year. The twelfth year, corresponding to 1517, had to begin on December 29, 1516, and so on to the year 1557, the last of that Mexican century, in which the Mexican year had to advance on ours as many days as there had been leap years. Parimente l'anno ottavo corrispondente al 1513 dovette cominciare a' 30. Dec. 1512, per la medesima ragione d'eflere staro quest' anno bisestile. L'aano dodescimo corrispondente al 1517 dovette cominciare a 29. Dec. 1515» e così fin' all'anno 1557, ultimo di quel secolo meslicano , nel quale l'anno meslicano dovette tanti giorni anticiparsi al nostro, quanti grano stati gli anni biseitili , Ora ne' 55 [p. 269] «del secolo messicano vi sono 13 bisestili: dunque quell' ultimo “anno del secolo doveva anticiparsi giorni tredici al nostro,e non 26, Non eta dunque superflua l' interposizione de' giorni tredici terminato il secolo, per aggiustar l’anno al corso solare. Sicchè Gemelli diff: bene in ciò che scrisse intorno all anticipazione dell’anno, benchè errafse nel ‘dire, che l’anno messicano cominciava a’ 10 Aprile; poichè cominciava , come tante volte abbiam detto, a' 26 Febbrajo. L' Autor delle Lettere crede, che i Messicani cominciavano. il loro anno dall’ equinozio di Primavera. Io fon del medefimo parere quanto al loro anno astronomico; ma non ho osato affermarlo ; perchè nol so. Gli antichi Storici Spagnuoli del Messico non erano Astronomi, e nelle loro storie non fi curarono tanto d’ esporre i progressi de' Meslicani nelle scienze , quanto i loro riti superstiziofi . La Ciclografia Messicana , composta dal grand’ Astronomo Siguenza dopo un diligente studio delle pitture messicane, e dopo moltissimi calcoli degli eclisli , e delle comete notate in quelle pitture, non è pervenuta a noi,
e: [p. 269] of the Mexican century there are 13 leap years: therefore that last year of the century had to advance thirteen days on ours, and not 26. The interposition of the thirteen days at the end of the century, to adjust the year to the solar course, was therefore not superfluous. So Gemelli spoke rightly in what he wrote concerning the anticipation of the year, though he erred in saying that the Mexican year began on April 10; since it began, as we have so many times said, on February 26. The author of the Letters believes that the Mexicans began their year from the spring equinox. I am of the same opinion as to their astronomical year; but I have not dared to affirm it, because I do not know it. The ancient Spanish historians of Mexico were not astronomers, and in their histories they did not take as much care to set forth the progress of the Mexicans in the sciences as their superstitious rites. The Mexican Ciclografía, composed by the great astronomer Sigüenza after a diligent study of the Mexican paintings, and after very many calculations of the eclipses and of the comets noted in those paintings, has not come down to us. I cannot forgive the author of the Letters the wrong that he does to this great Mexican in letter 3 of vol. II, where he discusses, on the faith of Gemelli, the pyramids of Teotihuacan. Carlos Sigüenza, says that author, judges such edifices to be anterior to the Flood. It is not true: how could Sigüenza judge such pyramids anterior to the Flood, believing the peopling of America posterior to the confusion of tongues, and the first settlers descendants of Nephtuim, great-grandson of Noah, as the Chevalier Boturini, who saw some works of Sigüenza, attests? Gemelli himself, on whom the author of the Letters relies, expressly contradicts him in vol. 6, bk. 2, ch. 8. No Indian historian, says this traveler, has known how to investigate the time of the erection of the pyramids of America; yet Don Carlos Sigüenza esteemed them most ancient, and a little after the Flood. Nor did Gemelli explain well the view of Sigüenza; for Dr. Eguiara, discussing in the Bibliotheca mexicana the works of Sigüenza

o: Non posso perdonare all’ Autor- delle Lettere il torto che fa a questo gran Messicano nella lettera }; del tomo II, dove ragiona sulla fede di Gemelli delle Piramidi di Teotihuacan . Carlo Siguenza, dice quell' Autore , giudica rali edifizj anteriori al Diluvio . Non è vero: come poteva Siguenza giudicar rali piramidi anteriori al diluvio, credendo posteriore la popolazione dell’ America alla confasione delle lingue, ed i primi popolatori discendenti di Nephtuim , bisnipote di Noè, siccome ne fa fede il Cav. Borurini, che vide alcune opere di Siguenza ? Lo stesso Gemelli, di cui fi prevale I’ Autor delle Lettere, gli contraddice espressamente nel tom, 6. lib. 2. cao. 8. Niîuno Strorico Indiano, dice questo Niaggiatore, ha saputo investigare il tempo dell’ erezione delle piramidi dell’ America; però D. Carlo Siguenza le stimò antichi/jime , e poco dopo il diluvio , Neppure il Gemelli spiegò bene il sentimento di Siguenza ; poichè il Dotr, Eguiara ragionando nella Biblioreca Messicana delle opere di SL è EL<1 3 guen[p. 270] guenza, € tralle altre di quella, che fcrifse sulla popolazioneé dell’ America, dice, che egli in ral opera fifa la prima polazione di quel Nuovo Mondo paulld post babylonicam con» fusionem, cioè alquanto dopo di quello, che da ad intendere Gemelli . Quanto poi ad altri articoli più rilevanti discussi nelle suddette lettere, ne ragioneremo opportunamente nelle no. stre diflertazioni, nellequali in parte ci accorderemo con quell Autore, ed in parte ci opporremo a' suoi sentimenti.

As for the other, more important articles discussed in the aforesaid letters, we shall treat of them at the proper place in our dissertations, in which we shall partly agree with that author, and partly oppose his views.
